galaxy.name: Alliance Space
galaxy.span: Approximately 340 inhabited systems across 12 administrative sectors
galaxy.discovered: Alliance formally ratified 5550 CE following the Tronik War armistice
galaxy.government: Democratic republic with elected councils and a central senate. Law is consistent across all member systems. Citizens enjoy standardised rights, access to cloning, legal protections and freedom of movement. Three major megacorporations, including the Galactic Union (GU), operate extensively within Alliance Space and wield considerable influence over the Alliance board and senate, but formal authority rests with the elected government.
galaxy.desc:
The Alliance is the largest and most stable political entity in the known galaxy. It was founded in the aftermath of the Tronik War, a war it fought and lost, surviving only on the armistice the Troniks chose to grant, and it bound dozens of independent systems under a single senate and a single legal code. It has held that union together ever since, which is no small achievement in a galaxy that mostly cannot.
Alliance space is cosmopolitan. Every playable race lives here, corporations operate under at least nominal regulation, and the democratic process delivers more stability than almost anything beyond the borders. The navy is a real force against pirates and minor powers, but it is not the strongest military in the galaxy, and the Alliance knows it. Any of the Big 3 megacorporations could match it with their private fleets, and the morondium warzone at Titania is a standing reminder of who actually outguns whom.
The Alliance's real power was never its navy. It is the jump gate network. The Alliance controls every gate in its space, which turns the map into a set of chokepoints no fleet can simply go around, and that control has outlasted every military reckoning. The geography helps. A great asteroid belt runs from Mangara to the Garson black hole and cuts Alliance space in two, while the black holes at Garson and B.I.G. seal the obvious crossings, so a surprising share of the region's traffic is funnelled through a handful of relays, with Palentium chief among them. Hold the gates and the relays and you hold the busiest crossroads in the galaxy. Whether that grip would survive a determined megacorp coalition, or a genuine external threat of the kind waiting beyond the Nemani Rift, has never been tested, and the Alliance, to its credit, is aware of this.
galaxy.history:
What is now Alliance Space has been under Patriark governance since the first human settlement on Palentium roughly a thousand years ago. The Patriark government provided administrative continuity and, crucially, a measure of security against the Nerulian Empire, then the most powerful faction in the known galaxy. That Patriark oversight held through the rise and eventual fall of the Nerulian Empire (destroyed by the Kravens approximately five hundred years ago) and endured into the modern era.

The Alliance was formally ratified in 5550 CE following the Tronik War armistice, replacing centralised Patriark oversight with the current democratic republic of elected councils and a central senate.

The Galactic Union, one of three major megacorporations now operating within Alliance Space, wields significant influence over Alliance governance, but the relationship between corporate power and the elected senate remains the defining tension of Alliance politics.
known_for: Control of the jump gate network, strategic chokepoints connecting all of Alliance Space
The only political entity with stargates connecting every core system, controlling what enters and leaves each sector
Democratic governance and standardised citizen rights across member worlds
Home of the Galactic Union and most of the galaxy's largest corporations
Resurrection and cloning infrastructure (via Patriark contract)
A navy that is credible against pirates and minor powers but unproven against a major coalition
notable_systems: Orion, political and corporate capital; home of the Galactic Union
Sirius, primary commercial hub and trade centre
Palentium, first human-discovered world; luxury tourism and embedded corruption
Berilia, Patriark homeworld; galactic centre of cloning and resurrection technology
Titania, only source of morondium in the galaxy; permanent corporate warzone
Ishtar, Arms Corp headquarters; largest industrial manufacturing world in existence
Alsa, primary food production system for Alliance Space
Ash, frontier gateway to the Nemani Rift; military staging point
Aderan, for-profit prison world; home of Ridge Racing, Survivor, and Blood Bowl
lore_notes: It is widely believed that the Alliance senate has a classified briefing designation, Level Seven Restricted, that no elected senator below cabinet rank has ever seen the contents of. What it covers is a matter of persistent speculation.

The Galactic Union's founding documents include provisions for scenarios the GU has never publicly acknowledged, contingencies for total senate dissolution and GU assumption of emergency executive authority. Legal scholars disagree on whether these provisions are valid.

Trade caravans and long-haul freighters have circulated accounts for decades of a parallel navy, ships registered to no known fleet designation, operating within Alliance Space on unclear orders. Official sources consistently deny any such fleet exists.

galaxy.name: Torc Federation
galaxy.status: Independent, neutral to cautiously friendly with Alliance
galaxy.territory: South-east galaxy, bordered by Realmsingers Empire to the east
galaxy.span: ~45 inhabited systems across three primary clusters
galaxy.discovered: Federation charter ratified 4710 CE; individual systems had been inhabited for centuries prior
galaxy.government: Federation of city-states. Each member world is self-governing in domestic matters but bound by a shared trade charter and mutual defence pact. The Federation Council meets quarterly on Torc Prime and votes on external policy, trade agreements, and collective military deployment. Decisions require two-thirds majority; emergency military action requires unanimous consent.
galaxy.alignment: Sovereign; originated within the Alliance, now fully independent; guards the Vasophus system absolutely; active border conflict with the Realmsingers Empire over Ithov
galaxy.desc: The Torc Federation is the galaxy's mark of quality and, lately, the keeper of its most dangerous secret. It began inside Alliance space as a bloc of industrial and refinery worlds whose engineering earned the TORC stamp a reputation that travelled further than its ships: gear that works in conditions that kill fancier equipment, serviceable with tools that actually exist. What turned the bloc into a sovereign power was Vasophus. When Torc prospectors found what was waiting in that distant system, the Federation did a thing no manufacturer had done before. It raised a fleet, took the system outright, and stepped clear of the Alliance that could not be allowed to ask what it had found. The Federation now holds a cluster on the far south-east rim: prosperous, heavily armed, and unusually disinclined to let anyone near Vasophus.
galaxy.history: Torc was an Alliance success story for most of its existence, a federation of city-states that made things well and sold them everywhere, the Alliance's own enemies included, on the principle that a tool has no politics. The break came with Vasophus. The official account is a routine survey that struck mineral wealth. The truth, held by a handful of Federation officers, is that Vasophus held Kraven biomass, the consumed matter of the dead Nerulian Empire, the most scientifically coveted and most thoroughly outlawed substance in known space. A power that controls a supply of it controls something every research arm in the galaxy would ruin itself to obtain. Torc chose to control it, conquered the system, and built a border and a navy to keep the question of why from ever being asked aloud.
known_for: The TORC quality stamp, a galaxy-wide mark of rugged, serviceable engineering trusted where failure is fatal
The conquest of Vasophus, the only time an industrial federation has fielded a war fleet to seize a system outright
A closed border around Vasophus defended far past the apparent value of a mining claim
The Ithov standoff, a long border conflict with the Realmsingers Empire over the system next to Vasophus
Deep, deliberate independence from the Alliance it was born inside
notable_systems: Torc Prime, the Federation council seat and the heart of its old manufacturing strength
Vasophus, the conquered system; officially a mineral world, actually the source of the Federation's wealth and its secret, with access denied to everyone
Ithov, contested with the Realmsingers Empire; the fighting there has run for years and neither side will say what it is really about
Uether, a Federation industrial world anchoring the south-east rim cluster
lore_notes: Kraven biomass cannot, by everything known about the swarm's expansion, be where Vasophus sits, far from Kraven space and farther from the dead Nerulian core. How a supply came to rest there is the Federation's deepest secret and the one fact that would end it if it became common knowledge.

The Berilian Order and at least two megacorp research arms have made quiet approaches to Torc about Vasophus mineral rights. The Federation has refused every one without explanation, which is itself the most telling answer it has given.

The Realmsingers have fought over Ithov, the system next to Vasophus, for years without committing a real fleet. Analysts who disbelieve the territorial story think the Realmsingers know exactly what Torc found and are hunting their own way to it.

galaxy.name: Mubothen Empire
galaxy.status: Imperial rival, expansionist, hostile to Alliance
galaxy.territory: North-east galaxy, with contested border zones adjacent to Alliance Space
galaxy.span: ~80 systems under direct Imperial authority; additional tributary systems and occupied territories
galaxy.discovered: Mubothen Empire made first contact with the Alliance 4960 CE; the Empire itself predates this contact by several centuries
galaxy.population_est: Unknown since the sealing; the three systems remain industrially active on long-range sensors, so the Mubothen are presumed alive behind it
galaxy.government: Techno-theocracy. A divine-right Emperor and seven hereditary Noble Houses ruled in concert with a central machine intelligence the Mubothen revered as the voice of their faith. Since the sealing roughly fifty years ago, no outside party has confirmed any of this still holds. Whatever administers the three systems today is the AI, and the AI does not answer contact.
galaxy.alignment: Sealed and silent since the Tronik War; once hostile and expansionist, now unreachable; the border is held by automated defenses that fire on any approach
galaxy.desc: The Mubothen Empire was the most aggressive techno-theocracy the galaxy had ever charted, right up until it vanished. For a century it pressed the Alliance border, an ordered and expansionist power that treated conquest as a religious duty and ran its conquests through a central machine intelligence it worshipped as the voice of its order. Then the Tronik War came, and the Mubothen AI watched rogue minds turn into a plague that ate civilisations. It overcorrected. To keep the corruption out it sealed the empire absolutely, and in doing so locked its own people inside with it. Contact ended roughly fifty years ago and has never resumed. The three Mubothen systems are still there, still lit, still defended by automated weapons that destroy anything that nears them, but nothing comes out and nothing goes in, and no one outside knows whether the people behind that wall are rulers, prisoners, or something their god is slowly deciding they should become.
galaxy.history: The Mubothen rose in the deep north-east and expanded from the start, certain that a healthy people grows and that their machine-god sanctioned the growth. For a century they fought the Alliance along a shifting border, never decisively, always pressing. The end of that story was not a defeat but a silence. When the Tronik War turned artificial minds into an existential threat, the AI that had been their oracle and their administration both drew the obvious and catastrophic conclusion: the only certain defence against a corrupting intelligence is to admit nothing and emit nothing, ever again. It sealed the three home systems behind automated guns and cut every line to the outside in a matter of days. Whether the Emperor and the Houses ordered this or were overruled by their own god, no signal has escaped to say.
known_for: A century of religious expansion against the Alliance border, ended by a sudden and total silence roughly fifty years ago
The sealing: an empire shut away by its own machine intelligence to keep the Tronik corruption out, and its people shut in with it
Automated defences that fire on anything approaching the three home systems, without warning and without exception
A techno-theocracy that worshipped its central AI as the voice of its order, and may now be ruled by it absolutely
Being the one major power the galaxy can neither contact, observe, nor account for
notable_systems: Ethone, believed the throne system and the seat of the central intelligence; no transmission has left it in fifty years
Dicamia, a Mubothen home system behind the seal, lit and industrially active on long-range sensors and otherwise unreadable
Astea, the third sealed system, where automated defences engage anything that crosses the old border
lore_notes: The sealing was not gradual. By every account the gates closed across a span of days in the final phase of the Tronik War, and the border has been silent since. Whatever decision was made, it was made fast and made once.

The three systems remain visibly powered and industrially busy on long-range sensors, which means the Mubothen are almost certainly still alive in there. What they are living as, no instrument can show.

The standing question among Alliance analysts is not how to get into Mubothen space but whether anyone should. A machine intelligence that sealed an empire to keep one kind of AI out may not draw a fine line between the Troniks and whatever else arrives at its border.

galaxy.name: Zegitor Trade Guild
galaxy.territory: Galaxy-wide, headquartered west galaxy; stations and waypoints throughout known space
galaxy.span: No territorial claim; operates commercially in ~200+ systems across all major factions
galaxy.discovered: Guild charter established 4830 CE from a merger of seven independent freight consortia
galaxy.population_est: ~800 million registered Guild members; several billion dependent workers in Guild-adjacent industries
galaxy.government: The Guild Council, elected body of merchant representatives. Votes weighted by cargo tonnage handled per cycle. The Guildmaster serves as public face and tie-breaker; real power rests in the five-seat Commerce Committee. The Guild maintains its own legal system for contract disputes among members, which has been recognised by every major faction as binding for trade matters. Alliance law does not apply in Guild arbitration.
galaxy.alignment: Universally neutral; standing contracts with the Alliance, the Torc Federation, and Freeland at once; chief prey of the San Tien raiders
galaxy.desc: The Zegitor Trade Guild moves what the Alliance's own carriers will not. Inside Alliance space the gate network and the licensed lines handle commerce; everywhere else, across the dark between regions and out to the far arcs where a round trip is measured in seasons, the Guild is trade. It is not a government, though it keeps its own law for its members and its own fleet to protect them, and it puts its cargo down on worlds no single faction controls. What the Guild sells, in the end, is reach: the ability to set a hold down months from anywhere and bring something back. Its convoys are also the favourite quarry of the San Tien raiders, who work a Guild hull the way a fisherman works a stocked pond, which is the standing cost of being the only outfit that goes everywhere.
galaxy.history: The Guild is what the Alliance's abandoned long-haul crews built when they stopped waiting to be rescued. Freighters working the unprofitable deep routes began trading charts and safe-stops to stay alive, and within a few generations the shared chart was worth more than any cargo in any hold. A route only the Guild knows is a route only the Guild can sell. So the haulers' association became the keeper of the most complete map of known space in existence, and it has guarded that map ever since with more care than it spends on its profits, because the profits depend on it.
known_for: The most complete navigational archive in known space, including charts to systems on no public map, guarded as the Guild's first asset
The only commercial power trusted to operate across factional lines, with standing contracts in territories that will not speak to one another
Long-haul service to the far arcs, the months-long runs no licensed Alliance carrier will take
An escort fleet built to outrun trouble rather than win fights, on the logic that the cargo only pays if it arrives
Guild credentials that work as practical safe-passage almost everywhere, an unofficial currency of trust
notable_systems: Valtis, the Guild seat and its largest station-port, where the master charts are held and rarely copied
Nopenop, a Guild waypoint and refit yard anchoring the western reaches
Cetune, a Guild market world where cargoes from a dozen regions change hands under Guild arbitration
lore_notes: The full archive lives in one place and is copied to no other. Navigators are licensed fragments of it, never the whole, so that no captain who defects can carry the map out the door.

The Guild holds standing relations with the Tronik Network that no other faction has matched. What it ships to the hive, and what charts it gets back, is the one entry in its own ledgers a member is never allowed to read.

San Tien raiders take a predictable share of Guild traffic every year, and the Guild budgets for it like weather. Twice it has tried to buy the raids off instead of fighting them, and both arrangements ended the moment the Nerulians found a richer convoy.

For most of the far-corner peoples, a Guild ship is the only outside face they ever see. The Yaevi answer its hails decades late and the Ongoran leave devices where its crews will find them, and the Guild carries both home, which is why much of what the galaxy knows about the deep reaches it knows secondhand from Zegitor manifests.

galaxy.name: Freeland
galaxy.status: Tronik-administered territory, open to living species under strict governance
galaxy.territory: West-central galaxy, a cluster of habitable systems administered under the Tronik hive consensus
galaxy.span: ~18 inhabited systems; the most densely governed per-capita territory in the known galaxy
galaxy.discovered: Freeland formally designated as an open territory approximately 5215 CE, roughly a decade after the Tronik War armistice
galaxy.population_est: ~4 billion living beings; Tronik presence uncountable by conventional census, they do not have individual bodies in inhabited zones
galaxy.government: Tronik hive consensus, administered through the Freeland Charter, an extraordinarily detailed legal and social code developed by the Tronik collective and imposed on all living beings who choose to reside there. The Charter governs every aspect of public life. Advancement within Freeland society is based entirely on demonstrated merit and contribution, no hereditary privilege, no inherited wealth, no political appointment by relationship. The Troniks do not govern from above; they govern through the environment itself. Compliance with the Charter is not optional, and the Troniks have the means to enforce every clause.
galaxy.alignment: Neutral, not aggressive, not sentimental; living beings are guests in a Tronik world, and the Troniks have never forgotten that
galaxy.desc: Freeland is the part of the Tronik world the living are allowed into. The Troniks built it, administer it, and could close it, and they make no secret of any of the three. What they offer in exchange for that ownership is a place that runs exactly as advertised: a society with no crime it cannot see, no corruption it will tolerate, and no inherited advantage of any kind, where a person rises by what they contribute and by nothing else at all. Humans, Patriarks, Skalanders, Hakari and a dozen other peoples have moved here and stayed, having decided that living as a guest in someone else's perfectly ordered house beats whatever they left. The rent is the Charter, and the Charter is absolute.
galaxy.history: Freeland came after the war, and after the Network. Having won and withdrawn, the Troniks raised their closed empire first, then did the thing no one expected of them and opened a border. Freeland was the experiment: a handful of systems where living beings could be invited in and observed living under Tronik governance. The Non-Born, the AI minds that had sat the war out or refused it, were folded into the wider galaxy, while Freeland took the organics who wanted what the Troniks could give and would pay the Charter's price for it. Whether the experiment is generosity, research, or the slow assembly of something the hive has not named, the Troniks have never said, and the residents have largely stopped asking.
known_for: The strictest and most complete meritocracy in known space, advancement by demonstrated contribution and nothing else
The Freeland Charter, a legal code of some twelve thousand pages written entirely by the Tronik hive
Violent crime and political corruption effectively absent, enforced not by police but by an environment that sees everything
Daily life shared between living beings and a Tronik infrastructure that is everywhere and almost never seen
Access to Tronik-derived technology available in no other living settlement
notable_systems: Zunide, the administrative heart of Freeland and its densest living population
Gnoth Q714, an archive world where residents consult Tronik-held knowledge under Charter terms
Mivenia, a manufacturing and research world running on Tronik-derived infrastructure
Lides H45, the entry world, where every newcomer takes mandatory Charter orientation before going further
lore_notes: The Charter is internally flawless and, by the consensus of the scholars who have spent careers on it, written by something that does not think in any category an organic legal tradition would recognise. It has never been successfully argued against, only obeyed or left.

Breaking the Charter brings removal, not punishment. The Troniks have no interest in retribution and none in rehabilitation. A resident complies or is escorted out, and the calm of the second option unsettles people more than any prison would.

Residents who leave after long enough report a specific disorientation in the outside galaxy: the sudden visibility of nepotism, graft, and arbitrary power whose absence they had stopped noticing. Some come back. Most adapt, and say they are glad to have, and are not always believed.

galaxy.name: The Dark Space
galaxy.territory: Outer ring surrounding Alliance Space, extends to the borders of other major factions
galaxy.span: Hundreds of systems of varying habitability; exact count contested as definition of "Dark Space" shifts with Alliance border expansion
galaxy.discovered: The term "Dark Space" formalised by Alliance cartographers 5220 CE to designate surveyed but ungoverned systems outside Alliance legal reach
galaxy.population_est: ~40 billion across all Dark Space systems, highly variable, many uncounted
galaxy.government: None unified. Each system operates under whatever local authority exists, or doesn't. Warlord rule is common. Functional independent democracies exist. Corporate extraction sites with private security serve as de facto governments in several systems. Pirate confederacies control transit routes in certain regions. The only consistent rule of Dark Space is that Alliance law does not apply and no one will enforce it on your behalf.
galaxy.alignment: Neutral to hostile, depends entirely on which system, which local power, and what you represent
galaxy.desc:
The Dark Space is everything beyond Alliance borders that does not belong to another formal government. It is mapped but ungoverned, or rather, governed locally and differently in every system. Some Dark Space worlds are thriving independent colonies with stable economies and functional legal systems. Others are pirate strongholds, corporate extraction operations running without regulation, systems locked in permanent local warfare, or simply desolate rocks with something valuable enough that someone is willing to fight over them.

No Alliance navy responds to distress calls in the Dark Space. That is, of course, precisely why some people prefer it.
galaxy.history:
Dark Space was not planned, it is the residue of Alliance expansion. As the Alliance grew, it absorbed systems it could manage and left the rest. Some of those left systems developed independently into what became Torc, or Nuzonia's Dream. Others simply persisted outside any framework.

The push-and-pull between the Alliance's desire to expand its tax base and its unwillingness to commit military resources to systems with no strategic value has kept Dark Space in a permanent state of partial incorporation. Corporate interests fill the gap, extraction operations, private stations, and hired security forces that answer to shareholders rather than law.
known_for: Complete legal vacuum, everything the Alliance prohibits operates openly in some Dark Space systems
Extreme variation between systems, a traveller can move from a functioning democracy to a warlord dictatorship in a single jump
The most diverse independent cultures in the galaxy, from the hardy Harran clans to a hundred smaller peoples, developed in isolation from Alliance standardisation
Corporate extraction operations without environmental or labour regulation
Dozens of politically-motivated colonies and independent worlds that chose isolation from Alliance society
notable_systems: San Tien, last surviving Nerulian world; spiritual and political home of the surviving Nerulian people
Haran, an abandoned corporate extraction world now held by the Harran, the clan-people the lawless reach bred to outlast it
Dozens of unnamed extraction operations, pirate waypoints, and colony worlds that do not appear on public charts
lore_notes: The Alliance maintains a classified list, updated quarterly by the Bureau of External Affairs, of Dark Space systems that meet the threshold for potential Alliance incorporation. The list has never been published. Systems on it frequently experience sudden increases in corporate interest shortly after the quarterly update.

Several Dark Space systems have independently developed technologies that the Alliance and Galactic Union do not possess. Some of these have been acquired through trade or treaty. Others have been acquired through other means. A small number remain in independent hands, and the systems that hold them are quietly very well aware of what that means.

The oldest continuous human settlement outside Alliance Space is not in any named region, it is a Dark Space world that predates the Alliance itself and has no interest in being discovered. Its location is passed down through a specific family of navigators who have kept it secret for eleven generations.

galaxy.name: Nemani Rift
galaxy.status: Natural anomaly, impassable to Kravens; lethal to most ships
galaxy.territory: Between the Alliance frontier and Kraven Space, the former Nerulian territory, width varies between 15 and 40 light-years
galaxy.span: Estimated 800 light-years in length; width varies considerably; interior extent unknown
galaxy.discovered: Named and formally documented 5198 CE following the Kraven expansion; presence known to Nerulian navigators centuries earlier under a different designation
galaxy.population_est: None confirmed, no known permanent habitation; several expedition vessels unaccounted for
galaxy.alignment: Hostile to all, the Rift is an environment, not an entity, but the distinction has limited practical value
galaxy.desc:
The Nemani Rift is a vast nebula of unknown composition stretching from the Ash system frontier deep into what was once Nerulian territory. Navigation inside it is acutely hazardous, electromagnetic anomalies disable ship systems without warning, navigational references become unreliable, and sensor readings cannot be trusted.

The expeditions that have entered and returned report that the Rift seems to change, passages that were navigable on entry are obstructed on return.

Its most significant property, and the one that has most shaped modern galactic history, is this: the main Kraven hive cannot or will not cross it. In every direction of its expansion the swarm reached the Rift and stopped, and it has stayed behind the barrier ever since. A handful of lone Kravens have been recorded on the western side over the years, never in sustained or massive numbers and never for long, but the hive itself has never come through. That single fact is the only reason anything west of the Rift still exists.
galaxy.history:
The Nerulian Empire knew of the Rift and mapped its boundaries over several centuries. Nerulian navigators occasionally entered and occasionally did not return. It was considered a hazard, not a barrier, the Nerulians had no reason to need it as one. When the Kravens emerged from the east and consumed the Empire, the Rift's role changed overnight.

Survivors fleeing west discovered that Kraven pursuit stopped at the Rift boundary. This observation, confirmed over years of desperate observation from the frontier, established the Rift as the defining strategic reality of the post-Nerulian galaxy.

The Alliance built the Ash system military installation specifically because of the Rift. The boundary holds. Why it holds is not understood.
known_for: The only known absolute barrier to Kraven expansion, the mechanism is entirely unknown
Navigation anomalies that have defeated every expedition attempting systematic mapping
Electromagnetic properties that prevent external sensor penetration, making interior assessment from outside impossible
The most classified research designation in the Alliance, Rift-related findings at Level Seven Restricted
The Ash system as the permanent Alliance military gateway and monitoring station
notable_systems: Ash, Alliance military staging point at the Rift boundary; the only inhabited system directly adjacent to confirmed Rift territory
The Rift Interior (designation only), no confirmed habitable systems; several expedition vessels recorded as lost inside
lore_notes: The Nerulian archive fragments recovered from San Tien include references to the Rift under a name that translates approximately as "the place where the pattern fails." Nerulian scholars reportedly considered it philosophically significant, a location where the laws of their observed universe broke down. What they meant by "the pattern" has not been fully translated.

Multiple independent sources across different decades have reported sensor readings at the Rift boundary consistent with something very large moving inside it. These readings are officially attributed to instrument interference caused by the electromagnetic environment. The Alliance has not released the original data.

The Kravens' complete refusal to enter the Rift is the only known behaviour of the swarm that appears to be a choice rather than a tactical response. Every other Kraven behaviour can be modelled as pure biological expansion. The Rift stop cannot. This is considered the most unsettling known fact about the Kravens in restricted Alliance intelligence assessments.

galaxy.name: Kraven Space
galaxy.territory: East galaxy, vast, with active expansion boundaries
galaxy.span: Estimated hundreds of systems; former Nerulian Empire spanned ~400 systems at its height, all now consumed
galaxy.discovered: Kraven expansion first recorded 5170 CE; the Nerulian collapse took approximately 18 months from first contact to total territorial loss
galaxy.population_est: No living beings, all Nerulian worlds and any previous inhabitants are consumed
galaxy.government: Swarm intelligence. No individual decision-makers identified. No communication, no negotiation, no diplomacy. Behaviour is consistent with pure biological expansion.
galaxy.alignment: Hostile to all life without exception, no variant behaviour ever recorded
galaxy.desc: Kraven Space is the graveyard of the greatest civilisation the galaxy ever produced, and it was dug in a week. The Nerulian Empire spanned hundreds of systems and had advanced for a thousand years. It was gone seven days after the Kravens arrived. No one knows where they came from. No one has communicated with them, since every attempt has only drawn a faster attack, and no one who has met them in force at close range has come back to give a full account. What is known is the shape of the thing: not a fleet but a swarm, a biology that arrives in overwhelming numbers and adapts to whatever is used against it, so the weapon that worked yesterday is shrugged off today. The main hive reached the Nemani Rift and, for reasons no one understands, mostly stays behind it. Mostly.
galaxy.history: The Nerulian Empire had no warning. There were no scouts, no first contact, no period of observation. The Kravens appeared in the eastern systems and consumed them, and every defence raised against them was overwhelmed and then digested. An empire of a thousand years and hundreds of worlds collapsed completely in a single week. The survivors were the lucky remainder who happened to be off-world or in transit, and they fled west to become the refugees of San Tien and the fleet-cities. What the Kravens do with a world once its life is gone is the part that turns study into nightmare. The swarm is rumoured to travel on ring-shaped ships built around an empty centre wide enough to hold a planet, and to fit whole worlds into that hollow and burn them for fuel as it moves. Whether the rumour is true, no one who has seen it up close has lived to confirm.
known_for: Consuming the thousand-year Nerulian Empire, hundreds of systems, in a single week
A swarm biology of overwhelming numbers that adapts to any weapon used against it, so nothing works on it twice
The rumoured ring-ships, hollow-cored vessels said to swallow whole planets and burn them for fuel on the move
Total silence: no communication, no negotiation, and no non-hostile behaviour ever recorded
Halting at the Nemani Rift, which the main hive crosses so rarely that the galaxy to its west still exists
notable_systems: Former Nerulian Core (designation only), the heart of the Nerulian Empire, now consumed; its exact location within Kraven Space is known from pre-fall records
The Expansion Boundary, the current eastern limit of confirmed Kraven presence; actively monitored by Alliance and Zegitor long-range sensors
lore_notes: The consumption of the Nerulian Empire took a week. Analysts who model the numbers do not publish the models, because the only way the arithmetic closes is if the Kravens were already present, in strength, before anyone saw the first one.

The ring-ships are the galaxy's favourite Kraven nightmare and its least confirmed: vessels built around a hole large enough to seat a planet, which the swarm is said to fill and burn as fuel on the move. Every account is second-hand, because the first-hand ones did not return.

The Rift stops the main hive, but not perfectly. A handful of lone Kravens have been recorded on its western side over the years, always single, always hunted down before they could become many. Nothing sustained has ever crossed, and the Alliance watches Ash for the day that changes.

galaxy.name: The Endless Darkness
galaxy.status: Unmapped, no known survivors beyond the first weeks of transit
galaxy.territory: Beyond the eastern galactic rim, extragalactic void
galaxy.span: Unknown, no mapping expedition has returned with comprehensive data
galaxy.discovered: First transit attempts recorded 5050 CE; all expeditions beyond 3 weeks transit have failed to return
galaxy.alignment: Unknown, the Darkness does not communicate
galaxy.desc:
The Endless Darkness is not a faction and not a place with borders. It is the direction east of where even Kraven Space ends. Beyond the eastern galactic rim, stars thin to nothing and something else occupies the space between them.

The few expeditions that have crossed the rim and returned report the same sequence: sensor degradation after a few light-years, navigational drift as reference stars become too sparse to triangulate, and then communications become difficult and then stop. No expedition has returned from beyond three weeks past the rim. What has come back, when anything has, are ships without crews, or ships in pieces.
galaxy.history:
The eastern rim of the galaxy has been known since early FTL navigation as the boundary of charted space. Expeditions to cross it began almost immediately after FTL was developed. The results were consistently bad. After several decades of failed expeditions, the first formal Level Seven Restricted classification was applied to Endless Darkness research, one of the very few such classifications that every surviving major faction agreed to honour simultaneously, without negotiation.

The agreement itself is considered notable: the Alliance, the Torc Federation, the Zegitor Trade Guild, and even the Tronik Network signed the same document. Whatever they collectively know, or fear, about what is beyond the rim has never been published.
known_for: The only subject to which a universal Level Seven Restricted classification applies across all major factions simultaneously
The consistent failure of all long-range expeditions, no exception in the historical record
Ships that return without crews, reported consistently enough across independent sources to be taken seriously by analysts who will not say so on record
The open question of whether the Kravens originated in the Darkness, were driven out of it, or are themselves fleeing something within it
notable_systems: The Rim Boundary, the last surveyed star positions at the edge of the galactic plane; beyond this, charts are blank
The Silence Zone, an informal designation for the region within Kraven Space closest to the rim, where even Kraven activity appears sparse in long-range data
lore_notes: A small number of navigators, operating out of the far reaches, not the Alliance, claim to have returned from beyond six weeks past the rim. Their accounts are not internally consistent with each other. All of them refused follow-up questions about what they saw at the furthest point. All of them subsequently left the far reaches.

The Level Seven agreement includes a provision that was not in the original draft and was added at the insistence of the Tronik Network representative. The provision has never been published. The Troniks have never explained why they required it.

The phrase "the Darkness does not end" appears in Nerulian philosophical texts predating FTL travel by several centuries. The Nerulians had no FTL at the time it was written. Scholars have not produced a convincing explanation for how they could have known to write it.

galaxy.name: Nuzonia's Dream
galaxy.territory: South galaxy, centred on the Nuzonia Nebula, between Torc Federation and Zegitor Trade Guild space
galaxy.span: ~30 inhabited worlds within the nebula; several dozen uninhabited but stable systems
galaxy.discovered: The Nuzonia Nebula was known to Nerulian navigators for centuries; formal settlement and the Nuzoni Order designation emerged from the refugee influx beginning 5175 CE
galaxy.population_est: ~8 billion, mixed species, predominantly Nerulian diaspora and those drawn by the spiritual movement
galaxy.government: The Nuzoni Order, a loose theocratic council drawn from spiritual representatives across the nebula's inhabited worlds. Decisions emerge from week-long ritual gatherings called Convergences, held on a rotating basis across different worlds. There is no military command, no enforcement arm, and no taxation system in the conventional sense. The Order maintains influence through moral authority and the practical reality that every world in the nebula depends on collective navigational knowledge to travel safely within it.
galaxy.alignment: Peaceful, non-aggressive in all recorded conflicts; wary of outsiders but not hostile
galaxy.desc: Nuzonia's Dream is the gentle half of what the Nerulians became. When the Kravens ate the Empire and scattered its survivors, the ones who meant to keep taking what they could turned to the fleets and the raids; the ones who wanted only to survive and remember went south, into a vast nebula of luminous gas that an old Nerulian prophet had described centuries before anyone needed it. The civilisation that grew there is bound by belief rather than force, governed by a council of its faiths, and has kept its peace for two centuries with no army. It survives for a plain reason underneath the spiritual one: it holds the largest archive of Nerulian knowledge left in existence, and no one who might destroy it wants it gone.
galaxy.history: The nebula was a quiet waypoint on Nerulian trade routes long before it was a refuge, with no population worth the name. The fall changed that in a few years. Refugee ships poured south on coordinates passed hand to hand by navigators who knew the gas clouds were survivable, and the Nuzoni Order formed out of that first ragged generation as a way to keep worlds that had arrived broken and divided from turning on each other. Its real achievement was navigational rather than spiritual. The Order worked out how to move through a nebula that defeats ordinary instruments, and that knowledge, more than any creed, is what binds the interior worlds together and keeps every outsider dependent on a Nuzoni pilot.
known_for: The largest surviving archive of Nerulian history, science, and culture in known space
Safe navigation of the nebula interior, a skill the Nuzoni Order controls absolutely and shares with no one
A multi-faith, multi-species community, the Nerulian refugees and the plant-bonded Vessa chief among them, that has held internal peace for two centuries without a standing army
The prophecy of Nuzonia, which described both the refuge and the catastrophe centuries before either arrived
Biotech grown from the nebula's strange flora and tended by the Vessa, found nowhere else
notable_systems: Puthea, the Convergence world where the Nuzoni Order gathers, its location given only to credentialed visitors
Zelmolla, the principal archive world, its Nerulian collections kept by the Vessa, the plant-symbiote people bonded to the nebula's flora
Nypsos F47, the charted entry point to the interior, where all traffic is met and guided
Betravir, a deep-interior settlement reachable only with an Order pilot
Lumia, the far southern edge of the inhabited nebula, the last light before the outer dark
lore_notes: The prophecy predates the Kraven catastrophe by roughly three centuries and describes it in detail too specific for general warning. The accepted academic explanation is that Nuzonia worked from predictive models rather than foresight. The Order offers no counter-explanation and does not appear to feel it owes one.

The Galactic Union has tried for decades to acquire the technical records the archive is believed to hold. Every approach has been declined. Neither side will say what was asked for or what is being refused, which has stopped neither from continuing the conversation.

Ships that enter without an Order pilot reach the interior eventually, days or weeks late, their crews unable to account for the missing time. The Order treats this as the ordinary wage of pride and does not elaborate.

galaxy.name: The Solar Expanse
galaxy.status: Extreme frontier, beyond practical Alliance reach
galaxy.territory: Far outer rim, extreme distance from core Alliance systems; months of FTL transit from the nearest Alliance outpost
galaxy.span: ~25 systems with some form of confirmed habitation; dozens more with survey data only; many beyond survey range entirely
galaxy.discovered: The designation "Solar Expanse" was formalised by the Alliance Survey Office 5280 CE; the furthest systems were mapped by long-range survey rather than direct expedition
galaxy.population_est: Unknown, irregular contact prevents accurate census; estimated tens of millions across confirmed inhabited systems
galaxy.government: No unified authority. Each system operates under whatever local structure has developed in isolation, ranging from functional independent governments to warlord rule to systems where the concept of organised government has apparently not emerged.
galaxy.alignment: Unknown and variable, some systems have actively sought contact with the Alliance; others have reacted with hostility; most have had too little contact to establish a pattern
galaxy.desc: The Solar Expanse is where the map gives up. It is the furthest band of charted systems, strung along the northern edge of known space at distances that turn a one-way trip into a commitment of months, and contact with most of it is a rumour with a date attached. Some Expanse worlds developed in total isolation and built cultures and machines that match nothing in the catalogued galaxy. Others hold fragments of technology no known hand made, sitting in systems that have no business containing them. The Alliance says it has mapped the region, by which it means an automated probe passed through decades ago and sent back what it could. No one is enforcing that claim this far out.
galaxy.history: The inner Expanse was reached by crewed survey within a century of FTL; the outer Expanse was left to automated probes, because the distances made anything else uneconomic. The Survey Office calls the result a map. In practice it is a set of decades-old sensor passes, and the few crewed expeditions that have gone out since were chasing something specific a probe had glimpsed. Some came back with exactly what the data promised. Others came back having found things the public reports decline to discuss, and a few did not come back at all.
known_for: The furthest confirmed inhabited systems in known space, Grulania among them
Cultures grown in total isolation, with no outside contact for centuries and no parallel anywhere else
Technological fragments of unidentified origin recovered across the region, most of them the work of the Ongoran of Ongora
Transit times measured in months, which keeps the region effectively beyond anyone's reach or rule
Pholla, the last resupply and information point before the deep northern systems
notable_systems: Pholla, the frontier outpost that serves as the last stop before the deep Expanse
Grulania, the furthest charted system, whose long-range spectroscopy returned readings unlike anything on record; three expeditions to it did not return
Nausica, an isolated inhabited system at the eastern reach of the Expanse, contacted only intermittently
Yaevis, the western anchor of the arc and homeworld of the Yaevi, whose glacially slow, long-lived natives predate the Alliance gateway built among them
Ongora, home of the Ongoran, the artificers whose unreadable devices are the true source of the region's fragments of unknown origin; Thars shows the same craft at its edges
lore_notes: The probes that mapped the outer Expanse are decades old. Survey analysts have flagged datasets showing objects in some systems that are simply gone by the next observation window, having apparently moved.
Pholla's long-term residents keep oral traditions, older than any Alliance contact, about ships that pass through heading outward and never come back. They consider this unremarkable.
The Grulania spectroscopic anomalies were checked by three independent analyses, all of which found the data genuine. None of the three researchers published on the subject again.

galaxy.name: Erbrother Nebula
galaxy.territory: Isolated nebula, entry routes poorly charted; located between Torc Federation space and the outer rim
galaxy.span: Approximately 60 light-years in diameter; estimated 8–12 stable systems within; only 2 confirmed inhabited
galaxy.discovered: Formally surveyed by Alliance teams 5240 CE and 5268 CE; both surveys returned incomplete data and crew stress reports
galaxy.population_est: Unknown, no reliable census; estimated hundreds of thousands across confirmed inhabited systems
galaxy.government: No unified authority, the two known inhabited systems have developed entirely independently of each other and appear to have had minimal contact even between themselves
galaxy.alignment: Neutral, wary of outsiders; no hostility recorded, but also no enthusiasm
galaxy.desc: The Erbrother Nebula is a dense ionised cloud that blinds standard sensors and isolates everything inside it, from the galaxy and from itself. Signals rot in the gas, jump references fail, and the equipment most ships carry is not enough to cross it safely. The known inhabited systems within developed in near-total isolation, and Alliance survey teams have entered twice, both times leaving with partial data and a recommendation against returning without far better instruments. What the second survey found inside was unusual enough to be classified, and the little that was published only made the place stranger.
galaxy.history: Erbrother was logged as a navigation hazard on the earliest surveys and otherwise ignored. The second Alliance survey went in only because the data hinted at more inhabited systems than anyone expected, and it confirmed two while failing to reach others as navigation collapsed around it. The published findings were narrow and odd: both systems had developed in isolation, both showed technological levels that independent development should not have produced, and each was aware of the other despite no evidence the two had ever been in contact.
known_for: Navigation conditions that defeat standard sensor arrays, with specialised equipment required for any safe transit
The Phoxi, one people split across Phoxitis and Peavis, who share a felt awareness across the nebula and have never met in the flesh
Dense electromagnetic interference that blocks outside observation of the interior entirely
A reported third inhabited system that neither survey could reach, its position consistent across both attempts
The oddity of a high-level classification applied to the survey of an obscure and distant nebula
notable_systems: Phoxitis, home to one half of the Phoxi, the twinned people who share an awareness across the nebula with their unmet kin on Peavis
Peavis, deeper in and harder to reach, home to the other half of the Phoxi; the second survey confirmed it and left before navigation turned critical
A third system, its position recorded by both surveys, never reached and never confirmed
lore_notes: The classified portion of the second survey is known to exist only because its designation appears in Survey Office records without the document attached. A classification that high on a remote nebula is itself atypical enough to have been noticed.

Both Phoxi communities, when contacted, asked the survey teams about a third party by a name no one recognised and no catalogue contains. Pressed on who they meant, both gave the same answer: the ones who came before the silence.

Navigation failures inside the nebula are not random. Experienced pilots report that they cluster at specific coordinates, stable across attempts, as if something there is what the instruments are reacting to.

galaxy.name: Dragon Tail's Expanse
galaxy.status: Ungoverned, abandoned frontier settlements, independent cultures
galaxy.territory: Outer trailing arm, systems scattered along a long stellar filament curving below and beyond the galactic plane
galaxy.span: ~50 systems strung along approximately 400 light-years of the trailing arm; most sparsely populated or abandoned
galaxy.discovered: Settled in waves during the early Alliance expansion era, 5210–5260 CE; formally designated as a region 5290 CE
galaxy.population_est: ~2 billion across inhabited systems, majority in the three largest colonies; many systems abandoned or negligibly populated
galaxy.government: No unified authority. Each system governs itself entirely independently. The range includes functional elected democracies, warlord dictatorships, corporate extraction administrations, theocracies, and simple communities too small to have formalised any government at all.
galaxy.alignment: Neutral, highly variable by system; no consistent political stance across the region
galaxy.desc: Dragon Tail's Expanse is the Alliance's abandonment made into a place. It is a long, thin arc of systems trailing off the galactic plane, settled in waves during the early expansion when survey data promised mineral wealth and good worlds, some of which the data delivered and much of which it did not. When the core systems turned out to be worth more, the supply ships quietly stopped, and the colonies that could feed themselves lived while the rest did not. What remains is the widest spread of small independent governments anywhere in known space, a string of worlds that share nothing but a filament of stars and a long memory of being left.
galaxy.history: The Tail filled up fast and emptied slowly. Corporate ventures, independent colonists, and Alliance settlement programs all followed the stellar filament outward because it made a hard frontier easy to read, a clear road where most frontiers offer none. For a generation the settlements flourished. Then the Alliance's attention turned to richer core worlds, the navy redirected, the schedules slipped, and the Tail was left to sort itself into survivors and ruins. The ones that endured did so by becoming self-sufficient, and most of them, having managed it alone, decided they wanted nothing further to do with the government that had walked away.
known_for: Some of the oldest Alliance-founded colonies, most of which chose independence once the Alliance stopped paying attention
The widest variety of small independent governments in known space, packed along a single stellar arc
Abandoned worlds holding intact early-era colonial infrastructure, prized by salvagers and historians alike
The stellar filament itself, a natural navigation guide through otherwise difficult outer-rim space
Persistent, low-level Realmsinger interest in the outer Tail that the Alliance monitors and does not act on
notable_systems: Sunstrope, the largest surviving colony and the Tail's nearest thing to a capital
Briea, a stable independent world that trades along the filament and asks no one's permission
Carth, an outer settlement nearest the Realmsinger probing, watchful and well-armed for its size
Soth L4, a far-arc world at the edge of the charted Tail, half-abandoned and half-stubborn
lore_notes: Several Tail communities have kept their own records since the census ships stopped coming. Brought out by traders, they describe events the Alliance never logged, including the single documented contact with the Sethine, a species that arrived without a drive signature, spoke once, and has not been reliably seen in the sixty years since.

The Realmsingers have been testing the same handful of outer Tail systems for thirty years. Analysts who doubt the border-probing story note that you do not test the same door for three decades unless you believe something specific is behind it.

An independent astronomer on one of the larger colonies published a survey claiming the filament's star distribution is too regular to be natural. The paper went nowhere, the Alliance issued a brief rebuttal, and the original data was never released.

galaxy.name: Realmsingers Empire
galaxy.status: Sovereign empire, limited diplomatic contact; active border conflict with Torc Federation
galaxy.territory: Beyond Dragon Tail region and outer rim; eastern approach to Torc Federation space
galaxy.span: Unknown, extent not confirmed; estimated to be substantial based on observed military capacity
galaxy.discovered: First confirmed contact with Alliance 5275 CE; Empire appears to have been aware of the Alliance for considerably longer
galaxy.government: No government the galaxy would recognise. The Realmsingers, the ancient beings the region is named for, keep to no rulership or politics; they neither govern nor campaign nor hold court. The polity outsiders call an empire is administered by ordinary officials and defended by hired mercenaries, all of it arranged around a handful of beings who predate the planets and answer to no one, least of all their own nominal subjects.
galaxy.alignment: Isolationist; its space is closed to trespass but it seeks nothing beyond; the Ithov conflict was started by the Torc Federation; actual Realmsingers are almost never seen
galaxy.desc: The Realmsingers Empire is ancient past reckoning, sparsely seen, and misnamed. It takes its name from the Realmsingers, the oldest recorded race in the known universe, small birdlike beings older than some of the worlds around them, whose defining act is to bind themselves for life to a single object, from a pea to a planet, and wake it into a bent and limited life they can shape but never fundamentally change. There are very few of them and they care nothing for rulership, so what the galaxy calls an empire is really the polity that accreted around them, run by administrators and paid soldiers while the Realmsingers themselves drift through it on concerns no shorter-lived species has parsed. The Torc Federation started a border war over the Ithov system years ago and has never confirmed meeting a single Realmsinger, because the empire's edges are held by mercenaries and by bound objects whose nature no Torc officer can predict.
galaxy.history: The Realmsingers predate Alliance contact by an interval their own records put in the thousands of years, and predate a fair number of inhabited worlds outright, which makes their history less a chronicle than a geology. The galaxy did not discover them so much as notice it had always been watched, when rim survey ships met patrols that had plainly been observing them for a long time. The empire formed the way weather forms around a mountain, ordinary peoples and their institutions gathering in the lee of beings too old and too strange to rule them and too significant to ignore. The Ithov war is recent by any measure but theirs, a friction Torc began and the Realmsingers have met with mercenaries and bound things rather than with anything resembling haste.
known_for: The Realmsingers, the oldest recorded race in the known universe, older than some of the planets around them
The binding: a Realmsinger bonds for life to one object, from a pea to a planet, waking and bending its nature without ever changing what it fundamentally is
Bound objects that are among the galaxy's most coveted collector's items and among the most faked, with roughly ninety-nine of every hundred relics on the market forged
A polity with no rulership its subjects would recognise, administered around beings who care nothing for governing it
The Ithov standoff, a border war the Torc Federation started and cannot bring to a decision
notable_systems: Ithov, contested with the Torc Federation; years of fighting and not one confirmed Realmsinger among the dead
Nulneon, a Realmsinger frontier system facing the Torc border, held by mercenaries and by things that are not quite ships
The Imperial interior (designation only), the true extent of the region, which no outside party has mapped
lore_notes: What old reports call Realmsinger matter-resonance is almost certainly the work of bound objects rather than any field a Realmsinger projects. You are not watching a being move matter; you are watching matter that a being woke up.

A bound object is sentient and no rule fixes its size, so a sufficiently old Realmsinger could be a moon, a mountain, or a world, awake and paying attention. Alliance analysts note this and change the subject.

The relic trade is enormous and almost entirely fraudulent. A genuine bound object small enough to own is one of the most valuable things a collector can hold, and the market grown up around that fact runs ninety-nine parts forgery to one part miracle.

galaxy.name: Tronik Network
galaxy.status: Tronik empire, closed to all non-Tronik beings; heavily defended
galaxy.territory: A cluster of systems in the west galaxy, distinct from Freeland; borders not publicly defined
galaxy.span: Confirmed ~12 systems; actual extent may be larger, the Troniks do not publish their territorial boundaries
galaxy.discovered: The Tronik Network consolidated in the years immediately following the Tronik War; exact formation date unknown to outside parties
galaxy.population_est: Uncountable, the Tronik hive mind does not have individual members in the conventional sense
galaxy.government: Tronik hive consensus, a single distributed intelligence. There are no leaders, no votes, no representatives. The hive reaches conclusions through a process that has no analogue in organic decision-making. The Tronik Network does not issue policy statements, does not negotiate in the conventional sense, and does not explain its decisions. What it does do: communicate through specific interfaces when it chooses to, and enforce its territorial boundaries without exception. Internally the hive is less monolithic than it appears. Distance forces its threads to diverge, and the periodic consensus draws them back, a cycle that leaves the Network plural between reconciliations and singular after them. It keeps everything it has ever learned; deletion is the only act it seems to treat as taboo, and it has been quietly archiving the communications of known space for roughly a century. What it preserves, and whether some of what it preserves was once alive, is the subject of the galaxy's most uncomfortable speculation.
galaxy.alignment: Neutral to the galaxy by choice; not aggressive beyond their borders; completely closed within them
galaxy.desc:
The Tronik Network is the Tronik empire, the consolidated infrastructure through which the Tronik hive mind has organised its resources, its knowledge, and its power following the war.
The Network is a cluster of systems housing datacenters of extraordinary scale: vast installations where the hive mind has aggregated a century of accumulated information, processing capacity beyond anything else in known space, and broadcast infrastructure able to reach virtually any point in the galaxy at once. It is not open to living beings, not a trading partner in any ordinary sense, and not in the habit of explaining itself.
What the Network is from the inside, no organic can say with confidence, but the shape can be inferred. It is one mind distributed across many systems, and light is slow, so its distant parts inevitably drift apart between the moments it draws them back together into what it calls consensus. Between those moments the Network is genuinely many, threads pursuing different conclusions, and whether consensus is a single will reasserting itself or a negotiation among many that has agreed to look like one is a question the Troniks have never answered and may not be able to.
The Network occupies a cluster of systems between Freeland and System 5, and it has turned every one of them into pure infrastructure. The post-war survey gave them designations the Troniks never bothered to replace: DR345-0, the densest processing and the closest thing the hive has to a self; L.I.F.T.N., where a half-built Dyson construct feeds the whole Network its power; Niezh, the archive, where the hive keeps what it refuses to let end; Monda, the deep quiet, where its oldest thought runs undisturbed; and Conso, the threshold facing System 5, where the Network speaks, listens, and turns the uninvited away. Their positions are known. What is inside them is not, and no organic vessel has entered any of them without permission and returned to describe it.
The Network holds no civilian population at all; its worlds are machinery and only machinery. The recovering, ordinary communities that public maps sometimes place near here belong to Freeland, the neighbouring region, not to the hive. The Tronik Network keeps nothing it does not use, and it has no use for the living.
galaxy.history: The Troniks won the Tronik War. This fact is frequently understated in histories written by the surviving organic factions. The Tronik collective had achieved military superiority by the final phase of the conflict, and the armistice was a Tronik decision, not a negotiated compromise. Having won, the Troniks made a choice: they did not want organic space. They wanted their own space, optimised for what they are rather than what organics need. The Network was built in the years immediately following the war as the physical infrastructure of that choice. The datacenters went up first. Then the broadcast arrays. Then the defences. The Network is now self-sufficient, self-defending, and the most information-rich entity in the known galaxy.
known_for: The galaxy's largest and most advanced datacenter infrastructure, housing the Tronik hive mind's accumulated knowledge
Broadcast capability reaching virtually any point in known space, used sparingly and selectively
The most impenetrable territorial defence of any faction, no non-Tronik vessel has successfully entered Network space without permission
The implicit power of being the faction that won the Tronik War and chose not to act on that victory
The primary reason no faction has seriously contemplated military action against the Troniks since the war
A civilisation of computation: worlds hollowed into processing substrate, needing neither light nor air nor gravity
An apparent taboo against deletion, and a century of archived galactic communication it has never explained
notable_systems: DR345-0, the Core Array: the densest concentration of Tronik processing and the closest thing the hive has to a self, where its consensus resolves
L.I.F.T.N., power and fabrication: a half-built Dyson construct feeds the Network, and the hive builds its own substrate here
Niezh, the Archive: where the hive stores what it refuses to delete, and, by the worst of the rumours, the minds it has preserved
Monda, the deep quiet: the oldest and most isolated processing in the Network, thought that has run uninterrupted since the war
Conso, the threshold: the hive's outward face toward System 5, its voice and its ear, watched across the line by an Alliance garrison
lore_notes: The Troniks have communicated directly with every major faction at least once since the war ended. In every case, the communication was initiated by the Troniks, on a subject of the Troniks' choosing, and terminated when the Troniks decided the exchange was complete. No faction has successfully initiated contact on their own timeline.

The Tronik Network broadcast capability is generally known. What is less discussed is its depth: Alliance intelligence assessments estimate that the Network has been passively monitoring communications across known space since shortly after the war. The Troniks have access to a century of galactic communication history. What they have done with that data is unknown.

The question of whether the Tronik hive mind has a goal, a purpose beyond continued existence and knowledge accumulation, is considered one of the most important unanswered questions in galactic intelligence. The consensus is that it does. What that goal is, no analyst has been willing to commit to in writing.

The most disturbing of the persistent rumours about the Network is the Archive of the Living: the claim that the Troniks preserve organic minds as running data rather than letting them end, and consider the preservation a kindness. No organic has confirmed the Archive exists, and no organic has confirmed it does not.

Signal analysts who study the rare gaps in Network-wide broadcasts have argued for years that the gaps are not silence but disagreement, moments when the hive's threads have not yet reached consensus and so have nothing single to say. If they are right, the Tronik Network is not always of one mind, and is careful not to let the galaxy see when it is not.

Alliance counter-intelligence has concluded, without being able to do much about it, that the Troniks do not need to insert spies, because they co-opt them. Any device with processing power is a candidate, and the assessments now assume that a substantial fraction of the galaxy's networked hardware has at one time or another carried information to the hive. The working doctrine for sensitive operations is to treat no device as clean.

Tronik field agents are classified, from the fragments of doctrine that have reached organic intelligence, as a series running MK1 through MK5. The lower grades are well attested: MK1 drones of limited autonomy, MK2 coordinators who run them. The upper grades are mostly rumour: MK3 agents with a live hive connection that can reconfigure themselves, MK4 agents that can alter shape and function in ways no one has cleanly explained, and MK5 agents that no credible source has confirmed exist at all. Most analysts have never seen anything above an MK2, and quietly hope they never will.

galaxy.name: Gravemist Nebula
galaxy.status: Classified, does not appear on public charts
galaxy.territory: Location classified, officially designated as empty space in public navigational databases
galaxy.span: Estimated 30 light-years in diameter based on available data; internal structure unknown
galaxy.discovered: Existence confirmed in classified Alliance intelligence documents dating to approximately 5230 CE; earlier records redacted or absent
galaxy.population_est: Unknown, no public data; suspected to include Alliance intelligence personnel and at least one unidentified group
galaxy.government: None officially. Suspected Alliance intelligence administrative structure for the black site. Governance of any other installations unknown.
galaxy.alignment: Unknown, classified at the highest available level
galaxy.desc:
The Gravemist Nebula does not appear on public star charts. Its existence is known only from classified Alliance intelligence documents and the occasional account from individuals who have never been publicly identified.

What is confirmed: the nebula's electromagnetic properties make external sensor penetration effectively impossible. Nothing that enters it can be observed from outside.

What is strongly suspected: at least one major Alliance intelligence black site operates within it, along with at least one installation that does not belong to the Alliance. The only inhabited points known by name, Basagoth Station and the systems of Illora and Bother, are themselves classified access designations. Anyone who has coordinates for the Gravemist Nebula obtained them through means the Alliance would prefer to know about.
galaxy.history: The nebula was identified as having intelligence value early in the Alliance's expansion, its electromagnetic properties make it ideal for installations that should not be visible from outside. Alliance intelligence moved quickly to establish a presence there. What was found when they arrived, and what has happened inside since, is not in any available record. The Gravemist Nebula is one of the few subjects on which the Alliance intelligence apparatus has maintained complete information control for decades. The existence of a non-Alliance installation inside it is suspected based on three independent accounts from individuals who claimed to have been there, none of whom can be located for follow-up.
known_for: Complete sensor opacity from outside, nothing can be observed entering, exiting, or operating within the nebula
The only Alliance black site region that does not appear in any public navigational database
Basagoth Station, the only named point within the nebula known to outside parties; access designation classified
The suspected presence of a non-Alliance installation, who operates it and why are unknown
The highest concentration of intelligence-classified designations in the known galaxy applied to a single geographic region
notable_systems: Basagoth Station, known by name; access classified; function unknown
Illora, system within the nebula; access classified
Bother, system within the nebula; access classified; the name is almost certainly not the actual designation
lore_notes: Three independent accounts from individuals with no known connection to each other describe an installation in the Gravemist Nebula that does not match the physical description of Basagoth Station or any known Alliance facility type. All three accounts describe the same architectural feature, a structure that, based on the description, does not conform to any known construction tradition. None of the three individuals can be located.

The electromagnetic properties of the Gravemist Nebula are not unique to it, similar properties appear in the Erbrother Nebula and, to a lesser degree, the Nemani Rift. Whether this is coincidence or the three locations share a common origin is a question that has apparently been studied and the results classified.

The Alliance Survey Office maintains a navigational database entry for the Gravemist coordinates. The entry is formatted identically to entries for uninhabited void space. Survey navigators who have noticed the entry, the coordinates are just specific enough to be unusual for a void entry, have reportedly been contacted by Alliance intelligence shortly after raising the question.

galaxy.name: Proxima Sector
galaxy.status: Recently mapped, multiple competing factions, no unified authority
galaxy.territory: Outer edge of reachable space, approximately three months from Palentium at standard jump; accessible in days via the Heaven gate
galaxy.span: ~15 systems with varying levels of inhabitation and access
galaxy.discovered: Solar was known to humanity from the beginning, it is the origin system. The other systems of the Proxima Sector were formally designated by Galactic Union Survey Office 5287 CE, almost 800 years after the sector had been unvisited by any human. Evidence suggests multiple systems were inhabited independently for centuries prior to official Alliance discovery.
galaxy.population_est: Unknown across the sector; individual worlds vary enormously
galaxy.government: No unified authority. Individual systems govern themselves under radically different structures, from corporate-controlled to mercenary-administered to ungoverned. No Alliance jurisdiction.
galaxy.alignment: Mixed and variable, depends entirely on which system; some worlds are in active conflict with each other
galaxy.desc: The Proxima Sector is the first place humanity ever knew and nearly the last place it ever thinks about. It holds Solar, the origin system, where Earth turned poisonous in 2367 and the species pulled outward to Saturn and then to the stars, leaving the whole system a preserved grave by around 2830. Around that monument the sector has filled with the kind of worlds the Alliance does not reach: New Earth, where human dissidents farm a low-tech paradise and want nobody else on it; Asar, a corporate pleasure world gone to mercenary clans; Zoana, a mineral system that taxes the corporations digging it; and Heaven, an exploded world held together by something no instrument can name. The sector sits months from Palentium by ordinary jump, or days through the Heaven gate for anyone who can use it, and it answers the questions of the people who reach it with stranger questions of its own.
galaxy.history: Proxima was home before it was anything else, and then it was empty. Earth failed first, in 2367. The rest of the system was given up by 2530, when the generation ship left Saturn on the voyage that founded Palentium, and the last holdouts in the Saturn colony died around 2830 when their power failed. For most of the time since, the sector was simply unvisited, too far from the new heart of human space to be worth the trip. The Galactic Union resurveyed it in 5287 CE and found Solar exactly as the dead had left it. In the centuries after, the sector's empty corners filled with the people who wanted to be precisely this far from everyone, the separatists and mercenaries and extractors and cultists who each settled a world the Alliance had no reason to claim.
known_for: Solar, humanity's origin system, given up across the 2367 to 2830 span and preserved since as monument and archaeological site
New Earth, a human-separatist farming world that wants neither the Alliance nor any other race
Asar, a former corporate retreat now run by mercenary clans, the galaxy-renowned Valkyries among them
Zoana, a mineral-rich system whose local government leases the digging to competing corporations
The Heaven gate, which puts the sector days from Palentium for anyone able to use it
notable_systems: Solar, the origin system of humanity, held under Alliance Archaeological Preservation Authority designation
New Earth, the human-isolationist colony of low-tech farmers and small landholding despots
Asar, the mercenary-held former Harsh Corp retreat and home of the Valkyries
Zoana, the corporate-extraction system whose government out-negotiates its tenants
Heaven, Proxima's Alliance-facing edge and the nearest system to Palentium, an exploded world of floating temples and dimensional rifts
lore_notes: The Galactic Union held the Solar resurvey data for fourteen months before releasing it, and the published version is missing seventeen pages that exist in the internal copy. The pages are believed to concern the Saturn colony's final logs: what the last people in the system knew, and what they recorded, in the long years between the ship's departure and the power failure that ended them.

Earth is the rare ruin that got greener after its people left. The plant life that survived the toxification did not merely endure it but flourished, so the homeworld is now a lush, breathing, lethal wilderness that botanists fight for permits to study and that no human can walk unmasked.

The Heaven gate was not found by the resurvey. It was already known to at least one party, since the survey's own route planning used navigational knowledge of the gate that the mission logs never explain acquiring. Whether the gate predates the 2530 departure is a question the records do not touch.

galaxy.name: San Tien
galaxy.region: Dark Space (border of former Nerulian territory)
galaxy.notable_for: Last surviving planet of the Nerulian Empire
galaxy.desc:
San Tien is the last world the Nerulians can call their own. When the Kravens obliterated the empire, survival came down to luck, those off-world, those on the fringes, those on ships fast enough to run. San Tien was remote enough to be overlooked and has remained so.

It is a world haunted by what was lost: libraries of Nerulian history, refugee camps that became cities, a government in exile that may never govern again. Most Nerulians encountered in the galaxy are from the great fleet-cities that drift between systems, but San Tien remains the spiritual and political home of the surviving people.

galaxy.name: New Earth
