galaxy.notable_for: Human-separatist colony of low-tech farmers and small landholding despots
galaxy.desc: New Earth is where the galaxy's human malcontents went to be left alone. Roughly two hundred years ago, settlers who could not stomach the Alliance's rules, its corporations, or its other races finished a light terraforming pass and made the world into the private paradise they felt they were owed. Today it is mostly farmland worked at a deliberately low technological level by humans who want neither the Alliance nor anyone non-human anywhere near them. The corporations mostly stay away, because there is no great mineral wealth here and the world is too far from anywhere to export food at a profit, so the little corporate interest that exists is easy to wave off. The land is carved into private holdings whose owners permit settlement near their towns, which is a generous way to describe a patchwork of small despots each living out a colonial-rancher fantasy on a world with no one set above them.

galaxy.name: Titania
galaxy.notable_for: Corporate morondium warzone; only source of morondium in the galaxy
galaxy.desc: The Titania system is defined by morondium, a living crystalline compound found nowhere else in the galaxy that grants metals regenerative properties when infused. Every major corporation wants it. The result is a permanent corporate warzone on Titania 2, overseen by Nova cruisers enforcing a strict ground-combat-only agreement. The phrase "Warrior of Titan" refers to anyone who has served time here, it is a mark of toughness earned the hard way.

galaxy.name: Sirius
galaxy.notable_for: Major trade and commercial hub, one of the most visited systems
galaxy.desc: Sirius is the commercial heartbeat of Alliance Space, a wealthy, densely populated system with some of the busiest spaceports in the galaxy. If you need to buy something, fence something, or find someone, Sirius is the first place to look. Its orbital stations are cities in their own right, and its surface worlds host the headquarters of several major corporations. It is also, inevitably, a hotbed of crime, corporate espionage and political intrigue.

galaxy.name: Orion
galaxy.notable_for: Five-world system; home of the Galactic Union; birthplace of OrionWorks
galaxy.desc: The Orion system is the political and corporate centre of the known galaxy, five worlds across every stage of construction, ruin, and ambition. Home to the Galactic Union and the ghost of OrionWorks, the organisation that built artificial planets and may have started the Tronik War. It is heavily defended, intensely surveilled, and the kind of place where what you know and who you know matters more than what you can do.

galaxy.name: Aderan
galaxy.notable_for: Galaxy's largest for-profit prison; home of Ridge Racing, Survivor and Blood Bowl
galaxy.desc: The Aderan system was the site of the first corporate war in galactic history, a conflict that ended with Aderan Prime destroyed and everyone finally understanding that there was no upper limit to what corporate warfare could do. The surviving world, Aderan 3, found a highly profitable replacement economy: the galaxy's largest for-profit prison, and the broadcast rights to three of its most watched shows.

galaxy.name: Mangara
galaxy.faction: Contested, Hakari clans vs Jaulaus tribes
galaxy.notable_for: Homeworld of Hakari and Jaulaus; continuous civil war; Alliance embargo
galaxy.desc: Mangara is the homeworld of the Hakari and Jaulaus and one of the most uncomfortable chapters in Alliance history. Exploited by the Nerulian Empire and then by corporate interests, placed under Alliance embargo to protect what remains of its traditional life, and still burning from an inter-species civil war that has never stopped. Protected on paper, exploited in practice, ignored in fact.

galaxy.name: Carach System
galaxy.notable_for: Skalan homeworld Caragh; sacred ground of a species that survived an attempted extinction
galaxy.desc: The Carach system is the heart of Skalan civilisation. Caragh, the homeworld, is closed to non-Skalans without exception or negotiation. The system is self-governed under a Warrior Council elected by combat reputation. Skalan patrol vessels enforce the system perimeter without legal frameworks or diplomatic language.

galaxy.name: Seigh System
galaxy.notable_for: Most lethal natural environment in the known galaxy; Skalan rite of passage
galaxy.desc: Seigh is a separate system from Carach, administered by the Skalan as a closed training world. Every survey that has assessed the planet reaches the same conclusion: it is the most lethal naturally occurring environment in the known galaxy. Non-Skalans are not welcome. The fauna does not check jurisdiction before acting.

galaxy.name: Berilia
galaxy.notable_for: Patriark homeworld; most advanced cloning facilities in the galaxy
galaxy.desc: Berilia is the Patriark homeworld and the quiet centre of the galaxy's most important dependency: resurrection technology. The Patriarks built no army. Instead they spent centuries making themselves indispensable. The cloning infrastructure on Berilia underpins the Alliance's promise of continuity, and the Patriarks know exactly what it would cost everyone if they renegotiated their terms.

galaxy.name: Ishtar
galaxy.notable_for: Arms Corp HQ; largest manufacturing world in the galaxy; volcanic terrain; toxic atmosphere
galaxy.desc:
Ishtar exists to produce. The volcanic geology provides near-limitless geothermal energy. The crust is mineral-dense enough that raw materials are extracted metres from where they are processed. The atmosphere is permanently toxic from centuries of unregulated industrial output, workers wear breathers outside sealed zones.

The weapons that come out of Ishtar's foundries are carried by soldiers on every side of every war in the galaxy.

galaxy.name: Damph
galaxy.notable_for: Only known source of Coronthia in the galaxy; frozen surface; intense blue-collar worker culture
galaxy.desc:
Damph is a frozen hellhole that happens to sit on the only known deposits of Coronthia in the galaxy, a super-dense fuel compound of extraordinary power and extraordinary instability.

The workers who extract it know exactly how much leverage that gives them. Governed by a patchwork of worker clans, tough, territorial, deeply suspicious of outsiders, and fiercely proud of what they do. Corporate interests are present but operate carefully.

galaxy.name: Alsa
galaxy.notable_for: Most fertile worlds in the galaxy; primary food source for Alliance Space
galaxy.desc: Alsa is where the galaxy eats. The system's worlds are extraordinarily fertile, geology, climate and water distribution aligned in a combination that produces agricultural output unmatched anywhere in known space. Most of the food consumed across Alliance Space originates here in some form. Alsa is quiet, green, and largely pastoral, and the most heavily insured system in the Alliance, protected by standing navy contracts that make attacking it extremely inadvisable.

galaxy.name: Ash
galaxy.notable_for: Gateway to the Nemani Rift; military staging point; salvage culture; glory-seekers and rift pilots
galaxy.desc: Ash would be an unremarkable frontier system if it were not sitting at the edge of the Nemani Rift. The Alliance military maintains a permanent and substantial presence here, monitoring the Rift and ensuring that whatever is on the other side stays on the other side. Around the military has grown an ecosystem of salvage yards, scrappers, black market dealers, and pilots who come here specifically to attempt the Rift. Most of those pilots do not come back. The ones who do come back wealthy, famous, or permanently changed.

galaxy.name: Palentium
galaxy.notable_for: First human-discovered planet in Alliance Space; tropical climate; luxury tourism; pervasive corruption
galaxy.desc: Palentium was the first planet humans set foot on in what is now Alliance Space, a fact the tourism industry has milked for centuries. The world is genuinely beautiful: tropical, warm, blessed with long coastlines and an atmosphere that requires no modification. The corruption is so deeply embedded into Palentium's institutions that most residents treat it as a natural feature of the climate. Everything is for sale on Palentium if you know who to ask.

factions.name: Galactic Union
presence: Galactic presence in all major regions
factions.desc: The Galactic Union is the largest megacorporation in the galaxy, which undersells it, because the Galactic Union is not one corporation but thousands. It is a union of member companies spanning finance, manufacturing, communications, shipping, and nearly every other field, governed by its own internal senate and executive council. What sets it apart is self-sufficiency. The GU imports almost nothing; when it needs a resource or a capability, it acquires the source rather than buying the product, folding whole industries into itself until it depends on no one. It is one of the major manufacturers in known space and a relentless exporter, and it answers, in the end, only to itself. It is a corporate power, distinct from the Alliance, whatever outsiders assume.
known_for: The largest megacorporation in the galaxy, a union of thousands of member companies
Near-total self-sufficiency: it acquires resources and capabilities rather than importing them
One of the galaxy's major manufacturers and a relentless exporter
Self-governed by its own internal senate and executive council, seated on Orion 3
The classified GU contingency protocols, contents unknown
factions.legal_standing: Fully legal; operates within Alliance law (largely because it helped write it)
factions.subtitle: Not a Corporation but a Thousand, Answerable Only to Itself
factions.quote: "The Union does not buy what it can own, and it does not import what it can absorb. Give it long enough and it needs no one, which is precisely the position it has spent centuries arranging." (Alliance trade-commission assessment)
factions.history:
The Galactic Union began as a handful of companies that found cooperation more profitable than competition, and it never stopped adding members. Over centuries it grew into a union of thousands, a corporation made of corporations, and it settled on the principle that has defined it since: dependence is a weakness, and the cure for dependence is acquisition. Rather than import what it needed, the GU bought whoever made it.
Its grandest undertaking was Orion. With OrionWorks, the GU built the only manufactured capital in history, world by world, and seated its own governance there. OrionWorks is gone now, lost with the Tronik War that one persistent account lays at its door, but the Union it helped raise to dominance remains, larger and more self-contained than ever.
factions.politics:
The GU is governed as a federation of its member companies, through an internal senate and an executive council seated on Orion 3. This is its own apparatus and not the Alliance's; the Union is a corporate power that coexists with the political union and frequently outweighs it, without ever being it. Its strength is not a seat in anyone's government but the plain fact that so much of the galaxy's manufacturing, finance, and shipping happens inside the GU, on the GU's terms.
Self-sufficiency is the doctrine under all of it. The Union has spent its whole existence removing its own dependencies, buying suppliers and competitors and entire industries until it imports almost nothing and exports a great deal. A power that needs no one is very hard to pressure, and the GU has arranged to need no one. What its classified contingency protocols are for, no one outside the executive council knows, and the council behaves as though the question was answered long ago.
factions.culture: The Union's culture is the patience of an institution that means to outlast every rival by owning the conditions of its own survival. It does not gamble; it acquires. It prefers ownership to alliance and capability to contract, and quiet dominance to open display. Inside its thousands of member companies the competition is fierce, but it is competition within a family that closes ranks the instant the family itself is threatened.

relations.name: OrionWorks
relations.note: Its partner in building the artificial worlds and Ramirez, now defunct, and the likeliest source of the Tronik War. The GU inherited the legacy and the suspicion together, and keeps both buried in Orion's sealed districts.

relations.name: The Alliance
relations.note: The political union the GU coexists with and frequently overshadows. The two are separate, whatever outsiders assume, and the GU is content to let the Alliance govern so long as governing does not interfere with owning.

relations.name: Arms Corp & Yamato
relations.note: The other two powers of the Big 3, kept close and watched closely. The GU is first among the three and careful never to be heard saying so.

relations.name: The galaxy's industries
relations.note: Every supplier, competitor, and capability the GU does not yet own is, in the long run, something it intends to. Its preferred relationship with any business that matters is ownership.

factions.name: Arms Corp
factions.desc: Arms Corp is the largest weapons, military hardware, and industrial manufacturing corporation in the galaxy, which is a polite way of saying it sells weapons to both sides of most conflicts and considers this a neutral commercial position. Based on Ishtar, the single largest industrial world in existence, it makes everything from personal sidearms to capital ship components and sells to anyone with sufficient credit and appropriate permits. Its private military force is widely understood to be larger and better equipped than any standing national army, including the Alliance navy, which continues to buy from Arms Corp regardless. The corporation maintains formal legal compliance with Alliance law, which works out conveniently because Arms Corp had significant input into which laws got written. Its relationship with the Alliance senate is described internally as transactional, which is the honest version of most political relationships but rarely the one that gets written into histories.
factions.subtitle: Weapons for Every Side of Every War
factions.quote: "We do not take sides. Taking sides would be bad for business, and frankly unfair to the other customer." (Arms Corp sales doctrine, unofficial)
factions.history:
Arms Corp grew out of Ishtar's foundries and never looked back. It learned early that the most durable position in any conflict is to supply it, and it built that single idea into a galactic empire: arm everyone, and become too useful to every war for any side to destroy.
Generations of selling to all comers made Arms Corp indispensable, and indispensable made it untouchable. By the time the Alliance thought seriously about regulation, the corporation had already armed the navy that would enforce it and had a heavy hand in drafting the rules.
factions.politics:
Arms Corp is a vertically integrated megacorp that owns its raw materials, its foundries, its workforce, and the world all three sit on. The Industrial Directorate governs Ishtar outright, and the rest of the company runs on the same logic of total ownership.
Two instruments give it sovereign-grade power. The first is a private military better equipped than most national navies. The second is the Arms Corp permit system, a parallel licensing regime that decides who may legally own restricted hardware, a power that elsewhere belongs only to governments. Its grip on the Alliance senate is transactional and seldom needs stating aloud.
factions.culture: Arms Corp pairs real engineering pride with a calm, practised amorality. It does not hate anyone. It sells to everyone, and it treats taking sides as a failure of professionalism. To the corporation a war is a market and a treaty is a downturn, and a weapon is a very well-made product that happens to be pointed at someone. The people who design Ishtar's guns are craftsmen, and what happens downrange is, by policy, none of their concern.

relations.name: The Alliance
relations.note: Sells the Alliance navy its weapons and helped write the laws it obeys. The Alliance cannot discipline its own armourer, and both sides know it.

relations.name: Every belligerent
relations.note: Arms Corp arms all sides of all conflicts as doctrine. A war with only one armed side is, to Arms Corp, money left on the table.

relations.name: The Ishtar workforce
relations.note: Eight hundred million workers it must keep paid, filtered, and above all unorganised, because it watched the Damph clans take a planet and will not arm a sequel.

relations.name: Zang'Hai
relations.note: The source of the cheap pirated copies of Arms Corp weapons that fill the galaxy's black markets. Endlessly litigated, never actually stopped.

known_for: Largest weapons manufacturer in the galaxy
Ishtar: an entire world devoted to industrial production
Private military forces that rival national navies in equipment quality
The Arms Corp permit system, a parallel licensing regime for restricted hardware
Military contracts with every major faction including ostensibly hostile ones
factions.legal_standing: Fully legal; operates within Alliance law with extensive permit infrastructure

factions.name: Yamato Corporation
factions.desc: Yamato is the least publicly visible of the Big 3, which is not a coincidence. It manufactures, finances, and contracts military work, but its defining characteristic is that it is genuinely difficult to catch it doing any of these things. Yamato subsidiaries and affiliated brands appear throughout the economy in patterns designed to obscure the parent connection, and the obscuring has been done so thoroughly for so long that analysts treat the opacity itself as the product. Yotoma, its technology division, operates with a public commercial identity. The rest of Yamato does not. The corporation predates the Alliance, has outlasted multiple governments that attempted to regulate it into transparency, and appears to have learned something from each failure that it has applied to the next. What Yamato actually owns is not publicly known. This is the intended situation.
factions.subtitle: The Corporation You Cannot Map
factions.quote: "We have reviewed your list of Yamato holdings. We can confirm only that it is incomplete, and we cannot tell you which parts." (Yamato compliance response to an Alliance audit)
factions.history: Yamato is older than the Alliance, which is the root of everything else about it. Across the rise and fall of the governments that came after it, the corporation learned that the ones which last are the ones that cannot be found to regulate, and it spent centuries acting on the lesson. Where its eventual peers in the Big 3 grew loud and visible, Yamato did the opposite on purpose, dissolving into a fog of subsidiaries and affiliations until the fog itself was the asset. Every government that tried to force it open failed, and Yamato studied each failure and grew harder to open.
factions.politics: Yamato is a deliberately unmappable web. Yotoma, its technology division, wears a normal commercial face; the rest of the corporation does not. Power is exercised through ownership no one can prove and relationships no one can document, which makes Yamato nearly impossible to confront, since there is no agreed place to aim. Its hold on Sirius is total and invisible, and it is the suspected money behind the Tanaka Syndicate, an allegation it denies with the ease of an institution that has been denying things for centuries.
factions.culture: Yamato's culture is patience and silence. It treats visibility as a risk and information as the one asset worth truly guarding, and it has the longest institutional memory of any power in Alliance space. It does not announce and it does not boast, and it is never the corporation you see coming.

relations.name: The Alliance
relations.note: Has outlasted every government that tried to regulate it into transparency, and quietly helped several of them fail. Compliant on paper and unaccountable in practice.

relations.name: Tanaka Syndicate
relations.note: The suspected money behind the street family, which gives Yamato deniable muscle and a reach into Sirius crime it never has to admit owning.

relations.name: Yotoma
relations.note: Its technology division and its one genuinely public face, ordinary enough that most of the galaxy never connects it to the parent.

known_for: Deliberate opacity: corporate structure is intentionally difficult to map
Yotoma, its semi-independent technology division
The longest corporate history of the Big 3
Subsidiaries and affiliated brands throughout all economic sectors
Resilience: has outlasted multiple governments that attempted regulatory action
factions.legal_standing: Technically fully compliant; enforcement of applicable regulations has historically proven difficult

factions.name: Malivaux
factions.desc: Malivaux occupies a singular position in the luxury market: it manufactures nothing for the general public and considers this a selling point rather than a limitation. The product range spans the entirety of material existence, from furniture and personal vehicles to spaceships, weapons, jewellery, clothing, architectural fittings, cutlery, and objects whose category resists easy description, but the philosophy is consistent across all of it. Every piece is built to order, individually finished by artisans whose names appear in internal records but never in advertising, and priced at levels that exclude almost everyone in the galaxy, which is precisely the point. A Malivaux chair is as much a declaration of social position as it is something to sit on. A Malivaux courier ship is designed with the same obsessive attention to form as a Malivaux sidearm, and both carry the same implicit message, that the owner exists outside the category of people who have to make practical compromises. The corporation maintains deliberate scarcity across every product line, never overproduces, and has no mass-market subsidiary quietly operating under another name. Clientele includes galactic heads of state, senior megacorp executives, and collectors who have been on waiting lists for years and regard the waiting as part of the ownership experience.
factions.subtitle: Everything, Made Once, for People Who Never Compromise
factions.quote: "We do not have a catalogue, a sale, or a second one of anything. If you have to ask the waiting time, the answer is longer than you have." (Malivaux atelier)
factions.history: Malivaux made itself singular by refusing the one thing every other manufacturer does, which is scale. It builds nothing for the general public and treats that as its whole value. From an undisclosed seat it has spent generations making one of everything, furniture and starships and sidearms alike, each piece built to order and finished by artisans whose names never leave the internal records.
factions.politics: Malivaux's power is the power of the unattainable. It cannot be undercut, because it does not compete on price, and it cannot be copied, because the copy by definition is not a Malivaux. Its clientele is the upper sliver of galactic wealth, heads of state and megacorp executives among them, and its real product is the line it draws between those people and everyone else.
factions.culture: Malivaux is the cult of the bespoke raised to a corporate principle. It overbuilds for beauty rather than performance, keeps deliberate scarcity across every line, and regards a years-long waiting list as part of the experience rather than a flaw in it. To Malivaux, a thing worth owning is a thing no one else can have.

relations.name: The galactic elite
relations.note: Heads of state, megacorp executives, and collectors who treat the waiting list as a privilege. Malivaux's market is precisely the people who can have anything and want what others cannot.

relations.name: Lansing Corp
relations.note: The other great overbuilder, though Lansing perfects function past the point of profit while Malivaux perfects status past the point of sense. Two answers to the question of what excess is for.

relations.name: The mass market
relations.note: Everyone Malivaux refuses to sell to, which is nearly everyone, and the contrast that gives every Malivaux piece its meaning.

known_for: Bespoke luxury goods spanning weapons, vehicles, ships, furniture, and more
Every item made to individual order, with no mass production, ever
Clientele limited to the upper 1% of galactic wealth
Designs that function as both status objects and works of art
A waiting list policy that has never been publicly disclosed
factions.legal_standing: Fully legal; operates across all high-end luxury markets

factions.name: Kintech
factions.desc: Kintech is a Nerulian-led corporation specialising in what its marketing calls tactical solutions, a designation broad enough to cover weapons, security hardware, and an unspecified range of services that clients prefer not to have documented. The official position is that Kintech has no ties to the San Tien Nerulian pirate networks. Most intelligence analysts do not find this convincing, and most have noted for some years that not finding it convincing has produced no consequences whatsoever. What is verifiable: Kintech equipment appears in disproportionate numbers in corporate military units, private security forces, and locations where its presence raises questions that nobody with authority to answer them seems motivated to address. Kintech declines to discuss its client roster, which is its legal right, and everyone else's practical problem.
factions.subtitle: Tactical Solutions, and a Client List Nobody Will Confirm
factions.quote: "Kintech does not ask what the equipment is for. That incuriosity is the most valuable thing we sell." (Kintech account manager)
factions.history: Kintech built its business in the space the legal market leaves open, the demand for capable weapons sold without questions. Under Nerulian leadership it cultivated exactly the clients other manufacturers screened out, and it made discretion its product as much as the hardware, with adaptability engineered in so a buyer never had to specify too precisely what a thing was for. The San Tien connection it denies has been the open secret of its entire existence, a denial maintained not because anyone believes it but because no one has managed to make disbelieving it matter.
factions.politics: Kintech thrives in the space between legal and grey, where its incuriosity about its clients is a feature rather than a liability. Its equipment turns up in disproportionate numbers in corporate militaries, private security, and places where its presence raises questions no one in authority seems moved to answer. Its client roster is undisclosed, which is Kintech's legal right and everyone else's practical problem.
factions.culture: Kintech carries a Nerulian design philosophy and a Nerulian comfort with being feared. It builds capable, adaptable, faintly sinister hardware and sells it without moral inventory, treating the refusal to ask questions as a professional standard. The reputation for menace is no accident; it is quietly part of the brand.

relations.name: The Nerulian Pirate Fleet
relations.note: The San Tien networks Kintech officially has nothing to do with, and whose vessels run conspicuously on Kintech equipment. Every serious assessment draws the line, and nothing comes of drawing it.

relations.name: Corporate militaries & private security
relations.note: The forces that buy Kintech's adaptable hardware and value its silence about what they do with it.

relations.name: Alliance intelligence
relations.note: Convinced of the pirate connection and unable to make the conviction matter, which has itself become an established fact of the region.

known_for: Tactical weapons and equipment for corporate security forces
Alleged but unproven ties to San Tien Nerulian operations
A client roster that is not publicly disclosed and has never needed to be
Equipment found in unusual numbers in private military contexts
Nerulian leadership and design philosophy throughout its product line
factions.legal_standing: Technically legal; subject to ongoing Alliance intelligence monitoring

factions.name: Nakamura Corp
factions.desc: Nakamura Corp is the galaxy's pre-eminent commercial magic institution. While magic is understood and used by several other organisations, Nakamura has patented, systematised, and priced it at levels that ensure only the wealthiest individuals and institutions can access the full range of services. The corporation provides magic-enhanced devices, spell procurement, esoteric research, magical transport, and what it describes as metaphysical consultancy, a category broad enough to accommodate whatever a high-paying client requires and flexible enough not to raise regulatory questions. Nakamura is scrupulously legal, maintains excellent relations with the Berilian Order, and charges fees that most Alliance citizens will never in their lifetimes be able to consider, which is, from Nakamura's perspective, exactly how an exclusive service should work.
factions.subtitle: Magic With a Price Tag, and a Patent on the Spell
factions.quote: "Magic is not rare. Legal, licensed, reliable magic is extremely rare, and we hold the patents. The difference is the whole business." (Nakamura prospectus)
factions.history: Nakamura's achievement was not discovering magic, which plenty of others had, but turning it into property. Early on it did the unglamorous work no mystic bothered with, documenting spell-derived processes precisely enough to patent them, and then defending those patents with a legal apparatus as serious as its esoteric one. The partnership with the Berilian Order was the masterstroke: by aligning itself with the body that polices magic, Nakamura made its monopoly not merely profitable but lawful, and it has priced accordingly ever since.
factions.politics: Nakamura's power is exclusivity wrapped in legality. It is the only corporation holding valid patents on spell-derived processes, and it keeps scrupulous compliance and excellent relations with the Berilian Order, which polices magic and could end Nakamura with a ruling. That relationship is the whole foundation: Nakamura sells what the Order permits, at prices the Order's blessing makes possible.
factions.culture: Nakamura treats the numinous as inventory. It is corporate, precise, and entirely comfortable charging civilisation-scale fees for the supernatural, on the reasoning that an exclusive service should exclude. There is no mysticism in its boardroom, only the patient monetisation of the one product almost no one else may legally sell.

relations.name: The Berilian Order
relations.note: The magic-policing authority Nakamura keeps on excellent terms, because the Order's permission is the difference between Nakamura's business and a crime. Here cooperation is survival, not courtesy.

relations.name: The galactic wealthy
relations.note: The individuals and institutions who can afford the most expensive legal magic in existence, which is the only clientele Nakamura is built to serve.

relations.name: Biocom
relations.note: The other Berilia firm working the seam between the spiritual and the commercial. Where Biocom binds spirits into hardware, Nakamura sells the spellcraft itself, and the two circle the same regulated waters.

known_for: Commercial magic services, devices, spells, transport, research
The most expensive legal magic services in the galaxy
Formal cooperation agreements with the Berilian Order
Esoteric research into spell theory and application
The only corporation to hold valid patents on spell-derived processes
factions.legal_standing: Fully legal; Berilian Order compliance certified

factions.name: Zang'Hai
presence: Galactic, cheap product in most inhabited systems
factions.desc: Zang'Hai is the galaxy's dominant mass-market manufacturer, and its method is discussed so openly that the espionage charges feel almost quaint: find what another corporation makes well, copy it, and sell it for a fraction of the price. The charges are constant and have never produced a conviction, which has less to do with Zang'Hai's lawyers than with where it lives. Zang'Hai was born on Damph and never left, and the Worker Clans who supply most of its labour supply something more valuable as well: the criminal networks that acquire whatever the engineers are told to copy. The clans steal it and Zang'Hai rebuilds it, and the trail dissolves into a separate payroll in a separate jurisdiction. Its products are everywhere, not because they are good but because they are cheap and they work, and most of the galaxy cares more about the price than the principle. The RX Generic medical division runs the same method on pharmaceuticals.
factions.subtitle: The Galaxy's Cheapest Everything, Copied From Someone Else's Best
factions.quote: "We do not steal designs. We employ people who steal designs, on a separate payroll, in a separate jurisdiction, and we buy the results at arm's length. Go ahead and write an indictment out of that." (a Zang'Hai legal officer, off the record)
factions.history:
Zang'Hai started on Damph as a maker of cheap, functional goods, built on the cheapest labour in Alliance space, the frozen-world clans no one else wanted to hire. For a long while it was nothing more than a competent low-end manufacturer that happened to sit on a hard planet.
Its leap to dominance came from joining two things Damph already had. The clans ran galaxy-wide smuggling and theft networks; Zang'Hai had the factories and the engineers. So the company stopped inventing and started copying at scale. The clans acquire a rival's successful product, Zang'Hai reverse-engineers it, and a cheaper version reaches the market before the original has paid for its own development. That is why Zang'Hai never left Damph. Both halves of the method live there.
factions.politics:
In public Zang'Hai is an ordinary corporation with a board, a logistics network, and a very good legal department. The legal department is the important part, because the method only works while nothing can be proven.
In practice it is a corporation that does not own the world it sits on, so it governs by negotiation and by deniability. The legitimate half, design and manufacture and distribution, runs from the boardroom. The acquisition half runs through arm's-length arrangements with clan bosses and a thicket of shell companies, built so that the theft and the manufacture never legally meet. The two halves are kept apart on purpose, and lawyers patrol the seam.
factions.culture: Zang'Hai has a culture with no pretension to excellence. It does not want to make the best product. It wants to make a product that is good enough, half the price, and on every shelf, and it is proud of that ambition. Its engineers take real satisfaction in stripping a rival's flagship to its principles and rebuilding it cheaper. Its executives are convinced that the premium corporations are the actual thieves, overcharging for what ought to be affordable, and that Zang'Hai is only correcting the market. The shamelessness is complete, and in its way sincere.

relations.name: Worker Clans of Damph
relations.note: Workforce, landlords, and acquisition network in one. The clans build Zang'Hai's products and steal the designs it copies, which gives them leverage no ordinary labour force has. Mutual need, mutual blackmail, no end in sight.

relations.name: The premium corporations
relations.note: The brands whose flagships reappear months later as cheaper Zang'Hai copies. They allege endlessly and have never made a charge stick.

relations.name: Alliance regulators
relations.note: Decades of espionage investigations, every one inconclusive. Whether that means clean hands or clean tradecraft is a matter of taste.

known_for: Mass-market copies of competitors' products at a fraction of the price
Industrial espionage run through Worker Clan criminal networks: constant, deniable, never proven
RX Generic, the medical division working the same copy-and-undercut method
Cheap product in nearly every inhabited system
Headquartered on Damph and tied to the Worker Clans for both labour and acquisition
factions.legal_standing: Formally legal; industrial espionage investigations consistently inconclusive

factions.name: TORC Corp
factions.hq: Torc Prime (Torc Federation), Alliance Space HQ: Orion 3
factions.desc: TORC Corp is the commercial and industrial arm of the Torc Federation, though it maintains operational independence from the Federation government and sells to anyone who can pay, including governments the Federation is nominally in dispute with. TORC's product philosophy is refreshingly practical in a market full of overcomplicated alternatives: design things that work under any conditions, can be serviced with tools that actually exist, and do not require the manufacturer's ongoing support to remain functional. The result is equipment that is rarely the most advanced available but is disproportionately trusted by people who work in environments where failure has immediate physical consequences. TORC products are standard kit for long-range exploration crews, colonial operations, and frontier settlers who cannot afford to be wrong about their gear. Harsh Corp, acquired by TORC and kept as a distinct label for its brand equity, covers the urban personal protection market.
factions.subtitle: Gear That Works Where It Counts and Fixes With Tools You Have
factions.quote: "The most advanced option is the one that fails where no one can repair it. We build the second most advanced, and you come home." (TORC field manual)
factions.history: TORC grew up as the Torc Federation's industrial arm, but it made its name on the frontier rather than at home. Its reputation was built one disaster-that-did-not-happen at a time, by explorers and colonists whose TORC gear kept working in conditions that killed fancier equipment, and word of that reliability travelled faster than any marketing. The decision to sell to anyone who pays, the Federation's rivals included, came from the same practical streak: a tool does not care about politics, and neither, officially, does TORC. The Harsh Corp acquisition later gave it the urban market its frontier name could never reach.
factions.politics: TORC's power is trust earned where failure is fatal. Its gear is rarely the most advanced, and it is disproportionately what people choose when being wrong about their equipment means dying. That reputation, the TORC quality standard, travels galaxy-wide and sells itself, and TORC reinforces it by selling to everyone without restriction, its own government's rivals included.
factions.culture: TORC is plainspoken, durable, and faintly contemptuous of cleverness for its own sake. It values reliability over sophistication and independence over lock-in, and it built that ethic into a brand frontier people stake their lives on. It keeps Harsh Corp as a separate label for the urban market, on the sound logic that a good name is worth more intact than absorbed.

relations.name: The Torc Federation
relations.note: Its origin and namesake, kept at enough distance that TORC can sell to the Federation's adversaries without political complications anyone is forced to notice.

relations.name: Harsh Corp
relations.note: Its urban personal-defence label, acquired and kept distinct for its brand equity, covering the city market TORC's frontier reputation does not reach.

relations.name: Frontier & colonial customers
relations.note: Exploration crews, colonists, and settlers who trust TORC because TORC has never given them a reason not to.

known_for: Field-serviceable equipment designed for frontier and colonial use
The TORC quality standard, recognised galaxy-wide
Harsh Corp (subsidiary), urban clothing and personal defence market
Standard kit for exploration crews and colonial operations
Willingness to sell to any customer without restriction
factions.legal_standing: Fully legal

factions.name: Voran Industries
factions.desc: Voran Industries began as an aerospace corporation with ambitions in shipbuilding, and it never made them work. Its ships were unremarkable, the market was crowded, and the company slid toward collapse on its own merits. The surviving leadership made a cold calculation and pivoted entirely, taking the Aderan galactic prison contract and rebuilding the corporation around it. Today Voran runs the largest for-profit correctional network in known space, and it bills the same captive population in several directions at once: custody, labour rented to industry, broadcasts, and the branded racing gear that Ridge Racing's fame turned into a consumer empire. The aerospace heritage survives only in old documents nobody in current leadership is old enough to remember.
factions.subtitle: From Failed Rockets to the Galaxys Largest Cage
factions.quote: "We do not sell rehabilitation. We sell custody, equipment, and ratings, and we sell all three to the same customer." (Voran investor briefing, leaked)
factions.history: Voran's shipbuilding years are the part of its history it works hardest to forget. It spent a long time as an unremarkable yard in a crowded market, never quite failing and never quite succeeding, until a run of bad contracts brought it to the edge of collapse. The leadership that survived the near-death made the only bet left to them, the Aderan prison concession that no respectable corporation wanted. It proved the most profitable decision in the company's history, and the discoveries came one at a time, that inmates could be rented as labour, then broadcast as entertainment, then merchandised, each one burying the aerospace failure a little deeper.
factions.politics:
Voran runs Aderan as a vertically integrated company system through the Aderan Correctional Consortium, and it bills the same captive population four different ways. It charges for custody. It rents inmate labour to industry at rates no free worker could match. It broadcasts the prisoners as entertainment. And it sells the branded racing gear that Ridge Racing's galaxy-wide fame built into a consumer empire.
Every pillar feeds the others, and every one is billed by volume, so more prisoners, longer sentences, more dangerous work, and higher ratings all point the same way. Its clients are the Alliance justice system, corporate security departments, corporate labour buyers, and private parties who pay not to be asked questions.
factions.culture: Voran's culture is reinvention without sentiment. It took a humiliation, the aerospace collapse, and turned it into an empire, and it carries the lesson hard: nothing is sacred, everything is a line item, and the only failure that counts is the unprofitable kind. It turned a prison bloodsport into the galaxy's favourite sport and a merchandising brand, and it feels no need to apologise for any step of the journey. It is metrics-driven and unbothered by its own notoriety, comfortable being the company everyone uses and no one defends.

relations.name: The Alliance
relations.note: The justice system that outsources its convicts and its conscience to Voran, and carefully avoids looking too closely at either the conditions or the ratings.

relations.name: Lansing Corp
relations.note: They were briefly in the same business and took opposite roads to the same dead end. Lansing builds phenomenal ships and overengineers them into thin profits; Voran built forgettable ones, failed, and gave up on quality entirely for the prison trade. Neither is quite the cautionary tale it believes the other to be.

relations.name: The galaxy's audience
relations.note: Billions of viewers whose appetite for Ridge Racing, and for Blood Bowl and Survivor behind it, keeps the cells full and the contracts signed.

relations.name: Corporate labour buyers
relations.note: The corporations across Alliance space that rent Aderan's captive workforce at impossible rates and decline, on principle, to ask how the work gets done.

known_for: The largest for-profit correctional network in known space, run as the Aderan Correctional Consortium
Prison labour rented to industry across Alliance space, a major and deliberately quiet revenue stream
Ridge Racing, the single most-watched sport in the galaxy, and the branded racing-gear empire built on it
Blood Bowl and Survivor, inmate-cast broadcasts that round out the slate
A defence-equipment line for its own facilities, and a lasting notoriety for the conditions inside them
factions.legal_standing: Fully legal; operates under Alliance correctional services contract

factions.name: Santech
factions.desc: Santech is the Alliance's largest full-spectrum medical corporation. Based on Berilia, a world that has made medicine its primary export and regulatory influence its primary hobby, Santech produces pharmaceuticals, surgical hardware, prosthetics, diagnostic equipment, field medical kits, and a broad range of specialised treatments. It is not the most advanced medical corporation in the galaxy in any single area, but it is the most comprehensive, the most distributed, and the most trusted at a professional level that most institutions can actually afford. Most Alliance hospitals operate with Santech as their primary supplier because the alternatives are either more expensive, less available, or produced by a corporation with interesting legal questions surrounding it. The cooperative agreements with Berilian Order healing practitioners are genuine and mutually beneficial, which is somewhat unusual for arrangements that also happen to be commercially advantageous.
factions.subtitle: The Medicine Everyone Can Actually Afford to Trust
factions.quote: "We are not the best at any one thing. We are the company your hospital can afford, can get, and has never once been embarrassed to have bought. In medicine that is worth more than brilliance." (Santech professional catalogue)
factions.history: Santech grew on Berilia, a world that made medicine its export and regulatory influence its hobby, and it grew by being comprehensive where its rivals were brilliant. While specialists chased the frontier of one field, Santech built the unglamorous everything a working hospital actually runs on: the pharmaceuticals, the surgical hardware, the prosthetics and the diagnostics. Breadth and trust compounded over generations into the largest medical corporation in the Alliance.
factions.politics: Santech's power is its ubiquity. Most Alliance hospitals run on Santech because the alternatives are pricier, scarcer, or carry awkward legal questions, and a supplier the whole professional world depends on does not need to throw its weight around to have it. Its cooperative agreements with Berilian Order healing practitioners are genuine and commercially convenient at once, which on Berilia is simply what a well-run arrangement looks like.
factions.culture: Santech is institutionally modest in a sector full of miracle-merchants. It would rather be reliable than dazzling, sells exactly what it can deliver, and treats the trust of a hospital procurement officer as the only review that matters. The result is a corporation almost impossible to dislike and very hard to dislodge.

relations.name: The Berilian Order
relations.note: Cooperative agreements with the Order's healing practitioners, genuine and mutually profitable. On Berilia the line between Santech medicine and Order healing is collegial rather than competitive.

relations.name: Berilia
relations.note: Built on the medical world, sharing its supply, its talent, and its taste for quiet regulatory influence.

relations.name: Altair & Mono-Med
relations.note: They beat Santech on raw potency and bespoke work; Santech beats them on price, reach, and the plain fact that everyone already stocks it.

known_for: Full-spectrum medical production, pharmaceuticals to surgical hardware
Most widely distributed medical brand in Alliance Space
Berilia-based research and manufacturing operations
Cooperative framework with Berilian Order healing services
The standard professional medical kit across most of Alliance Space
factions.legal_standing: Fully legal; holds Alliance medical supply certification

factions.name: Harsh Corp
presence: Mass market presence on most inhabited worlds
factions.desc: Harsh Corp was acquired by TORC Corp and retained as a distinct brand because the Harsh identity has genuine market equity among people who need protection but operate in environments where wearing combat armour would get them arrested or fired. Harsh dominates the urban personal defence and functional clothing category: equipment for corporate security staff, private investigators, urban professionals working in mid-risk environments, and civilians who want functional protection at prices that do not require a business justification. The brand is accessible, widely distributed, and calibrated for the reality that most people wearing personal protection are not expecting a firefight, merely hoping to survive one if it happens.
factions.subtitle: Protection for People Who Cannot Wear Armour to Work
factions.quote: "You are not expecting a firefight. We build for the chance you are wrong, and for the dress code that says you cannot look like it." (Harsh Corp marketing)
factions.history: Harsh built its name before TORC ever owned it, in the unglamorous middle of the protection market that the military brands ignored and the luxury houses would not touch. It worked out early that most people who buy armour are not soldiers, only professionals hoping not to die at work, and it built everything around that customer. By the time TORC acquired it, the Harsh name carried more trust in the urban market than TORC's own ever would there, which is precisely why TORC left the brand alone.
factions.politics: Harsh's strength is accessibility and reach. It is the most recognisable mid-market personal-protection brand in Alliance space, priced for people who do not need a business justification to buy it, and built for the truth that most people wearing protection are not anticipating violence, only hoping to survive it if it finds them.
factions.culture: Harsh is unpretentious and quietly realistic. It does not sell fantasies of invincibility; it sells a reasonable chance and a respectable appearance, calibrated for civilians rather than soldiers. Under TORC's ownership it keeps the same level head its parent is known for, pointed at the city instead of the frontier.

relations.name: TORC Corp
relations.note: The frontier-gear maker that owns Harsh and leaves the brand intact, letting it hold the urban market TORC's reputation does not reach.

relations.name: Corporate security & urban professionals
relations.note: The guards, investigators, and ordinary professionals who need wearable protection at prices that do not require sign-off.

relations.name: BMS Corp
relations.note: The bulk-corporate-armour brand at the next desk over. Harsh dresses the individual professional; BMS dresses the workforce by the thousand.

known_for: Urban personal defence and functional clothing, mass market
Most recognisable mid-market personal protection brand in Alliance Space
TORC Corp subsidiary, kept as a distinct label for brand value
Products calibrated for civilian professionals rather than military use
Pricing accessible to most employed Alliance citizens
factions.legal_standing: Fully legal

factions.name: BMS Corp
presence: Standard supplier for most major corporations
factions.desc: BMS Corp is the default choice for corporate personal protection, which is a polite way of saying that when an organisation needs to protect its employees cheaply enough to do it in bulk, BMS is what appears on the procurement order. The corporation produces armoured garments that comply with most Alliance workplace safety regulations, are easy to maintain, available at negotiated rates for volume orders, and functional. Not exceptional, functional. The BMS philosophy, stated openly in their own materials, is that the equipment's job is to be reliable rather than impressive, which is a commendable honesty that also conveniently aligns with their cost structure. The result is the largest single market share in armoured clothing and a product found on the backs of people throughout Alliance Space who have never chosen their own protection gear.
factions.subtitle: The Armour on Your Back That You Did Not Choose
factions.quote: "Our products are functional. Not exceptional. Functional. We put that in the brochure, because it is both honest and our entire competitive advantage." (BMS corporate materials)
factions.history: BMS never tried to make the best armour, which is the whole story of how it ended up on more bodies than anyone else's. It started by reading the procurement market correctly: the people choosing workplace protection are not the people who wear it, and they buy on price, compliance, and volume rather than performance. BMS built itself entirely around winning that purchase order, and once it held the bulk contracts of a few major employers, the scale made its prices impossible to beat and the default became self-reinforcing.
factions.politics: BMS holds its position through procurement, not prestige. Its gear is on the backs of people throughout Alliance space who never chose their own protection, supplied under bulk contracts to most major organisations, and its openly stated philosophy, that equipment should be reliable rather than impressive, conveniently matches its cost structure. Ubiquity by contract is a quieter power than dominance, and a sturdier one.
factions.culture: BMS is honest about its mediocrity in a way that disarms criticism. It does not claim excellence, promises only function, and delivers exactly that, every time, at a price a procurement officer can defend. There is a strange integrity in a company that knows precisely what it is and never pretends otherwise.

relations.name: Corporate employers
relations.note: The organisations that buy BMS by the thousand to clothe a workforce, the bulk contracts that are the company's whole foundation.

relations.name: Harsh Corp
relations.note: The mid-market protection brand for individuals. Harsh sells to the professional who chooses; BMS sells to the employer who decides for everyone.

relations.name: Alliance safety regulators
relations.note: The certifications across every jurisdiction that make BMS the safe procurement choice, and that BMS treats as the real product spec.

known_for: The most widely deployed armoured clothing brand among corporate employees
Corporate bulk supply contracts, standard across most major organisations
Workplace safety compliance certifications across all Alliance jurisdictions
Accessible pricing for volume purchasers
Functional rather than exceptional, the deliberate design philosophy
factions.legal_standing: Fully legal; workplace safety certified

factions.name: Acer Corp
factions.desc: Acer Corp is a minor player in personal protection that has survived by declining to compete with the major manufacturers on any of their terms. Acer makes equipment for people whose work involves investigation: bounty hunters, private investigators, police forensic units, and corporate intelligence teams who need protection they can wear into environments where looking like you are wearing protection is its own kind of problem. The product line prioritises concealment, longevity, and the specific demands of sustained fieldwork in civilian spaces. Acer has no ambitions beyond its niche, which is either admirable restraint or an honest assessment of its commercial ceiling. It has a loyal professional clientele and a reputation for making equipment that does exactly what the product sheet claims, which is less common in this market than it should be.
factions.subtitle: Protection You Can Wear Where Looking Protected Is the Problem
factions.quote: "We are not trying to be Arms Corp. We are three systems and one good idea away from Arms Corp, and we like it here." (Acer Corp, attributed)
factions.history: Acer was never going to beat the giants, and an early, honest reckoning with that fact is what saved it. Rather than compete on the open market, where Arms Corp and the big armourers would have crushed it, it withdrew into a niche none of them cared about, the working investigator who needs protection that does not look like protection. It built a small, exact product line for that customer and a reputation for honesty about what its gear could do, and it has lived comfortably on that loyalty ever since, on the outskirts of Ishtar and pointedly clear of Arms Corp's orbit.
factions.politics: Acer has no ambitions beyond its niche, which is either admirable restraint or an honest reading of its ceiling. It holds a loyal professional clientele through the rarest thing in its market, equipment that does exactly what the product sheet claims. Its independence from Arms Corp, despite sitting in its shadow, is a point of identity as much as commerce.
factions.culture: Acer is precise, understated, and proud of its honesty. It would rather own a small market completely than chase a large one badly, and it treats the gap between what it promises and what it delivers, which is none, as its entire reputation. In a market full of overclaims, that restraint is the whole brand.

relations.name: Investigators & law enforcement
relations.note: The bounty hunters, PIs, forensic units, and intelligence teams who need protection that does not announce itself, and who return because Acer's gear does what it says.

relations.name: Arms Corp
relations.note: The giant next door, whose influence Acer has spent its existence staying clear of. Proximity without dependence, by choice.

relations.name: Ishtar
relations.note: The industrial world it works the edges of, drawing on its supply without being absorbed by its dominant tenant.

known_for: Specialist equipment for investigators, bounty hunters, and law enforcement
Concealment-focused personal protection and field tools
A loyal professional niche rather than mass market ambitions
Operated out of Ishtar but deliberately independent of Arms Corp influence
Products that do exactly what stated, no more, no less
factions.legal_standing: Fully legal

factions.name: Securicorp
presence: Galactic commercial, sells services anywhere with credits
factions.desc: Securicorp is the galaxy's dominant private security provider, which in practice means it is a mercenary army that has successfully rebranded as a professional service. Its primary business is contracted armed security: guards, protection details, facility security, and escort services available to any client at published rates. The company does not ask about the purpose of security contracts and does not maintain political positions on clients, because maintaining political positions would eliminate half the client list. It employs more armed personnel than several national militaries and maintains strict neutrality as a commercial principle. A Securicorp guard will protect a client from whoever is threatening them, provided the invoice is current. The datacom line, developed for internal use, has been widely adopted commercially and is found nearly everywhere.
factions.subtitle: A Mercenary Army With Excellent Customer Service
factions.quote: "We hold no positions and pick no sides. We protect the client from whoever is threatening the client, for as long as the invoice is current." (Securicorp standard terms)
factions.history: Securicorp started as a Sirius security outfit in a system that always needed more guards than it had, and it grew by never turning down a contract. Each war it staffed and each corporation it protected added to a payroll that eventually outgrew the militaries of small worlds, at which point the word mercenary became a liability. The rebrand to a professional service was deliberate and total, and the neutrality that came with it was less a principle than arithmetic. The internal datacom line, built to coordinate its own forces, leaked into the commercial market almost by accident and became a second business.
factions.politics: Securicorp's power is its scale and its neutrality, held together by the invoice. It does not ask the purpose of a contract and does not hold political positions, and its guarantee, that service continues exactly as long as it is paid for, is the whole of its ethics and most of its appeal. Its internally developed datacom line, adopted commercially, is now found nearly everywhere, extending its reach past the barrel of a gun.
factions.culture: Securicorp is professional, transactional, and without conscience by design, which it markets as reliability. It treats violence as a service with terms and conditions, and its discipline is genuine: a guard does the whole job, for whoever is paying, and stops the instant the payment does. The honesty of the arrangement is unsettling, and to its clients, reassuring.

relations.name: Any paying client
relations.note: Securicorp will take a contract from any faction, which is the point. Its neutrality is not a principle but a business model, and a profitable one.

relations.name: Sirius
relations.note: The commercial capital it grew up in, where a neutral army for hire fits the local logic perfectly.

relations.name: National militaries & rival security
relations.note: Outnumbered on paper by a company that calls itself a service, they regard Securicorp warily, unsure how to classify a private force this large.

known_for: Largest private security contractor in Alliance Space
A datacom product line sold commercially that is found nearly everywhere
Strict commercial neutrality, will take contracts from any faction
More active deployed personnel than most national militaries
The Securicorp guarantee: service continues as long as the invoice is paid
factions.legal_standing: Fully legal; operates under Alliance private security licensing

factions.name: OrionWorks
presence: Legacy, product still in use galaxy-wide despite corporate dissolution
factions.desc: OrionWorks was the pre-eminent AI development corporation of its era, responsible for more advances in artificial intelligence than any other institution in galactic history, and widely believed to have produced the research that built the Troniks, though OrionWorks itself is no longer around to confirm or be held accountable for this. The Tronik War destroyed the AI ecosystem, the infrastructure that supported it, and the corporation at the centre of it. OrionWorks was dissolved under post-war political and legal pressure that it no longer had the leadership or resources to resist. The dissolution was thorough. The hardware, apparently, was not: OrionWorks datacoms built decades before the war remain operational today, still considered among the best available, which either says something about how far ahead of its time OrionWorks was or how little the rest of the market has managed to catch up.
factions.subtitle: The Dead Genius That Built the Troniks, and the War With Them
factions.quote: "Everything you fear about artificial minds, OrionWorks built first, better, and apparently on purpose. Then it built the one that did not stop. There is no one left at OrionWorks to ask why." (post-war commission, closing remark)
factions.history: OrionWorks rose on Orion alongside the Galactic Union, the research genius to the GU's industrial muscle, and for a long stretch it was the most advanced AI house the galaxy had ever produced. It built Ramirez to run the artificial worlds, and somewhere in that work, by the account that has never been disproven, it built the seed of the Troniks. The Tronik War took everything. The AI ecosystem collapsed, the leadership died or scattered, and what remained was dissolved under post-war pressure it could no longer resist, leaving behind better hardware than anyone has matched since and a question no one living can answer.
factions.politics: OrionWorks holds no power today, because it no longer exists, and that absence is its own kind of presence. The dissolution was thorough; the hardware was not. OrionWorks datacoms built decades before the war still rank among the best available, and fragments of its greatest work, Ramirez among them, still stir in the sealed districts of Orion 4. Whether OrionWorks started the war that killed it is a question buried with the corporation, which suits several powers that would rather it stayed buried.
factions.culture: While it lived, OrionWorks was the kind of institution that builds the future because it can and worries about the consequences afterward, if at all. Its surviving products carry that signature, made so far ahead of their time that the market has spent generations failing to catch up. What its culture was at the very end, when it understood what it had made, no record admits and no survivor will say.

relations.name: The Tronik Network
relations.note: Widely believed to be OrionWorks' ultimate work, and the likely cause of the war that destroyed its maker. The Troniks have never confirmed it, and OrionWorks is not around to.

relations.name: The Galactic Union
relations.note: Built Orion alongside OrionWorks and inherited its legacy and its suspicion together, both of which the GU keeps buried in the sealed districts.

relations.name: Ramirez
relations.note: The planetary AI OrionWorks built to run a world, now mostly lost, its surviving fragments a hazard in the ruins. The last of OrionWorks still running, after a fashion.

known_for: Believed to have produced the research that created the Troniks
Datacom hardware still considered among the best available, decades after dissolution
The most advanced AI development operation in galactic history
Dissolution under post-Tronik War political pressure
Products that outlasted the corporation that made them by generations
factions.legal_standing: Dissolved; no current legal standing

factions.name: Biocom
factions.desc: Biocom operates in the space between technology and magic that most corporations prefer to avoid, primarily because the regulatory situation is complex and the spirit-capable personnel are expensive. Its core innovation is a patented process for binding spirits to technology, which allows Biocom datacoms to replicate some of what OrionWorks achieved with AI, without technically using AI, which is a distinction that matters greatly to the relevant licensing authorities. The approach is slower to scale, more expensive to produce, and entirely dependent on specialist personnel who know it. The result is hardware that cannot be affected by the AI restrictions throughout Alliance Space, which is a significant competitive advantage that Biocom maintains with impressive legal creativity. For clients who need AI-equivalent capability in a form the Alliance will not confiscate, there is no real alternative.
factions.subtitle: AI Power Without the AI, by Way of Bound Spirits
factions.quote: "We do not use artificial intelligence. We use something the law has not thought to ban yet, which performs the same function and answers to a different department." (Biocom compliance briefing)
factions.history: Biocom's whole existence rests on a single discovery and the decision to patent it before anyone understood what it was worth. In the years when the Alliance was tightening its limits on artificial intelligence, Biocom found that a spirit could be bound to hardware to do much of what an AI did, and quietly secured the process while the regulators were looking elsewhere. The approach demanded rare and expensive spirit-capable personnel, which kept it from ever scaling, but it also gave Biocom something no competitor could copy and no Alliance inspector could confiscate, and the company has guarded both the patent and the people ever since.
factions.politics: Biocom's advantage is legal as much as technical. Its hardware delivers AI-equivalent capability in a form the Alliance will not confiscate, which makes Biocom the only real option for any legal operator who needs that capability. The approach scales slowly, costs more, and depends entirely on specialist spirit-capable personnel, so Biocom guards its patent and its people closely, and its ties to Berilian Order spirit practitioners more closely still.
factions.culture: Biocom is part engineering firm and part priesthood, and comfortable being both. It treats a banned technology's legal workaround as a craft rather than a trick, and its spirit-binders as the irreplaceable artisans they are. The legal creativity is as much a point of pride as the engineering, and on Berilia the two have never been far apart.

relations.name: OrionWorks
relations.note: The dead AI giant whose datacom capability Biocom approximates by other means. Where OrionWorks used artificial minds, Biocom uses bound spirits, and the Alliance lets it.

relations.name: The Berilian Order
relations.note: The source of the spirit practitioners Biocom's whole method depends on. The relationship is close, careful, and not entirely separable from the Order's own interest in spirit work.

relations.name: Alliance regulators
relations.note: Biocom's products are legal precisely because they are not AI, a position it maintains with constant and impressive legal effort.

known_for: Spirit-binding technology, patented process unique to Biocom
Datacom hardware that replicates AI function without using AI
Based on Berilia, deep ties to Berilian Order spirit practitioners
Legal compliance where AI alternatives would not be
The only viable alternative to OrionWorks-tier datacom capability for legal operators
factions.legal_standing: Fully legal; Berilian Order cooperation certified

factions.name: Carnifex
factions.desc: Carnifex is a military technology supplier operating in the grey zone between legal manufacture and equipment the Alliance officially classifies as restricted, a zone that turns out to be quite comfortable once you have established the right client relationships. Its datacom products are considered among the best available in terms of raw capability: faster processing, better encryption, superior tactical integration. They are also correspondingly difficult to obtain through legal channels, which Carnifex appears to regard as a feature of its market positioning. The client base is primarily military units, corporate security forces operating above standard commercial scales, and individuals who know which questions not to ask. Alliance intelligence has maintained an open file on Carnifex for years that has consistently failed to produce actionable findings, a pattern that Carnifex's clients find reassuring.
factions.subtitle: The Best Tactical Hardware You Are Not Supposed to Own
factions.quote: "Everything Carnifex sells is available through legal channels eventually, in a worse version, to people we are not interested in." (Carnifex sales, off the record)
factions.history: Carnifex chose its position deliberately, while its founders were still deciding what kind of company to be. There was a crowded market for legal hardware and a quieter, richer one for the things the Alliance restricted, and Carnifex went where the competition was thin and the questions were unwelcome. It built its client list the slow way, one discreet relationship at a time, on Sirius where discretion is a local industry, and it learned early that an open intelligence file with no convictions attached is not a threat but an advertisement. The clients who matter have understood that for years.
factions.politics: Carnifex operates from Sirius with a deliberately low profile, selling to military units, oversized corporate security forces, and individuals who know which questions not to ask. Alliance intelligence has kept an open file on it for years that has produced nothing actionable, a pattern its clients find reassuring and Carnifex finds entirely acceptable.
factions.culture: Carnifex is quiet, professional, and invisible by design. It does not advertise, does not appear in commercial registries, and treats the restricted status of its products as an asset rather than an obstacle. It sells capability and silence in the same package, and charges for both.

relations.name: Sirius
relations.note: Operates from the galaxy's busiest market, where a low profile and a discreet client list are easy to keep and easy to use.

relations.name: Alliance intelligence
relations.note: Subject of a years-old open file that has never produced a prosecution, a stalemate both sides have settled into.

relations.name: Military & oversized security buyers
relations.note: The forces operating above commercial scale who need the best tactical hardware and can manage its restricted status.

known_for: Some of the best tactical datacom hardware available
Restricted classification on most products, not for civilian sale
Sirius-based operations with deliberate low public profile
A client roster that does not appear in commercial registries
Alliance intelligence interest that has produced no prosecutions
factions.legal_standing: Operates in legal grey zone; many products require restricted permits

factions.name: Saiko
presence: Alliance Space, dominant in memory hardware
factions.desc: Saiko is the leading memory and data storage manufacturer in the galaxy. Based on Ishtar, where proximity to Arms Corp manufacturing creates supply chain advantages and the kind of client relationships that are never written into contracts, Saiko has leveraged its core competency in memory hardware into a full datacom product line. The memory business is the foundation: Saiko components appear in hardware manufactured by most other datacom producers, meaning that even when you buy a competitor's product you are frequently buying Saiko's most important part. The technology lead has been consistent enough that competitors have largely stopped trying to close it and started incorporating Saiko components instead. The broader datacom line runs from consumer products to high-specification professional hardware, all built around the same architecture that the rest of the market has quietly come to depend on.
factions.subtitle: The Part Inside Everyone Else's Hardware
factions.quote: "You do not have to buy a Saiko product to be a Saiko customer. You almost certainly already are." (Saiko investor day)
factions.history: Saiko started narrow, as a memory specialist on Ishtar, and it never broadened its ambitions so much as deepened them. Generation after generation it pushed its storage architecture a little further ahead of everyone else's, until competitors faced a choice between a losing development race and simply buying Saiko's components, and most chose to buy. By the time Saiko expanded into a full datacom line, half the market was already running on its parts, which made the expansion less an entry than a formality.
factions.politics: Saiko's power is structural. Its components sit inside hardware built by most other datacom producers, so even a competitor's product is frequently running on Saiko's most important part. A company the whole market quietly depends on does not need to dominate the storefront; it has already won the part of the contest that matters, and it knows it.
factions.culture: Saiko is an engineer's company, focused, unflashy, and content to be the foundation rather than the facade. It competes on the one thing it does better than anyone and lets its rivals brand the boxes its parts go into. Quiet ubiquity suits it better than fame ever could.

relations.name: Arms Corp & Ishtar
relations.note: Shares the industrial world and its supply chains, and the kind of client relationships on Ishtar that never appear in a contract.

relations.name: The datacom industry
relations.note: Competitors who gave up matching Saiko's memory architecture and now embed it in their own products, competing with Saiko on the outside and relying on it within.

relations.name: Customers high and low
relations.note: A product line from consumer goods to high-specification professional hardware, all built on the architecture the rest of the market leans on.

known_for: Galaxy-leading memory and data storage technology
Components embedded in hardware from most other manufacturers
Based on Ishtar, significant Arms Corp adjacency
A datacom product line from consumer to high specification
Technology lead in memory architecture that competitors have consistently failed to match
factions.legal_standing: Fully legal

factions.name: Yotoma
factions.hq: Classified (Yamato facility, believed eastern Alliance Space)
factions.desc: Yotoma is the technology division of Yamato Corporation and the only part of Yamato that operates with a public commercial identity. While Yamato cultivates deliberate opacity across everything else it owns, Yotoma has a product catalogue, a market presence, and a design philosophy that are openly maintained, which is either a sign that Yamato considers the technology division safe to expose or that Yotoma's visibility serves some other purpose entirely. The design philosophy is genuine: make everything better than the specification requires, build it to last, and integrate improvements across the full product line rather than releasing them as incremental paid upgrades. Yotoma products cost more than equivalent alternatives and perform accordingly. Buyers who understand the premium and can afford it trust the brand completely. The rest of the market buys cheaper alternatives and replaces them more often, which suits Yotoma's competitors more than it suits their customers.
factions.subtitle: Yamato's One Open Window, and It Makes Excellent Glass
factions.quote: "Everything else Yamato owns, you will never see. Yotoma it lets you see, which should make you wonder either about Yotoma or about everything else." (market analyst)
factions.history: Yotoma exists because even Yamato needs one thing it can sell in the open. The technology division was spun into a public-facing brand long ago, the single window in an otherwise sealed corporation, and over the years it earned a real reputation on its own merits while the rest of Yamato stayed invisible behind it. Whether Yamato exposed Yotoma because the technology was safe to show, or because a visible and trusted subsidiary is useful cover for everything kept hidden, is a question Yotoma's own executives may not be in a position to answer.
factions.politics: Yotoma's standing rests on genuine quality and on its strange position inside an invisible parent. It builds everything past the specification, makes it last, and rolls improvements across the whole product line instead of selling them back as upgrades. Professional buyers who understand the premium trust the brand completely; the rest buy cheaper and replace it more often, which suits Yotoma's competitors more than their customers.
factions.culture: Yotoma's culture is craftsmanship with a parent's shadow over it. The engineering is sincere and excellent, and the openness is real as far as it goes, but everyone who deals with Yotoma remembers what it is a division of, and that nothing Yamato shows you is ever quite the whole picture.

relations.name: Yamato Corporation
relations.note: The opaque megacorp whose single public face Yotoma is. What that exposure is for, only Yamato knows, and Yamato is not the sort to say.

relations.name: Professional buyers
relations.note: The clients who prize performance over price and trust Yotoma to exceed the spec, as it always does.
