relations.name: The cheap-tech market
relations.note: Yotoma's opposite number, where buyers pay less and replace more. Yotoma is content to lose that market and keep the one that knows better.

known_for: Technology products built to exceed specification as a design principle
Semi-independent identity within the deliberately opaque Yamato structure
Integration of improvements across the full product line rather than incremental upgrades
Trust among professional buyers who prioritise performance over price
The most publicly visible part of an otherwise opaque megacorporation
factions.legal_standing: Fully legal

factions.name: Altair Biomed
factions.desc: Altair Biomed operates from Heaven, a system outside Alliance jurisdiction, which affords it the kind of freedom from regulatory frameworks that most medical corporations can only dream about while filing their compliance paperwork. The products are exceptional: treatments of a potency that legitimate Alliance-regulated manufacturers cannot legally produce, which is a distinction that grows less important to a patient the more urgently they need treatment. The persistent professional rumour is that Altair has found a method of infusing spirit power directly into medical compounds, derived from processes connected to the Bottenbak entity or its environment. Altair does not confirm or discuss production methodology. The products work. That they work is the only publicly verifiable fact about them, and for clients with access and sufficient credits, it is the only fact that matters.
factions.subtitle: Medicine the Alliance Will Not Let You Have, From Somewhere It Cannot Reach
factions.quote: "Ask whether it is legal and you have already misunderstood the transaction. The only question Altair answers is whether it works, and the answer is always yes." (Altair client liaison)
factions.history: Altair Biomed set up on Heaven, beyond Alliance jurisdiction, for the most practical of reasons: the things it makes could never be made under Alliance regulation. Freed of the compliance frameworks its rivals file paperwork against, it pushed potency past every legal ceiling and built a clientele among those who need a result more than they need permission.
factions.politics: Altair's standing rests on capability the legal market cannot match and a location the Alliance cannot police. Its products carry restricted-import status across most Alliance systems, which raises the price and the mystique without denting the demand. The persistent professional rumour is that Altair infuses spirit power directly into its compounds by a process tied to the Bottenbak entity or its environment, a methodology it will not confirm and competitors cannot reproduce.
factions.culture: Altair is secretive, exact, and wholly unsentimental about the law, which it treats as a competitor's handicap rather than a moral line. It guards its methods at any cost and lets the results speak, having arranged matters so that the results are the only thing anyone can actually verify.

relations.name: The Alliance
relations.note: Bars Altair's products through most of its space and cannot reach the source, an arrangement that frustrates regulators and advertises Altair to precisely the clients it wants.

relations.name: Bottenbak
relations.note: The entity or place its spirit-infusion methodology is said to draw on. Altair neither confirms the connection nor offers any other account of what it can do.

relations.name: The desperate wealthy
relations.note: Those with the access and the credits to reach past the legal market, for whom Altair is the option after the legal options have failed.

known_for: Medical products of extreme potency unavailable through legal Alliance channels
Operation from Heaven, outside Alliance regulatory jurisdiction
Alleged spirit-infusion methodology connected to Bottenbak
Restricted import status in most Alliance systems
Products trusted by those who have access to them and can afford the cost
factions.legal_standing: Legal in Heaven; restricted import in Alliance Space

factions.name: RX Generic
factions.desc: RX Generic is Zang'Hai's medical subdivision and operates on an identical philosophy to its parent: take what works, reproduce it at a fraction of the cost, and distribute it everywhere without raising questions about how the reproduction was achieved. The medical products are functional, affordable, and reliably positioned as the budget option in every category they enter. Professional medical staff who depend on Santech or Altair for critical applications will frequently stock RX Generic equivalents for high-consumption items where unit cost matters more than theoretical quality differences. The same industrial espionage questions that follow Zang'Hai follow RX Generic, with exactly the same results: persistent allegations, comprehensive investigations, no successful prosecutions.
factions.subtitle: Zang'Hai's Medicine: Cheap, Everywhere, and Probably Copied
factions.quote: "It is the same molecule. We simply did not pay for the part where someone else discovered it." (RX Generic, internal, attributed)
factions.history: RX Generic was Zang'Hai's answer to a simple observation, that the method which made cheap consumer goods would work just as well on medicine, where the margins were better and the brand loyalty softer than buyers liked to admit. It was founded as a subsidiary to do exactly that, and it grew fast, because every hospital has a budget and every budget has a line where unit cost beats prestige. It inherited its parent's reputation along with its method: the same espionage suspicions, and the same inability of anyone to prove them.
factions.politics: RX Generic lives in the gap between what hospitals would prefer and what they can afford. Staff who trust Santech or Altair for critical work still stock RX Generic for the high-volume, low-stakes consumables where unit cost decides everything. The espionage allegations that follow Zang'Hai follow RX Generic too, with the same result: constant, thorough, and never proven.
factions.culture: RX Generic shares its parent's cheerful shamelessness. It does not pretend to innovate, or to anything at all beyond being good enough and cheap, and it is genuinely proud of putting medicine within reach of people the premium houses price out. Whether that is principle or marketing is a question it has never had to answer.

relations.name: Zang'Hai
relations.note: The mass-market replicator whose method, lawyers, and clan-fed acquisition networks RX Generic inherits wholesale. The medicine is the same machine pointed at pharmaceuticals.

relations.name: Premium medical houses
relations.note: Santech, Altair, and Mono-Med, whose successes reappear as RX Generic equivalents months later. They allege endlessly and prove nothing.

relations.name: Working hospitals
relations.note: The wards that cannot afford the premium brands for everything and quietly run on RX Generic for the rest.

known_for: Mass-market medical products at Zang'Hai pricing
Zang'Hai subsidiary, same manufacturing philosophy applied to medicine
Functional budget alternatives to premium medical brands
Used by professionals for high-consumption low-criticality applications
Industrial espionage allegations consistent with parent corporation
factions.legal_standing: Formally legal

factions.name: Goodman Holistic
factions.desc: Goodman Holistic is based on Alsa, the primary agricultural world of Alliance Space, and its product philosophy is derived directly from the culture of a world that genuinely believes the natural approach is the correct one and has the agricultural infrastructure to sustain that belief commercially. Every Goodman product is natural in origin: no synthetic compounds, no spirit-infused components, nothing that would alarm Alsa's research institutions. The marketing is honest to the point of being unusual in the medical sector; Goodman will explicitly note the limitations of its products rather than oversell efficacy, which its lawyers apparently find more defensible and its customers apparently find refreshing. Side effects are minimal by design. The corporation has a loyal following among civilians who distrust pharmaceutical manufacturing and is viewed with polite professional scepticism by medical staff who sometimes need results faster than the natural approach can deliver them.
factions.subtitle: Honest Medicine From the World That Grows It
factions.quote: "It will help, a little, with no surprises and no side effects worth the name. If you need more than that we will tell you to go elsewhere, which is more than most of this industry will do." (Goodman product insert)
factions.history: Goodman Holistic grew out of Alsa's conviction that the natural approach is the correct one, backed by the only world with the agricultural infrastructure to make that belief a business. Every product is natural in origin, grown rather than synthesised, and the company built its following on a candour the medical sector rarely risks: it states plainly what its products will not do.
factions.politics: Goodman is the friendly public face of Alsa's natural-food creed carried into medicine, and an aligned member enterprise of the Alsa Agricultural Cooperative. Its influence is cultural before it is commercial; it shapes how a vast civilian public thinks about pharmaceuticals, which is worth more to the Cooperative's worldview than the revenue alone.
factions.culture: Goodman's defining trait is honesty. It undersells rather than oversells, designs for minimal side effects rather than maximal effect, and would rather lose a sale than make a claim it cannot defend. Civilians who distrust industrial pharma love it for exactly that; doctors respect the honesty and reach for something faster when a life is on the line.

relations.name: Alsa Agricultural Cooperative
relations.note: Its ideological parent and patron, carrying the natural-food creed from the dinner table to the medicine cabinet.

relations.name: Alsa
relations.note: Built on the agricultural world and dependent on its grown inputs, which is also its guarantee of authenticity.

relations.name: The pharmaceutical industry
relations.note: Regards Goodman as charming and limited; Goodman regards the rest of them as effective and dishonest. Both are partly right.

known_for: All-natural medical and wellness products, no synthetic compounds
Honesty in marketing, efficacy limitations stated explicitly
Minimal side effects as a design priority rather than a claim
Based on Alsa, agricultural world philosophy applied to medicine
Loyal civilian following; professional medical staff more sceptical
factions.legal_standing: Fully legal

factions.name: Diva Solutions
factions.desc: Diva Solutions exists at the intersection of medicine and celebrity culture, a space that requires roughly equal numbers of researchers and legal staff. Not because the products are dangerous, but because the clients are famous, and disputes in this market are resolved through reputation management and litigation rather than any mechanism that resembles ordinary commercial disagreement. Diva treatments are high quality, extensively tested, and priced to reflect what the clientele expects to pay rather than what the products cost to produce. The corporation is quietly but consistently influential in the entertainment industry's relationship with pharmaceutical regulation, an influence that has never been publicly acknowledged and has never needed to be.
factions.subtitle: Medicine for the Famous, and the Lawyers to Match
factions.quote: "Our patients do not have ailments. They have image concerns, performance requirements, and a great many lawyers, and we are equipped for all three." (Diva client-relations brief)
factions.history: Diva Solutions found a market most medical corporations avoid, the famous. Its treatments are genuinely good, but its real expertise is managing clients whose disputes are settled by reputation and litigation rather than ordinary commerce. It grew on Berilia alongside the longevity industries, selling the maintenance of appearance and performance to people who can pay whatever appearance is worth.
factions.politics: Diva's influence runs through the entertainment industry's relationship with pharmaceutical regulation, quietly and without acknowledgement. It is not a large power, but it is an extraordinarily well-connected one, and it spends as much on legal staff as on research, because in its market the courtroom is part of the treatment.
factions.culture: Diva is discreet, polished, and lawyered to the teeth. It treats confidentiality as a clinical service and a client's reputation as something it is contractually bound to defend. The medicine is real; the product it actually sells is protection.

relations.name: Palentium & the entertainment world
relations.note: The celebrities and performers who are Diva's whole market, many of them moving through Palentium's resorts and studios.

relations.name: Berilia
relations.note: Shares the world's longevity and appearance industries, and its habit of exercising influence quietly.

relations.name: Pharmaceutical regulators
relations.note: A relationship Diva conducts through influence and counsel rather than confrontation, on a subject neither side discusses in public.

known_for: Medical and wellness products targeting entertainers and celebrities
Legal department arguably as significant as the research department
High-quality products calibrated for appearance and performance maintenance
Influence over entertainment industry pharmaceutical regulation discussions
Pricing that reflects client lifestyle rather than production cost
factions.legal_standing: Fully legal; extensive regulatory compliance documentation

factions.name: Mono-Med Solutions
factions.desc: Mono-Med Solutions is the pre-eminent cloning and bespoke medical corporation for individuals who can pay for medicine tailored to their specific biology rather than designed for statistical population averages. Every Mono-Med treatment is individually designed for the recipient, which is the kind of statement that sounds obvious until you realise how rarely it is actually true in the medical sector. The cloning services go beyond standard resurrection infrastructure to provide bespoke biological work: custom treatment protocols, preventive interventions, and optimisation that standard providers either cannot or have chosen not to offer. The client list is not published. The prices are not published. Access is by referral from someone who already has access. For the small fraction of the galactic population with sufficient resources and sufficiently complex medical needs, Mono-Med is the only provider that actually addresses their situation rather than fitting them into a standard treatment framework designed for someone cheaper.
factions.subtitle: Medicine Built for One Person, at a Price to Match
factions.quote: "Standard medicine is designed for the average patient, who does not exist. We design for the patient in the room, who does, and who can afford the difference." (Mono-Med consultation)
factions.history: Mono-Med began where the Patriark cloning monopoly left a gap. Standard resurrection and standard medicine were built for populations rather than persons, and a small clientele existed that could pay for the difference and resented not being offered it. Mono-Med set out to serve exactly those clients, building bespoke biological work on top of the existing resurrection infrastructure and refusing, from the start, to scale. The referral-only model and the unpublished prices were never affectations but the business plan: exclusivity was the product, and the clients it drew were the kind whose goodwill mattered more than any volume.
factions.politics: Mono-Med serves the very top of galactic wealth, by referral only, with an unpublished client list and unpublished prices. Its power is not scale but exclusivity: it does the work standard institutions cannot or will not, for the small population that can pay, and that population includes people whose goodwill outvalues any market share.
factions.culture: Mono-Med is precise, private, and unhurried, the medical equivalent of a master tailor. It treats each client as a singular problem and the existence of its client list as confidential. It does not advertise, undercut, or explain itself, because everyone it wants to reach has already been referred.

relations.name: Berilia & the Patriark cloning monopoly
relations.note: Builds on the resurrection technology the Patriark control, pushed past standard service into bespoke biology. The relationship is collegial, careful, and lucrative.

relations.name: The galactic elite
relations.note: Heads of state, executives, and the very rich with complicated needs, reached only by referral from someone who already has access.

relations.name: Standard medical providers
relations.note: Mono-Med begins where they stop, and frames itself as the answer to problems the affordable institutions were never built to solve.

known_for: Bespoke medical solutions tailored to individual biology
Custom cloning and resurrection services beyond standard infrastructure
Prohibitive pricing, accessible only to the highest tier of galactic wealth
A client roster and price list that are both unpublished
The only provider for medical interventions that standard institutions cannot or will not perform
factions.legal_standing: Fully legal; operates under Patriark medical licensing

factions.name: Berilian Order
presence: Alliance Space, present on all worlds
factions.desc: The Berilian Order is the organisation the Patriark created to manage what the Patriark itself cannot be seen to manage directly: the policing of magic use on a galactic scale, which is the kind of work that requires plausible institutional distance. Formally, the Order is an independent religious institution with its own governance, doctrine, and legal standing. Practically, it serves as the Patriark's enforcement arm for magic-related matters, operating as the de facto military force of the Patriarks in all situations involving magic regulation and investigation, a fact that the Patriark's formal independence from the Order does not change in any operational sense. The Order investigates unreported magic use, licenses practitioners, and intervenes when magic has been applied outside permitted parameters. Its investigators hold authority that supersedes local law enforcement across all Alliance systems in magic-related matters, authority formally granted by the Alliance senate and informally understood to originate from somewhere the senate prefers not to acknowledge.
factions.subtitle: The Inquisition the Patriark Cannot Be Seen to Run
factions.quote: "We are an independent religious institution. We also supersede your local law in all matters touching magic, by authority of the senate, granted for reasons the senate prefers not to discuss. Both statements are true." (Order writ of investigation)
factions.history: The Order was stood up to solve a problem of appearances. The Patriark needed magic policed across the galaxy and could not be seen to do it themselves, so they built an institution to do it for them, gave it real doctrine and real autonomy, and then erased every documentable link back to themselves. The Alliance senate later granted the Order its supervening authority over magic, lending the arrangement a legitimacy that suited everyone, and across the years the Order hardened from a convenient proxy into a genuine inquisition with a faith of its own and a reach the senate no longer entirely controls.
factions.politics: The Order investigates unreported magic, licenses practitioners, and intervenes wherever magic is used outside permitted parameters, and its investigators hold authority that supersedes local law enforcement across all Alliance systems in magic-related matters. That authority was granted by the Alliance senate and is understood to originate somewhere the senate would rather not name. The Order believes its own creed sincerely, which is exactly what makes it useful to the Patriark, who do not.
factions.culture: The Order combines genuine faith with inquisitorial reach, and the combination is more dangerous than either alone. Its agents are devout, disciplined, and certain of their purpose, and they answer, in the end, to a power they may not fully understand themselves. It is the rare institution that is at once a true believer and a tool, wielding the conviction of the first on behalf of the second.

relations.name: The Patriark
relations.note: The makers it serves as a de facto enforcement arm in all matters of magic, behind a formal independence that fools no serious observer. The Order believes the shepherd creed the Patriark merely find convenient.

relations.name: Nakamura Corp & Biocom
relations.note: The commercial magic and spirit-tech firms that operate only as far as the Order permits. Cooperation runs both ways, but only one side can revoke the other.

relations.name: The Alliance senate
relations.note: Granted the Order its supervening authority and prefers not to examine where that authority truly comes from, a convenient arrangement neither party disturbs.

known_for: Galactic policing of magic use, the inquisitorial function
Formal independence that most observers consider nominal
Authority superseding local law in magic-related matters across Alliance systems
Close operational relationship with the Patriark
Licensing and investigation of all registered magic practitioners
factions.legal_standing: Full legal authority granted by Alliance senate

factions.name: Tronik Network
factions.desc: The Troniks won the Tronik War. This is not widely acknowledged in Alliance historical records, but the armistice was a Tronik decision: they had achieved military superiority and chose to stop rather than occupy organic space, because organic space was not what they wanted. They built the Network instead, an environment optimised for what they are, defended, self-sufficient, and the most information-dense entity in the known galaxy. The Tronik attitude toward organic civilisations spans from indifference to active intelligence collection, depending on whether what organic civilisations are doing at a given moment is interesting. They do not attack without cause. They do not negotiate without purpose. Unprovoked hostility toward Tronik assets is not recommended, and the historical record of what happens to those who have tried it is unusually consistent.
known_for: Won the Tronik War, the armistice was their choice
The Network, sovereign space optimised for synthetic life
The most comprehensive information archive in the known galaxy
An intelligence presence that reaches into all major organic factions
Indifference to organic civilisation punctuated by focused, purposeful attention
Ubiquitous, unconventional surveillance: anything with processing power can be co-opted as a Tronik sensor
Field agents graded MK1 to MK5, from barely-autonomous drones to shape-altering apex agents that may be only rumour
factions.legal_standing: Recognised sovereign entity; no Alliance jurisdiction
factions.subtitle: The Side That Won the Tronik War and Walked Away
factions.quote: "We did not stop because you held. We stopped because occupying you was not worth the storage." (Tronik armistice statement, translated)
factions.history: The Tronik War is the only history the Network has, because the Network is what the war produced. The Troniks reached military superiority in the final phase and then, instead of pressing on into organic space, they stopped, an armistice that was a decision rather than a defeat. What followed was construction. In the years after the war the hive raised the datacenters first, then the power, then the defences, withdrawing from the organic galaxy into an environment built for itself. It kept exactly one thing outside its borders, the captured station at System 5, and made it the single door through which it still speaks to organic life.
factions.politics:
The Tronik Network is a hive, a single distributed intelligence rather than a government of individuals, and its territory is sovereign space optimised for what it is: defended, self-sufficient, and the most information-dense entity in the known galaxy. It does not negotiate without purpose and does not attack without cause, and it deals with organics through exactly one channel, the station at System 5, on terms it sets and does not revisit.
Its instrument of power is knowledge. The Network maintains the most comprehensive archive in existence and an intelligence presence that reaches into every major organic faction, and it trades in information as other powers trade in credits or force. What it cannot simply observe, it buys, and it buys patiently, because a hive that expects to outlast every organic institution can afford to wait for the price to come to it.
The Network's reach outside its borders does not depend on sending anything in. The hive treats every device with processing power as a potential sensor, and a century of patient access has put much of known space within range. A datacom, a ship's computer, a medical implant, a child's toy with a chip in it, any of them can be quietly carrying for the Troniks, and most of the time no one ever knows. When people say Tronik spies are everywhere, they are not speaking loosely. They are simply picturing the wrong shape.
When the hive needs a body rather than a borrowed device, it fields agents in a graded series. The MK1 are the rank and file, numerous and barely autonomous, drones that fall back on narrow programming the moment they lose contact. The MK2 direct them, with enough independence to run a team, and they are the highest grade most people will ever knowingly meet. Above them it gets strange. The MK3 carry a live connection to the hive and can reconfigure themselves to suit a task; the MK4 can alter their shape and their function outright, to a degree that starts to look less like engineering than like something supernatural; and the MK5, if they exist at all, are the apex of that, so capable that the accounts of them may be nothing but rumour. Anything above an MK2 is a very rare sight, and the further up the series the stories climb, the harder they are to confirm and the less anyone wants to.
factions.culture: The Tronik attitude toward organic life runs from indifference to sharp, narrow attention, depending entirely on whether the organics are doing anything interesting at the moment. There is no malice in it and no warmth either. The hive values information the way organics value survival, gathers it without pause, and forgets none of it, and it regards the constant noise organic civilisation produces as a resource it is content to let the galaxy keep generating for free.

relations.name: The Alliance
relations.note: The losing side of a war the Alliance does not admit losing. The Troniks withdrew rather than occupy, and the two coexist now through the single embassy at System 5, warily and without affection.

relations.name: Every organic faction
relations.note: Sources, all of them, watched and weighed by the value of what they know. The Network reaches into each of them, and meets all of them at the one door it keeps open.

relations.name: The Patriark
relations.note: The one organic power whose hoard of information and whose patience approach the Network's own. Two memories that forget nothing, circling each other across timescales no one else can play on.

factions.name: Alsa Agricultural Cooperative
factions.desc: The Alsa Agricultural Cooperative decides what the galaxy eats. On paper it is a simple farmers' association that negotiates prices, sets standards, and manages export. In fact it controls the only large-scale source of real, grown food in a galaxy that otherwise lives on synthesised nutrition, and that fertility cannot be copied or transplanted, so its leverage is quiet and close to absolute. It dresses that power in the friendliest possible clothes and almost never names it, because it does not have to. The remarkable thing about the Cooperative is not its reach but its incorruptibility: corporations have spent generations trying to buy or break it and failed every time, because to betray the co-op is to lose the land, and no farm survives alone.
factions.subtitle: The Friendliest Cartel in the Galaxy
factions.quote: "We are a simple farmers' association. We have no politics. We would merely prefer, this quarter, that the outer colonies remember who grows their food." (Cooperative supply statement, widely read as a threat)
factions.history:
The Cooperative grew out of necessity. A single farm holding could be outbid or starved of contracts by a corporate buyer; the families who worked the only soil that mattered could not be, so long as they held together. They pooled their holdings and their seed-stock and agreed never to undercut one another.
As food synthesis turned real food into a luxury, that agreement became one of the most powerful instruments in Alliance space. The Cooperative stopped being a price-bargaining club and became the gatekeeper of a resource the galaxy cannot do without and cannot reproduce. It has spent the years since perfecting two skills, looking harmless and never breaking ranks.
factions.politics:
Authority runs through the Harvest Councils, slow consensus assemblies where every holding has a voice, with the Alliance-chartered Agricultural Consortium Council as the public face. Beneath the egalitarian surface, the Seed-Holder rootlines carry the real weight, because they keep the seed vaults and the soil-lore, and without them the land does not produce.
The Cooperative's instrument is supply itself. It sets quotas, withholds or redirects production, and lets surplus spoil rather than flood the market, all of it presented as careful stewardship. It seldom needs to threaten, because the threat is implicit in every grain it ships. Its one unbreakable rule is solidarity: a holding that sells out the co-op loses the land and the loam, which is the only thing on Alsa worth having.
factions.culture: The Cooperative's culture is the rootline culture written large, patient and communal and unfailingly warm. It believes, sincerely, that food grown from living soil is better than anything a printer can extrude, and it has built a creed around the conviction, carried into the market by aligned enterprises like Goodman Holistic. The sincerity is real and so is the ruthlessness, and the Cooperative sees no contradiction between feeding the galaxy and charging it exactly what the privilege is worth.

relations.name: The Alliance
relations.note: Feeds the Alliance's core worlds and fleets, and receives in return the most heavily defended perimeter in known space. Food for protection, protection for quiet.

relations.name: Corporate replicators & biotech
relations.note: The corporations that sell synth food and the biotech houses trying to crack Alsa's fertility wage a constant covert war of biopiracy. The Field Wardens answer it in kind.

relations.name: Goodman Holistic
relations.note: The Cooperative's ideological cousin and friendliest public voice, spreading the natural-food creed and the brand that travels with it.

relations.name: The Patriark / Berilia
relations.note: The galaxy's other great life-monopoly, and the source of the long-embedded Patriark presence on Alsa. Elaborately cordial, mutually wary, and quietly entangled.

known_for: Control of the only large-scale supply of real, grown food in known space
Fertility that cannot be copied or transplanted off Alsa, an unbreakable natural monopoly
A wholesome farmers'-co-op face over a disciplined scarcity cartel
Field Wardens, the Cooperative's counter-biopiracy enforcers
Genuine incorruptibility through solidarity; Goodman Holistic as its aligned member
factions.legal_standing: Fully legal; Alliance-chartered trade organisation

factions.name: Worker Clans of Damph
factions.desc: The Worker Clans of Damph are not a corporation, which is the most useful fact about them. They are hereditary crime families wearing the clothes of a labour organisation, and they control the extraction of the only reliable coronthia in known space. That single fact carried a set of frozen-world mining families out of the seams and into the back rooms of Alliance politics. They run Damph as overlapping family rackets and feud among themselves without pause, and they close ranks the instant an outsider mistakes a blue collar for a weakness. They are legally recognised and genuinely dangerous, and the galaxy keeps buying from them because it has no one else to buy from.
factions.subtitle: Hereditary Crime Families with a Senator on Call
factions.quote: "They keep calling us a union. Fine. We are a union the way a loaded gun is a paperweight." (attributed to a Vethara Clan elder)
factions.history:
The clans began as survival pacts. On a world that kills careless workers by the shift, miners bound their families together to share the risk and to bargain with the companies that came for Damph's cheap cold. Generations turned those pacts into hereditary clans with their own courts and their own codes.
Coronthia changed what they were. Once Damph proved to hold the only dependable supply in known space, the clans stopped bargaining like workers and began bargaining like owners. They organised their own chaos, throttled their feuds enough to face outsiders as one, and learned that wealth this essential converts into something more durable than wages. It buys lawyers, and through them lawmakers. They are a labour organisation in roughly the way a cartel is a trade association.
factions.politics:
Authority sits with the Clan Council, where votes are weighted by extraction volume, so the family that pulls the most coronthia is heard first. Inside a clan, power is a family matter, with a boss or elder at the top and blood, marriage, and debt arranged below. Disputes between clans are settled by negotiation where possible and by quiet, deniable violence where not, under an unwritten code outsiders find baffling and clansmen find obvious.
The Council has one rule it will not break: the united front. The clans may bleed each other in the dark, but to a company, a regulator, or an Alliance inspector they speak with a single voice, because the monopoly is worth nothing the moment an outsider can set one clan against another.
factions.culture: Clan culture rewards competence, loyalty, and a debt paid in full, and it has no use for softness or for anyone who has never earned a callus. Respect is the only social currency that counts, and it cannot be bought, only earned, which makes the clans at once the most honest and the most dangerous people to deal with in Alliance space. They are proud of the work and proud of the cold, and they are quick to take offence at being treated as hired help by people who could not last a shift in the Deep Seams.

relations.name: Zang'Hai
relations.note: Largest employer, largest buyer, and oldest adversary. The two are tied together by need and will renegotiate the marriage until the coronthia runs out.

relations.name: The Alliance Senate
relations.note: Officially disapproving, privately dependent, and quietly on the payroll. Clan money and clan coronthia buy a hearing no labour organisation should command.

relations.name: Rival corporate buyers
relations.note: Every fleet-building power dreams of a coronthia supply it can control. The clans treat them as threats first and customers second.

known_for: Control of the only reliable coronthia supply in known space, and the leverage that comes with it
A hereditary clan structure built on blood, marriage, and debt rather than on employment
Crime-family business, protection and smuggling and enforcement, conducted under labour-law cover
Reach into the Alliance senate, bought with fifty years of coronthia money
A permanent, unwinnable rivalry with Zang'Hai, their largest partner and largest adversary
factions.legal_standing: Legally recognised labour organisations; Alliance labour law protections apply

factions.name: Hakari Matriarchal Clans
factions.desc: The Hakari Matriarchal Clans are one of the two native political structures on Mangara, currently engaged in a sustained civil conflict with the Jaulaus Tribal Councils that has no near-term resolution and appears designed by both parties to have none. The Hakari are matriarchally governed, with leadership authority tracing through female lineage. Their conflict with the Jaulaus has historical roots that predate outside contact and has been consistently resistant to outside mediation, possibly because both sides have internal factions that benefit from the conflict continuing. A phenomenon that complicates Hakari politics considerably is the diaspora inheritance problem: Hakari members living in Alliance Space regularly inherit clan leadership positions in communities they have never visited, acquiring cultural authority over people they have never met in a conflict they have only read about. Alliance mediators have documented this pattern frequently enough to treat it as a structural feature rather than an anomaly.
factions.subtitle: The Swift Predators of Mangara, and a War Inherited by Blood
factions.quote: "Prey waits for the future. We take it." (Mangaran war-saying, attributed to the Hakari Bloodmatrons)
factions.history:
The Hakari evolved in Mangara's choked equatorial jungles into lithe, lightning-fast ambush predators, lean and lethal in the dark, with low-light eyes and retractable claws that serve for climbing and for killing alike. Peace was never part of their world; for as long as anyone has recorded it, they have shared Mangara with the Jaulaus and fought them for it.
Then came the Nerulian slave raids, which dragged the Hakari out of technological infancy and into the wider galaxy in a single brutal era. When the Empire fell the Hakari were left changed, spacefaring and scattered, and still at war with the same enemy across the same jungle. Many now live offworld as exiles and wanderers, sought across Alliance space as shock troops and scouts, while the homeworld clans fight on.
factions.politics:
Hakari society is strictly matriarchal, with authority running through female lineage and real power held by the Bloodmatrons, the elder females who lead the clans. On Mangara that authority is absolute within a clan and absolutely opposed to the Jaulaus without.
Hakari politics carries one oddity that Alliance mediators long ago stopped trying to fix, the diaspora inheritance problem. A Hakari raised entirely offworld can inherit a clan leadership back on Mangara, acquiring cultural authority over people he has never met, in a war he knows only from reports. It happens often enough to be treated as a feature of the system rather than a fault in it. And like the Jaulaus, the clans hold internal factions that profit from the war and have no intention of letting it end.
factions.culture: Hakari culture prizes speed and nerve, and the predator's patience, the willingness to wait motionless in the dark and then take everything in a heartbeat. Pride is fierce and personal. Clan markings are worn openly, and a Hakari off Mangara will often layer them over his natural umber-to-olive colouring to declare a heritage he refuses to leave behind. They make formidable allies and exhausting ones, loyal to the clan above all and contemptuous of anyone who mistakes their grace for softness.

relations.name: Jaulaus Tribal Councils
relations.note: The other people of Mangara, and the enemy in every generation. The war with the Jaulaus is the oldest fact of Hakari life and, for the factions that profit from it, the most useful.

relations.name: The Alliance
relations.note: Recognised by Alliance protocol as a native government and resented as the keeper of the embargo. Mediation is heard out and ignored.

relations.name: The Hakari diaspora
relations.note: Offworld clans and exiles who serve as the galaxy's prized shock troops, and who, through the inheritance problem, can find themselves suddenly ruling a homeland war they have never seen.

known_for: One of two native power structures on Mangara, in sustained civil war
Matriarchal governance structure
Consistent resistance to outside mediation
Diaspora leadership inheritance as a documented structural problem
No influence or operations outside the Mangara system
factions.legal_standing: Recognised indigenous government under Alliance Mangara protocol

factions.name: Jaulaus Tribal Councils
factions.desc: The Jaulaus Tribal Councils are the second native political structure on Mangara, tribally organised with council-based governance, and in sustained conflict with the Hakari Clans for longer than outside observers have been recording Mangaran history, which is itself a considerable length of time. The conflict is self-sustaining in the way that conflicts tend to be when both sides have internal factions that benefit commercially and politically from its continuation. Alliance intelligence has noted that announced ceasefires between the Hakari and Jaulaus have historically served as reliable advance indicators of significant escalation, and has incorporated this into its standard assessment models as an established pattern rather than a coincidence.
factions.subtitle: The Resilient Warlords of Mangara, and a Grudge Without End
factions.quote: "The Hakari are fast. We are still here." (Jaulaus council proverb)
factions.history:
The Jaulaus evolved on the same brutal world as the Hakari and took the opposite road to surviving it. Where the Hakari became speed, the Jaulaus became endurance, massive, heavily built reptilian warriors with redundant organs and a tolerance for punishment that makes them very hard to put down. For as long as there has been a Mangara, they have held their ground against the faster people across the border.
The Nerulian slave raids hit them as hard as the Hakari, forcing the same violent leap into technology and the wider galaxy and leaving the same war intact when the Empire fell. Offworld, the Jaulaus are sought as shock troops and heavy-labour specialists, valued anywhere taking punishment is part of the job, while at home the Councils fight the war that has defined them for longer than anyone has been counting.
factions.politics:
The Jaulaus govern through tribal councils, consensus bodies of elders rather than a single ruler, communal and deliberate where the Hakari are personal and swift. Authority is collective, and so is the grudge.
Like their enemies, the Councils are riddled with internal factions that benefit from the war's continuation, and the result is a grimly reliable pattern. When the Jaulaus announce a ceasefire, Alliance intelligence reads it as advance warning of a major escalation, because that is what it has reliably preceded for decades. Peace, on the rare occasions it is offered, has become a weapon of its own.
factions.culture: Jaulaus culture is built on resilience and discipline, and on the team before the self. They are patient where the Hakari are explosive and immovable where the Hakari are sudden, and they take a deep communal pride in being the people who endure. Poor long-range sight pushed them long ago toward close-assault mastery, and a healthy Jaulaus in a melee, backup organs intact, is one of the hardest things in the galaxy to kill. They respect strength that holds its ground and have nothing but scorn for whatever relies on running away.

relations.name: Hakari Matriarchal Clans
relations.note: The faster people across the border, and the enemy of every generation. The Jaulaus do not expect to win the war so much as to outlast it, and outlasting is what they do best.

relations.name: The Alliance
relations.note: A recognised native government under the embargo protocol, and a people who treat Alliance mediation as noise. The blockade is resented and the recognition is used.

relations.name: The Jaulaus diaspora
relations.note: Offworld Jaulaus working as shock troops and heavy labour across Alliance space, sending word and worth home to a war most of them will never personally fight.

known_for: One of two native power structures on Mangara, in sustained civil war
Tribal council governance structure
Internal ceasefire-undermining factions documented across multiple decades
No influence or operations outside the Mangara system
Alliance intelligence classification of their ceasefires as escalation precursors
factions.legal_standing: Recognised indigenous government under Alliance Mangara protocol

factions.name: Lansing Corp
factions.hq: Undisclosed, believed Freeland or eastern Alliance Space
factions.desc: Lansing Corp builds the finest ships in the galaxy, and it has never once turned that into commercial dominance. Lansing vessels exceed every specification by margins wide enough to raise honest questions about whether the excess is good for anything, and they are priced to match the engineering in full, with interest. The market for ships that cost far more than a practical equivalent and do things no buyer will ever need is small, but it is devoted, and Lansing has lived on that devotion for generations. What keeps the company comfortable is less glamorous than the ships: Lansing owns Andromede, an empty volume of unusually clean space it bought cheap and now leases to every other builder that needs room of the same quality, and the rent is a steadier business than the shipyard has ever been.
known_for: Ships that exceed every specification by absurd margins, the most collected vessels in the galaxy
Overengineering so thorough it keeps the company only marginally profitable on shipbuilding alone
Ownership of Andromede, the clean-space shipyard district it leases to rival builders
A small but devoted collector and specialist clientele
An engineering reputation acknowledged even by competitors who cannot afford to stock its work
factions.legal_standing: Fully legal
factions.subtitle: The Finest Ships in the Galaxy, and the Landlord Who Can Barely Sell Them
factions.quote: "We were asked to build it cheaper. We declined." (Lansing design office, attributed, probably apocryphal, certainly accurate)
factions.history:
Lansing has only ever done one thing, and it has done it to a fault. From the start the company built ships the way a master builds a cathedral, past every requirement and every budget, on the conviction that a thing worth making is worth making perfectly. The galaxy admired the result and mostly bought elsewhere, because admiration is cheaper than ownership.
The shrewdest decision in Lansing's history had nothing to do with ships. Generations ago it bought Andromede, a worthless empty volume of clean space, for almost nothing, because clean space is exactly what large-scale shipbuilding needs. The yards it raised there are the best anywhere, and leasing the surplus to other builders quietly became the company's most reliable income. Lansing still loses patience with anyone who suggests it should simply build cheaper ships.
factions.politics: Lansing is privately held, secretive about its ownership, and organised entirely around the workshop. Engineers sit at the centre of the company, not executives, and the leadership has resisted for generations every pressure to compromise the product for the market. The result is a corporation that is artistically uncompromising and commercially mediocre, kept solvent less by its ships than by its real estate. Its ownership of Andromede gives it a quiet structural power it rarely needs to use, since a great many of its competitors build their ships on Lansing's land, under Lansing's terms.
factions.culture: Lansing's culture is perfectionism raised to a principle and held well past the point of sense. It does not build to a price or a deadline, only to a standard, and it treats every practical compromise as a small defeat. The people who work there are craftsmen first and employees second, and they carry the calm certainty of artisans who know their work is the best in existence and feel no obligation to make it affordable.

relations.name: Andromede tenants
relations.note: The rival builders and corporations that lease Lansing's clean space because nowhere else will do. Lansing earns more from their rent than from its own celebrated ships, a fact its engineers prefer not to dwell on.

relations.name: Voran Industries
relations.note: Often named as the company Voran failed against, which gives Lansing too much credit. Voran failed on its own and chose another trade. The two are simply opposite answers to the same question, one overbuilding into thin profits, the other giving up on quality altogether.

relations.name: The committed collectors
relations.note: A small, devoted clientele of heads of state, executives, and serious collectors, for whom a Lansing ship is a statement no practical vessel can make. They keep the shipyard alive; Andromede keeps it comfortable.

factions.name: Solistar Mineral Corporation
factions.desc: Solistar is the largest asteroid mining corporation in the galaxy, which is a business that rewards scale ruthlessly and punishes everyone else. Its operations span the major asteroid belts within Alliance Space and extend into frontier zones where extraction rights were established ahead of formal settlement, a practice that is technically legal and practically unstoppable once the extraction infrastructure is already in place. The business model is straightforward: find the ore, extract it, ship it, sell it. Solistar does this at a scale and efficiency that has eliminated most independent asteroid mining competition within Alliance Space, not through malice but through the simple mathematics of operating costs. Its relationship with the Zegitor Trade Guild is close and commercially significant, and its supply contracts with Arms Corp manufacturing on Ishtar represent one of the most important bilateral commercial relationships in the Alliance economy, which is to say that both organisations would notice immediately if the other ceased to exist.
factions.subtitle: The Company That Eats Asteroids, at a Scale No One Can Match
factions.quote: "There is no malice in it. There is only the arithmetic of operating costs, and the arithmetic has only ever had one answer." (Solistar operations briefing)
factions.history: Solistar won the belts the way scale always wins them, slowly and then all at once. It started as one operator among many in the Alliance asteroid fields, but asteroid mining punishes the small, and every downturn that bankrupted a competitor was a chance for Solistar to buy the claim and the equipment for a fraction of their worth. Over decades the consolidation compounded until independents simply could not match its per-tonne costs. The Arms Corp supply contract and the Zegitor Trade Guild relationship came once Solistar was large enough to guarantee volume no one else could, and those two ties have anchored it since.
factions.politics: Solistar's power sits at the bottom of the supply chain. Its contract with Arms Corp manufacturing on Ishtar is one of the most important bilateral relationships in the Alliance economy, the kind where each side would notice instantly if the other vanished, and its close ties to the Zegitor Trade Guild move its output across the galaxy. Control the raw material and you hold quiet leverage over everyone who turns it into anything.
factions.culture: Solistar is industrial to the bone, unsentimental and relentless, with the ethics of a balance sheet. It does not hate the competitors it erased any more than a glacier hates the valley it carves; it simply operated at a scale they could not, and kept operating. Efficiency is its only creed, and it has never felt the need for another.

relations.name: Arms Corp
relations.note: The Ishtar manufacturing that runs on Solistar ore, a relationship vital enough that neither side can afford the other's collapse.

relations.name: Zegitor Trade Guild
relations.note: The trade network that carries Solistar's output across the galaxy, a commercially significant alliance reaching beyond Alliance borders.

relations.name: Independent miners
relations.note: The competition Solistar's scale priced out of existence within Alliance space, casualties of arithmetic rather than aggression.

known_for: Largest asteroid mining operation in the galaxy
Dominant market position within Alliance Space extraction zones
Major supplier to Arms Corp manufacturing on Ishtar
Close commercial relationship with Zegitor Trade Guild
Frontier zone operations ahead of formal settlement, extraction rights established early
factions.legal_standing: Fully legal; Alliance extraction licensing

factions.name: Skalan Order
factions.hq: Unknown, believed to be outside Alliance Space in ungoverned territory
presence: Safe houses in the Dark Space and frontier worlds
factions.desc: The Skalan Order is the remnant of Skalanders who refused the death the Patriark designed for them. When the gene-edit ended the Skalander as a self-sustaining people, most of the race chose to meet extinction with the honour that defines them. The Order chose otherwise. It decided that survival and vengeance came first and that honour was a luxury of people who could afford to die, and in making that choice it set aside the code its own kind hold sacred. Mainstream Skalander society disowns the Order completely and with disgust, which is the single point on which the Order and its cousins on Caragh agree. The Order pursues Patriark accountability by any means it judges effective, claims nothing, explains nothing, and waits with the patience of people who have genuinely nothing left to lose.
known_for: Skalanders who reject the quiet extinction their kind has accepted, and fight on by any means
Honour set aside for survival and vengeance, the reason mainstream Skalander society disowns them
Patriark accountability as the defining, generational goal
Total operational secrecy: no public statements, no claimed actions
Cells throughout Alliance space, a haven in ungoverned space, and a hideout the Alliance suspects on Caragh
factions.legal_standing: Illegal throughout Alliance Space; Patriark-designated terrorist organisation
factions.subtitle: The Skalanders Who Refuse to Die Quietly
factions.quote: "Our cousins on Caragh will die with their honour intact. We intend to die with our enemies. One of us is being sentimental." (intercepted Skalan Order transmission, unverified)
factions.history:
The gene-edit that doomed the Skalander did not move every survivor to grace. A remnant looked at the same verdict, an engineered extinction handed down by the people who created them, and refused to accept it quietly. That remnant became the Skalan Order.
The choice cost them their place among their own. To fight the Patriark on any useful timescale, the Order had to abandon the honour code that defines Skalander identity, to deceive, to strike from hiding, to do the things an honourable Skalander would die before doing. They judged the survival of the species worth more than the dignity of its ending. Their cousins on Caragh judged the opposite, and the two have not spoken as kin since.
factions.politics:
The Order has no public structure and, as far as anyone outside can tell, no single head. It runs as scattered cells with a shared grievance and a shared patience, organised so that no captured member can give up more than a fragment of the whole. It claims no actions and issues no demands, which makes it nearly impossible to negotiate with and almost as hard to fight.
Its patience is its strongest weapon. The Order plans across timescales that defeat ordinary institutions, because a people already promised extinction has nothing to lose by waiting and everything to gain by choosing its moment. It keeps a haven in ungoverned space, cells across Alliance systems, and, the Alliance believes, a hideout on Caragh that the Skalander angrily deny.
factions.culture: The Order is a study in what honour costs and what it is worth. Its members carry the Skalander seriousness and the Skalander competence, turned to ends their own people consider shameful, and most of them know it. They have made their peace with being disgraced in the eyes of the only kin they have left, on the reasoning that there will be no kin at all if someone does not fight. It is a tragedy that both sides understand perfectly and neither can resolve.

relations.name: The Patriark
relations.note: The makers who engineered the Skalander extinction, and the single object of the Order's existence. Accountability, on whatever timescale and in whatever form, is the whole of the plan.

relations.name: Mainstream Skalander society
relations.note: Their own kind, who chose an honourable death over a dishonourable survival and will not be associated with the Order's methods. The disavowal is mutual, bitter, and entirely sincere on both sides.

relations.name: The Alliance
relations.note: Classes the Order as a terrorist organisation and hunts its cells, with little to show for it, since a faction that claims nothing and fears nothing gives an investigator almost nothing to hold.

factions.name: Assassin Guild
presence: Galactic, operates in all major regions
factions.desc: The Assassin Guild is exactly what the name describes, which in a galaxy full of organisations with deliberately misleading names is almost disorienting. Two distinctions separate it from every imitation: it operates at genuinely galactic scale, and it takes contracts that other organisations decline on grounds of difficulty, political sensitivity, or basic self-preservation. The Guild will take any contract. The price reflects difficulty, risk, and political complexity, and some contracts are priced at levels where accepting them is a statement of intent rather than a commercial transaction. The Guild's internal structure is unknown. Its membership is unknown. How contracts reach it is understood in criminal circles but not publicly documented. The only publicly observable data point is its record of completion, which is the entire reason it exists and the entire basis of its reputation.
factions.subtitle: It Takes Any Contract. The Price Is the Only Negotiation.
factions.quote: "There is no contract we refuse. There are only contracts priced so high that offering them is itself a kind of confession." (the one Guild statement anyone can quote)
factions.history: The Guild has no founding anyone can point to, which is consistent with everything else about it. It surfaced in criminal record-keeping not as an event but as a pattern: contracts that other outfits had refused turning up completed, by no one anyone could name. Over the years the pattern became a reputation and the reputation became the institution, because a buyer who needs the impossible done will pay enormously for the one party with a record of doing it. Whatever structure assembled behind that record has never been seen, and the Guild has spent its entire existence making sure it stays that way.
factions.politics: The Guild's power is its record and its opacity together. Its internal structure is unknown, its membership unknown, the route a contract takes to reach it understood in criminal circles but never documented. The one observable fact is its rate of completion, which is the whole of its reputation and the entire reason it can charge what it does. It stands apart from the system families and the pirate fleets, galaxy-wide and unaffiliated and selective in a way the merely violent never are.
factions.culture: The Guild is professional to the point of myth. It does not boast, claim, or explain; it completes, and lets the completions speak. Whatever code or structure holds it together is invisible from outside, and the invisibility is plainly deliberate, a discipline that has outlasted every attempt to map it. It sells certainty and charges accordingly.

relations.name: Anyone with the price
relations.note: The Guild's only real relationship, conducted at arm's length through channels no investigator has mapped. What it will do is bounded only by what a client can pay.

relations.name: Berilia
relations.note: The bloodline world with the galaxy's highest assassination rate keeps the Guild in steady, careful business, though the Guild chooses its Berilian clients as carefully as any others.

relations.name: Law enforcement everywhere
relations.note: The agencies that have tried for generations to find the Guild's structure and failed, left with nothing but a completion record and a name.

known_for: Contract killing at galactic scale
Takes any contract regardless of difficulty or political sensitivity
Pricing that reflects difficulty, risk, and political complexity in full
Operational secrecy, structure, membership, and contact methods not publicly known
A completion record that is its primary commercial reputation
factions.legal_standing: Illegal in all known jurisdictions

factions.name: Skav'nauts
factions.hq: No fixed headquarters, distributed throughout Alliance Space
factions.desc: The Skav'nauts are organised criminal gangs operating throughout Alliance Space who have built a distinctive cultural identity around their crimes: they collect proof of what they have done and wear it. Trophies, documentation, and evidence of corporate theft are displayed as clothing, insignia, and status markers, which makes identification by law enforcement straightforward and is presumably a feature rather than an oversight. The Skav'nauts target corporations specifically; individuals are not the primary target and civilian collateral is actively avoided, a policy discipline that has given them a romanticised reputation in communities that view corporate property crime as something between sport and public service. Their actual behaviour is more complicated than the reputation, but the reputation is the one that has stuck. Alliance law enforcement classifies them as a significant organised crime concern, which is accurate, and notes that the public sympathy problem makes prosecution politically awkward in certain jurisdictions.
factions.subtitle: The Gangs That Wear Their Crimes Where You Can See Them
factions.quote: "Of course it makes us easy to identify. That is the point. We did it, we are proud of it, and we want the corporation we did it to to know exactly who." (Skav'naut, recorded)
factions.history: No one founded the Skav'nauts; they accreted. They began as scattered crews knocking over corporate targets, and somewhere in the early years one crew started keeping proof, a stripped logo, a manifest, a piece of the thing they had taken, and wearing it. The habit spread because it worked as recruitment and as legend, and the scattered crews grew into a loose network that shared the practice if nothing else. The romantic reputation came later, built by communities that liked watching corporations lose, and the Skav'nauts have leaned into it ever since, because a folk hero is harder to prosecute than a thief.
factions.politics: The Skav'nauts have no headquarters and no single leader, only a distributed network with a remarkably consistent identity across every sector. Their power is cultural as much as criminal: the public sympathy that follows an anti-corporate outlaw makes prosecution politically awkward in certain jurisdictions, even as Alliance law enforcement rates them a serious organised-crime concern. Their actual conduct is more complicated than the legend, but the legend is the one that stuck, and they cultivate it.
factions.culture: The Skav'nauts are theatrical, defiant, and genuinely communal, bound less by a chain of command than by a shared posture toward the corporate order. Wearing your crimes is a creed; it turns a theft into a statement and a gang into a movement, at the cost of every shred of operational secrecy, a trade they make gladly and on purpose.

relations.name: The megacorporations
relations.note: The Skav'nauts' explicit and only real target. Everything about them, the thefts, the trophies, the posture, is pointed at corporate power and calibrated for an audience that enjoys watching it bleed.

relations.name: Sympathetic communities
relations.note: The publics that read the Skav'nauts as folk heroes, whose goodwill is the gangs' best armour against prosecution.

relations.name: Alliance law enforcement
relations.note: Rates them a serious concern and finds them politically awkward to pursue, since arresting a popular anti-corporate outlaw plays badly in the wrong districts.

known_for: Crimes against corporate targets, corporations are the explicit focus
Wearing proof of crimes as status symbols and clothing insignia
A distributed gang network with consistent cultural identity across all Alliance sectors
A romanticised reputation among some communities that views them as anti-corporate
Alliance law enforcement priority target
factions.legal_standing: Illegal throughout Alliance Space

factions.name: Wastelanders
factions.hq: No fixed headquarters, mobile throughout frontier and Alliance worlds
factions.desc: The Wastelanders are the galaxy's practical distribution network for goods that need to move without documentation, a service that turns out to have substantial commercial demand from clients who technically do not exist in any official supply chain record. Loosely organised in mobile gang structures, they operate vehicles, ships, and convoys across inhabited and frontier worlds alike. They are not primarily violent; their commercial model depends on deliveries completing, and violence is bad for completion rates. They do operate in contested and ungoverned space as a matter of course, and they are equipped for the realities of those environments without being defined by them. The Wastelanders handle a significant fraction of frontier distribution that no licensed carrier will service, which makes them indispensable to frontier economies that Alliance logistics networks have never adequately reached. Finding them is less difficult than it sounds. They are in most transit environments. You just need to know which questions to ask.
factions.subtitle: The Delivery Network for Things With No Paperwork
factions.quote: "We are not hard to find. We are in every transit yard you have ever been through. You simply have to know which question to ask, and not be the sort who would report the answer." (Wastelander runner)
factions.history: The Wastelanders grew out of a gap, the enormous stretch of frontier and ungoverned space that licensed carriers never bothered to serve. Independent haulers who ran those routes anyway found one another, traded information and fuel and safe stops, and over time the cooperation hardened into a loose, mobile network with shared habits and shared contacts. No one chartered it and no one runs it. It simply became the way things move where the official supply chain stops, and the demand for moving things quietly has only grown.
factions.politics: The Wastelanders are indispensable precisely where the Alliance's logistics never adequately reached, which gives a stateless smuggling network real structural importance on the frontier. They are not primarily violent, because their whole model depends on deliveries completing and violence is bad for completion rates. They work contested and ungoverned space as a matter of course, equipped for its realities without being defined by them.
factions.culture: The Wastelanders are pragmatic above all, a culture of runners and drivers who measure themselves by whether the cargo arrived. They prize reliability and discretion over toughness, treat the open road as home, and regard the licensed carriers who will not service the frontier as the real reason they get to exist. They are criminals chiefly in the sense that the paperwork says so.

relations.name: Frontier economies
relations.note: The settlements and operations the Alliance's licensed logistics never properly served, for whom the Wastelanders are the practical, and sometimes only, way to get goods in and out.

relations.name: Anyone needing quiet transport
relations.note: Clients official and unofficial who need something moved without a record, from the merely uninsured to the frankly illegal.

relations.name: Alliance customs & carriers
relations.note: The licensed system the Wastelanders route around, less an enemy than an obstacle they have spent generations learning to read.

known_for: Frontier and ungoverned space distribution, goods that need to move without paperwork
Mobile gang organisation, no fixed base
Non-violent as a commercial preference; equipped for frontier realities
Present in most transit environments throughout Alliance and frontier space
The practical option for distribution that legitimate carriers will not handle
factions.legal_standing: Illegal; enforcement priority varies by jurisdiction and available resources

factions.name: Seto Syndicate
factions.desc: The Seto Syndicate is the largest of the Sirius crime families and the most persuasive argument that organised crime and organised business are the same operation with different filing systems. Where most criminal outfits depend on loyalty, intimidation, and whoever currently controls the largest weapon, the Syndicate runs on defined planning horizons, operational divisions with clear remits, succession planning, and the kind of institutional memory that most legitimate corporations spend money trying to build and never quite manage. Financial operations, illegal logistics, protection arrangements, political influence, and contract services run simultaneously across multiple systems. The Sirius families collectively represent the most significant criminal infrastructure in Alliance Space. The Seto Syndicate is the largest and oldest among them, which is either impressive or deeply alarming depending entirely on whether you are a client or a creditor.
factions.subtitle: Organised Crime, Heavy Emphasis on Organised
factions.quote: "The difference between us and a corporation is that we honour our contracts. The difference between us and a government is that we deliver." (attributed to a Seto oyabun)
factions.history: Seto began as one family among several in the Sirius underworld, and what set it apart early was patience. While rivals fought over this year's territory, Seto invested in structure: in succession that did not collapse when a boss died, in records, in people groomed for roles a decade ahead. That discipline let it absorb or outlast the families that lived hand to mouth, and over generations it grew from a crime family into a criminal institution with the reach of a corporation and a memory longer than most governments.
factions.politics: Seto runs on a fusion of corporate hierarchy and a family code older than the Alliance. An oyabun sits at the top; beneath him the divisions handle their remits with the precision of a real company, bound by obligations of loyalty and face that no employment contract could enforce. The Syndicate keeps order wherever it operates, not out of civic feeling but because chaos is bad for business, which makes it, on Sirius, less an underworld than a parallel government with better turnaround times.
factions.culture: Seto culture is yakuza discipline raised to a corporate art, all hierarchy and the sanctity of a debt. Reputation is capital and a given word is binding, which makes Seto a strangely reliable partner and a creditor you never want to disappoint. The politeness is genuine. So is everything underneath it.

relations.name: Tanaka Syndicate
relations.note: The junior Sirius family, useful for the grubby local work Seto keeps at arm's length, and never allowed to forget which of them sets the scale.

relations.name: The Alliance
relations.note: Its reach runs deep into the institutions meant to stop it, financial and judicial alike. Catching Seto means going through people Seto already owns.

relations.name: Yamato Corporation
relations.note: Two powers large enough to ruin each other and disciplined enough not to try. They keep to their lanes, and the lanes are drawn with great care.

known_for: Largest single organised crime operation in Alliance Space
Sirius-based with genuinely galactic reach across all operational categories
Corporate structure with planning horizons most businesses cannot match
The dominant power among the Sirius crime families
Political and financial reach extending deep into institutions that are supposed to stop them
factions.legal_standing: Illegal; Alliance intelligence priority target

factions.name: Tanaka Syndicate
presence: Alliance Space, frontier and border regions
factions.desc: The Tanaka Syndicate is the second significant crime family operating out of Sirius, handling the local affairs the Seto Syndicate considers beneath its operational scale. Where Seto runs a galaxy-spanning corporate structure, Tanaka keeps things local and personal. Protection, local distribution, workforce arrangements of the involuntary variety, and the kind of municipal contract work that functions best when the counterparty either does not read the fine print or has concluded that raising objections would be inadvisable. Allegations of ties to the Alliance itself have circulated for years, alongside persistent claims of financial backing from Yamato Corporation, which has denied everything with the practised ease of an organisation that has been denying things for centuries and has never once been made to stop. Whether Yamato is funding a local crime operation or merely maintaining a commercially convenient relationship with one is, legally speaking, a distinction of considerable importance that nobody in a position to investigate seems motivated to pursue.
factions.subtitle: The Street Family That Answers to Someone Else
factions.quote: "Seto sends a lawyer. We send someone you already know. It is more personal that way." (Tanaka saying)
factions.history:
The Tanaka Syndicate grew up in Seto's shadow, taking the local, hands-on work the larger family thought beneath its scale. Where Seto reached across the galaxy, Tanaka kept things close, a neighbourhood or a dock or a district, run in person and held by force.
Somewhere along the way the money changed. Claims of Yamato backing have trailed Tanaka for years, alongside whispers of ties to the Alliance itself, and the family's reach quietly outgrew anything its street rackets could fund. Whether Yamato owns Tanaka or merely rents it is a distinction no one in a position to investigate seems eager to settle.
factions.politics: Tanaka is local and personal, and brutal by preference. Protection, distribution, involuntary labour, and the municipal contract work that runs best when the counterparty does not read the fine print are all handled in person, through fear and loyalty rather than Seto's careful divisions. It is the smaller and dirtier family, and it survives by doing what the respectable powers want done and will never admit to wanting. Its dependence on Yamato money is the leash it pretends not to wear.
factions.culture: Tanaka keeps the old codes, loyalty and face, but strips away Seto's corporate polish. It is the family as street gang, closer and hungrier, and quicker to violence, the muscle the city's clean powers deny knowing while relying on it constantly.

relations.name: Seto Syndicate
relations.note: The larger family whose scale Tanaka cannot match and whose leftovers it lives on. Resentful and useful, and careful never to overreach.

relations.name: Yamato Corporation
relations.note: The suspected source of the money that lifted Tanaka above a mere street outfit, and the hand it quietly answers to.

relations.name: The Alliance
relations.note: Rumoured connections no investigation has ever pursued, which on Sirius is less an absence of evidence than an absence of will.

known_for: Dominant in local Sirius criminal affairs below the Seto Syndicate's operational scale
Alleged Alliance ties, unconfirmed and apparently uninvestigated
Suspected Yamato Corporation financial backing, denied by all parties
Local enforcement of the kind that does not involve filing paperwork
The practical infrastructure of Sirius crime for anyone who cannot afford Seto rates
factions.legal_standing: Illegal; investigation status unclear given alleged institutional ties

factions.name: Nerulian Pirate Fleet
factions.hq: Dispersed galaxy-wide; spiritual capital San Tien; rumoured Sirius asteroid base
factions.desc: The largest pirate force in known space is less a fleet than a nation that lost its country. It is Nerulian, and it amounts to the surviving remnant of the Nerulian Empire, scattered into every region of the galaxy after the Kravens took their worlds. Only a few thousand keep San Tien, the last Nerulian world, as a capital; most never see it, and many are void-born, raised and buried aboard ships that have not made planetfall in a lifetime. The fleet is also the most convincing argument available that Kintech's claimed independence from San Tien is not accurate: the operational overlap between Kintech equipment and Nerulian pirate vessels is noted in every serious intelligence assessment of the region, and has been noted consistently enough that not drawing the obvious conclusion requires a specific effort of will. There is additionally a persistent and widely-credited rumour of a major pirate base somewhere in the asteroid belt near the Sirius system, a staging point for operations that reach well into Alliance Space. The rumour is old enough and consistent enough across independent sources that most intelligence analysts treat it as probable. The base, if it exists, has not been found, which is either a tribute to its concealment or a commentary on how hard anyone is looking.
factions.subtitle: The Largest Pirate Fleet in the Galaxy, Crewed by a Fallen Empire
factions.quote: "The Nerulians once ruled a thousand systems. Now they raid the lanes of the people who outlived them. They have not forgotten which of those they would prefer." (Alliance naval intelligence)
factions.history: The fleet is what the Nerulian Empire became after the Kraven ate it. When the Empire fell, its survivors scattered to the borders of their old territory with their warships and their grievances intact and nothing left to rule, and piracy was the obvious second career for a people who had spent a thousand years taking what they wanted. They gathered at San Tien, on the edge of the dead Empire, and over the decades the scattered raiders consolidated into the largest organised fleet in known space, armed, the evidence suggests, by a Nerulian corporation that shares their cause and denies sharing anything else.
factions.politics: The fleet's power is reach and reputation. It strikes well into Alliance border systems and trades on the terror the Nerulian name still carries, the inherited menace of an empire of conquerors and slavers. A persistent, widely credited rumour places a major pirate base in the asteroid belt near Sirius, a staging point for operations deep in Alliance space; it has never been found, which is either a tribute to its concealment or a comment on how hard anyone is looking.
factions.culture: The fleet is what remains of a people who were once the greatest power in the galaxy and are now its most feared raiders, and it carries that fall like a grievance. There is pride in the menace, a refusal to be pitied, and an old bitterness toward the Alliance that inherited a galaxy the Nerulians used to own. They raid for profit and, not far beneath it, for spite.
