The Aderan Correctional Consortium operates the galaxy's largest for-profit prison facility here, housing criminals from across known space under contracts from the Alliance justice system, corporate security departments, and private clients who do not always specify what the inmate did. What makes Aderan 3 famous beyond the prison industry is the broadcasting. Three of the most watched programmes in the galaxy, Ridge Racing, Survivor, and Blood Bowl, are recorded here, using inmates as participants.

planets.name: Ashvel
planets.atm_note: Trace carbon dioxide, negligible pressure
planets.temperature: Cold, roughly -40°C to 8°C
planets.access_note: Unrestricted, nothing of commercial value confirmed.
hazards: Thin atmosphere provides no radiation shielding
Surface temperature extremes
No infrastructure within recovery range
planets.desc: A small, barren rocky world between the Aderan Prime debris field and the surviving worlds of the system. Called Ashvel in navigational logs, the name predates the corporate war, when it was surveyed and found unremarkable. The Consortium has not expressed interest in it. It orbits in silence, unchanged by everything that has happened in the system around it: the corporate war, the destruction, the prison empire, the broadcasting.

planets.name: Gorthon
planets.atm_note: Dense hydrogen-helium envelope with ammonia cloud bands
planets.temperature: Cryogenic cloud tops, roughly -110°C to -180°C; far hotter in the deep atmosphere under pressure
planets.economy: None, no fuel licensing in this system
planets.access_note: No commercial infrastructure. Outer system.
hazards: Standard gas giant hazards, pressure, radiation, gravity gradient
planets.desc: A large gas giant in the outer Aderan system, named Gorthon in navigational records. Unlike Sirius, no commercial fuel operation has been established here, the Aderan system's reputation for corporate conflict and the Consortium's tight grip on access have made independent operators reluctant to invest in infrastructure they might not be allowed to use. Gorthon orbits without infrastructure, observed by the Consortium's security network as a matter of routine patrol coverage.

planets.name: Crethis
planets.temperature: Frozen, roughly -80°C to -30°C
planets.access_note: Extreme outer system.
hazards: Extreme cold
Isolation
planets.desc: A frozen outer world named Crethis at the edge of the Aderan system's charted territory, primarily ice and rock, far enough from the system's activity to be effectively invisible to the Consortium's monitoring network. Its distance from everything commercial makes it an occasional rendezvous point for vessels that prefer not to appear in Aderan's approach records. Whether the Consortium is aware of this use is a question that experienced operators leave unanswered.

catalogue_systems.name: Berilia System
catalogue_systems.desc: Berilia is the Patriark homeworld and the quiet centre of the galaxy's most important dependency: resurrection technology. The Patriarks built no army. Instead they spent centuries making themselves indispensable. The cloning infrastructure on Berilia underpins the Alliance's promise of continuity, and the Patriarks know exactly what it would cost everyone if they renegotiated their terms.
catalogue_systems.subtitle: Homeworld of the Patriark, and the Quiet Owner of Resurrection
catalogue_systems.quote: "They sell the rest of us a second life and call it mercy. Among themselves they use the same machinery to settle arguments. You learn quickly on Berilia: a body is a position, not a person, and positions change hands." (Adjutant Vess Corellin, Alliance trade legation, recalled at her own request)
catalogue_systems.history:
Berilia is the homeworld of the Patriark, though the word covers two very different peoples, and the difference explains the planet. They began as the Arcor. Threatened with extermination by the Nemanian Empire, the Arcor engineered a warrior offshoot to fight the war for them, and that offshoot became the Skalander. When the danger passed the species did not reunite. The warriors kept the fighting; the scholars kept Berilia and the older name. Those early Patriark were what the reputation still describes, a patient and studious people who preferred to advise from a distance and to outlive their mistakes rather than answer for them.
That reputation has since become a sales pitch. The Patriark who run Berilia today are politicians before they are anything else. Over many centuries they turned their grasp of biology into the one service no one in the galaxy can do without, reliable resurrection, and the money and leverage that followed changed them. A gap opened between the old houses, who still believe the stewardship creed, and the newer regimes, who treat heredity as a thing to be improved and sentiment as a weakness. From the outside the two are hard to tell apart. Only one of them still means what it says.
catalogue_systems.politics:
Berilia is governed by the Patriark Directorate, a council drawn from the major bloodline houses. In theory it deliberates for the long good of the species. In practice it is a slow and courteous struggle over which gene-lines deserve to continue, and in what form, conducted by people who count their plans in generations.
Status is inherited but never safe. A house is judged by the quality of its bloodline, and the judgment is exact. When an heir disappoints, the newer regimes do not disown him. They rebuild him, quietly, into the same body with the flaws corrected, and present the improved version at the next gathering as if nothing had happened. An heir who cannot be improved is simply not mentioned again. None of this is ever admitted, because on Berilia a scandal is more dangerous than a death.
What keeps the arrangement survivable is the Patriark relationship with death, which is also why Berilia records more assassinations for its population than any world in Alliance space. A Patriark mind does not end with its body. Given a willing host or a waiting clone, it goes on. Killing a rival therefore settles very little. It removes him from his position and forces him through a rebuilding he may not control, which is usually the point. The real instrument of power is not the weapon but the resurrection behind it: who is allowed a backup, and in what body they come back. Most of the killing is hired out, and there is no shortage of professionals. Everyone understands the system. No one of standing names it.

dominant_race.name: Patriark
dominant_race.lore:
The Patriark sell the galaxy one flattering picture of themselves, the Ancient Shepherds, deathless and wise, steering younger species clear of catastrophe. The Berilian Order believes the picture completely. Most Patriark treat it the way any old institution treats its founding story, as useful advertising.
What is true is that a Patriark mind genuinely persists. They do not age, and poison does nothing to them. When the body dies the mind can pass into a willing host and live on beside the host's own, carrying its memory and skill with it. That is an intimate and awkward arrangement, and it is the reason the Patriark perfected cloning in the first place, since a blank body of one's own is far preferable to sharing someone else's. Selling that same continuity to every other species for a price made them quietly rich and quietly indispensable, which suits a people who would rather own the lever than be seen holding it.
The Berilia-born Patriark of the present are political animals before they are anything else, polished and very hard to read, an effect the Veil only deepens. Whether the one across the table treats you as a guest or as an asset is exactly the thing you are not meant to be able to tell.

race_standing.note: Home, and the only people on Berilia whose continuity is genuinely assured, provided they stay useful to their house.

The Patriark seeded humanity and left before it had writing, and they regard the old experiment with a proprietary, faintly amused affection. A human is welcome as a client and useful as labour, and never mistaken for an equal.

The brother-race the Arcor built and then left to die out. A Skalander on Berilia is treated with great courtesy and watched closely, because his presence raises the one subject no Patriark will discuss aloud.
Heirs of the empire that once tried to wipe the Arcor out. Berilia has a long memory. A Nerulian is served and shown the door.
A mind that cannot be charmed or read is a real problem for a culture built on managing what others perceive. The Patriark value Psylon for that incorruptibility and never quite trust it.
Hired in numbers as security and couriers. Respected for their lethality and kept to those roles.
Useful as guards and as heavy labour. Their bluntness passes, by Patriark standards, for restful company, which is not quite a compliment.

The quiet joke of the cloning capital. Bodies grown without a birth are everywhere on Berilia and count for nothing socially, while the houses that prize pure descent depend on artificial bodies absolutely and would rather not examine the contradiction.

relations.name: Berilian Order
relations.note: Affiliated and sincere. The Order actually believes the shepherd creed the houses merely sell, which is precisely what makes it useful to them.

relations.name: The Alliance / Galactic Union
relations.note: The Alliance leans on Berilian resurrection and cannot easily do without it. The Patriark have never needed a fleet, because the possibility of revising their terms does the work a fleet would.

relations.name: Assassin Guild
relations.note: Berilia keeps the galaxy's busiest market in hired killing, but the Guild is a separate matter, galaxy-wide and unbought, and it picks its own clients. When it takes an interest in a Berilian affair, the houses pay attention.

catalogue_systems.gm_notes: Run Berilia as good manners laid over a knife. Nothing is openly hostile; everything is an assessment. Violence is indirect and almost never final, and a contact who is murdered may surface weeks later, slightly altered and unwilling to discuss it. The real danger is never the weapon. It is owing the wrong house a favour, or learning something a bloodline would rebuild a relative to keep quiet.

planets.name: Berilia
planets.atm_note: Clean oceanic atmosphere, notably high oxygen, low particulates. Pleasant to most species.
planets.temperature: ~15°C to 30°C (mild, oceanic)
planets.grav_note: Below standard, Patriark physiology adapted. Non-Patriarks find the low gravity pleasant.
planets.demographics: ~85% Patriark, remainder mixed, diplomatic staff and medical tourism
planets.economy: Cloning and resurrection services, biological research, pharmaceutical production, political consultation
planets.access_note: Visitor permits available but processed with comprehensive background checks. The Patriarks are careful about who they let in.
hazards: Patriark political manipulation, every interaction may be an intelligence-gathering exercise
Legal frameworks heavily favour Patriark citizens on home soil
Corporate surveillance targeting cloning research is constant
The dependency economy means the Patriarks hold significant leverage over anyone needing their services

notable_locations.name: The Cloning Spires
notable_locations.desc: The most advanced cloning and resurrection facilities in the galaxy. The actual processes are proprietary and kept from outside observation. The output, reliable resurrection across multiple species, is a dependency the Alliance cannot afford to disrupt.

notable_locations.name: The Archive of Lives
notable_locations.desc: Records of every individual who has passed through Berilia's cloning facilities. The archive is extraordinarily sensitive. The Patriarks maintain it as a private resource. Others have tried to access it. None successfully.

notable_locations.name: Berilia Wet Docks
notable_locations.desc: The main port, built to accommodate the oceanic environment. Ships dock at surface platforms; cargo and passengers are ferried by submersible to the main cities below. An unusual and disorienting entry experience.

notable_locations.name: The Directorate Hall
notable_locations.desc: The seat of Patriark governance. Accessible to invited diplomatic visitors. The real decisions that affect the galaxy are made here by people who have been planning them for decades.

specialties.name: Tide-Grown Delicacies
specialties.desc: Rare shellfish and kelp cultivars raised on Berilia oceanic farms and served at Directorate functions. Exquisite, absurdly expensive, and a quiet way of showing which house can afford them.

specialties.name: Beryl Reserve
specialties.desc: A pale, nearly flavourless spirit the Patriark prize for its subtlety. The offworld joke is that drinking it is like Patriark conversation: you are never quite sure what just happened.

hooks: The Patriark Archive of Lives is believed by intelligence professionals across the galaxy to be the most complete record of individual identities ever assembled, containing not just cloning data but biographical detail accumulated through decades of client interaction. It is widely assumed that the Patriarks use this archive as an active intelligence asset, not merely a service record. No external party has ever successfully accessed it, and the Patriarks have never confirmed or denied its full scope.

Medical researchers and cloning specialists have noted for decades that the published output of Berilia's cloning facilities contains statistical anomalies inconsistent with the biological error rates their own research predicts. The leading explanation among specialists who study the field is that the Patriarks routinely produce results they do not publish, results whose nature is the subject of considerable speculation.

It is an established fact among the galaxy's intelligence community that getting any operative onto Berilia without the Patriark Directorate's awareness is essentially impossible, their background screening process is more thorough than any government security clearance in Alliance Space, and the Patriarks share information about suspicious applicants between themselves in ways that have caught multiple attempts by different agencies to place assets on-world.
planets.desc: Berilia is a predominantly oceanic world and the homeworld of the Patriark, a species whose evolutionary environment shaped them into some of the most capable political operators in the galaxy. The Patriarks have no meaningful military force. They have never needed one. Instead, over centuries, they accumulated something more durable and more difficult to counter: leverage. The Patriark-owned cloning infrastructure on Berilia is the most advanced in existence. Resurrection technology that the rest of the galaxy depends on runs through Berilia in some form. The Patriarks built this dependency deliberately, over generations, as policy.

planets.name: Berilia II
planets.atm_note: Sulphur dioxide and volcanic gas, lethal without full respiratory protection
planets.temperature: Up to ~600°C at the surface (active volcanism)
planets.economy: None, the Patriarks have no interest in industrialising their system
planets.access_note: Unrestricted. No infrastructure. Patriark patrol vessels monitor system traffic.
hazards: Active volcanism throughout
Toxic atmosphere
Extreme surface temperatures
planets.desc: A volcanically active inner world in the Berilia system, frequently illuminated by lava flows visible even from orbit. The Patriarks have never developed it, their philosophy of careful stewardship extends to leaving hostile worlds undisturbed. Their patrol vessels ensure it stays that way.

planets.name: Berilia III
planets.atm_note: Dense hydrogen-helium envelope with striking blue-white banding
planets.temperature: Cryogenic cloud tops, around -150°C
planets.access_note: No infrastructure. Patriark vessels occasionally use its gravity well for orbital manoeuvring.
hazards: Gas giant pressure and radiation zones
planets.desc: A large gas giant with several moons, visible from Berilia's ocean surface as a bright blue-white disc. The Patriarks have catalogued its moons but show no interest in colonisation or exploitation. It serves as a reference point for system navigation.

catalogue_systems.name: Mangara System
catalogue_systems.faction: Contested, Hakari Clans vs Jaulaus Tribes
catalogue_systems.desc: Mangara is the homeworld of the Hakari and Jaulaus and one of the most uncomfortable chapters in Alliance history. Exploited by the Nerulian Empire and then by corporate interests, placed under Alliance embargo to protect what remains of its traditional life, and still burning from an inter-species civil war that has never stopped.
catalogue_systems.subtitle: Two Peoples and One Jungle, in a War That Will Not End
catalogue_systems.quote: "Outsiders keep asking when the war will end. They have misunderstood. The war is not something that happens on Mangara. The war is Mangara." (an Alliance mediator's closing report, filed under Abandoned)
catalogue_systems.history:
Mangara is the homeworld of the Hakari and the Jaulaus, two predator peoples who shared one brutal equatorial jungle and were already at war with each other long before anyone from outside arrived to make it worse. The jungle bred both into lethal, watchful survivors, and it bred a border war that has been redrawn in blood more times than anyone has counted.
Then the outside arrived. Before the Alliance existed, and before their own empire fell, the Nerulians raided Mangara for slaves and sold its peoples through the Nemanian markets. That predation is the grim reason Mangara developed as fast as it did. Dragged out of technological infancy in a single brutal era by the demands of its slavers, the Hakari and Jaulaus were forced into industry and offworld contact within a few generations. Shared suffering did not unite them. They carried the war into the new era unchanged.
When the Nerulian Empire fell and the Alliance rose, corporate interests moved in to strip what the slavers had left. In the end the Alliance sealed the system under embargo, an exclusion zone meant to protect what remained of traditional Mangaran life and, just as much, to quarantine a civil war it had given up trying to end. The embargo holds, mostly. The war holds entirely.
catalogue_systems.politics:
Mangara has no unified government and never has. Power belongs to the two native structures, the Hakari Matriarchal Clans and the Jaulaus Tribal Councils, each governing its own people and territory, each set against the other in a civil war with no front line and no end.
The important thing about that war is that it is built not to end. Both sides hold internal factions that profit from its continuation, so peace is bad for business on both sides. Alliance mediators documented this for decades and gave up, and Alliance intelligence now reads an announced ceasefire as a reliable warning of a coming escalation rather than a step toward peace.
Officially the embargo seals Mangara off to protect it. In practice it also freezes the conflict in place and feeds a healthy black market. Smugglers run weapons past the blockade to both sides, who buy eagerly, and corporate survey teams probe the under-watched edges of the system for whatever they can quietly take. Everyone outside claims to want the war over. Almost no one outside profits from its ending.

dominant_race.name: Hakari and Jaulaus
dominant_race.lore:
Mangara belongs to two peoples, and they have never agreed on anything except that it is theirs. The Hakari are lithe, lightning-fast ambush predators, matriarchal and proud. The Jaulaus are massive, resilient reptilian warlords, communal and immovable. The jungle that made them made them opposite, and made them enemies, and the war between them is older than any record of it.
What they share is a history of being prey to something worse. The Nerulian slave raids that scarred both peoples should have united them and never did, and the centuries since have only deepened the divide. To understand either people you have to understand the other, because each has spent its whole existence defined against the one across the border. Their fuller stories live with their governments, the Hakari Matriarchal Clans and the Jaulaus Tribal Councils, who are also the war's two combatants.
The war is only part of it. The gravity wears down anything not bred for it, and the sky drops rock without warning, since Mangara's orbit carries it through a dense asteroid belt and lethal meteor showers fall almost daily. Sudden death is a fact of Mangaran life, which goes some way toward explaining why neither people frightens easily.

race_standing.note: One of the two native peoples, at home in their own territory and the enemy in Jaulaus country. A Hakari on Mangara is never neutral to anyone.
The other native people, sovereign in their own territory and the foe in Hakari lands. There is no neutral ground for a Jaulaus on Mangara either.

The former slavers who raided Mangara for generations. It is the one thing the Hakari and Jaulaus agree on without reservation: a Nerulian who sets foot here is in mortal danger from both sides at once.

An outsider, and on Mangara an outsider is a smuggler, a corporate scout, or an Alliance enforcer, none of them trusted. Tolerated when useful, such as when running arms to one side, and watched the rest of the time.
Smooth offworld operators in a place that learned the hard way what offworld interest costs. Received with deep suspicion by peoples who were once a resource to be harvested.
Fellow warriors with a code, which earns a wary respect from both natives. About as close to safe passage as an outsider gets on Mangara, which is not very close.
Cold offworld minds on a world that trusts no offworlder. Hired by smugglers and welcomed by no one.
Rare here, and to peoples once treated as disposable bodies, an uncomfortable reminder. Outsiders either way, and outsiders are not trusted on Mangara.

relations.name: The Alliance
relations.note: Maintains the embargo that seals Mangara off, officially to protect it and practically to quarantine a war it cannot end. Resented as a jailer and leaned on as a shield, in roughly equal measure.

relations.name: The Nerulians
relations.note: The former slavers whose raids both built and scarred Mangara. The Empire is gone; the hatred is not, and it is the one thing the two native peoples share without reservation.

relations.name: Smugglers & corporate survey teams
relations.note: The embargo created a black market. Smugglers arm both sides and corporate scouts strip the under-watched edges of the system. To outsiders, Mangara's misery is simply a business.

catalogue_systems.gm_notes: Run Mangara as a war that is the setting, not the backdrop. The embargo makes it a forbidden and dangerous place even to reach, and once there nothing is neutral ground. The crucial truth for players is that the locals do not want the war ended, because too many on both sides profit from it, so bringing peace to Mangara is a fool's errand the natives will quietly sabotage. Strong plots: running the blockade, arming or extracting from one side, corporate biopiracy in the lethal jungle, and getting caught between two peoples who agree on nothing except hating Nerulians. Keep the sky dangerous too, since meteor showers fall almost daily and being caught in the open is a hazard in its own right. And do not forget the Hakari diaspora twist, where an offworld character can inherit clan authority over a community they have never met, in a war they have only read about.

planets.name: Mangara
planets.atm_note: Breathable but degraded, centuries of industrial exploitation visible in atmosphere quality
planets.temperature: Hot and humid, roughly 28°C to 45°C, brutal in the deep canopy
planets.grav_note: Markedly higher than standard. Outsiders tire fast and bruise easily, and it is a large part of why both native peoples are as physically formidable as they are.
planets.demographics: Mixed Hakari and Jaulaus, no reliable census, both groups distributed across territories
planets.government: None, clan and tribal governance, no unified authority
planets.economy: Subsistence agriculture, conflict economy, illicit corporate extraction via intermediaries
planets.access_note: Alliance embargo, ships require Alliance waiver to enter system. Landing without waiver treated as hostile. Corporate vessels operate through legitimate-looking intermediaries.
hazards: Active inter-species civil war, all outsiders treated as potential threats by both factions
Alliance patrol ships operate in-system, entry without waiver risks boarding
Corporate intelligence extraction operations, unknown actors active throughout
Ecological degradation, significant terrain sectors toxic from historical extraction
Deep population hostility to outsiders runs across both species

Frequent meteor showers from the system's dense asteroid belt. Mangara passes through the debris daily, and strikes range from harmless streaks to ground-cratering impacts; open terrain is never entirely safe.

notable_locations.name: The Contested Line
notable_locations.desc: The rough border between current Hakari-dominant and Jaulaus-dominant territories. It has moved continuously for centuries. Crossing it without appropriate cultural knowledge is extremely hazardous.

notable_locations.name: Old Extraction Sites
notable_locations.desc: The ruins of Nerulian-era and corporate mining and extraction operations, now mostly abandoned. Both species consider them sacred ground, reminders of what was taken from them.

notable_locations.name: Port Neutral
notable_locations.desc: A small, barely-functional port that somehow both sides allow to operate. Corporate intermediaries, smugglers, and the occasional genuine relief worker pass through here. The Alliance doesn't officially acknowledge its existence.

specialties.name: Jungle Pharma (Smuggled)
specialties.desc: Rare medicinal and toxic compounds wrung from Mangara's hyper-lethal biosphere, worth fortunes offworld and the prime reason corporate teams risk the embargo at all. Most of it leaves the system in a smuggler's hold.

specialties.name: Bloodvine Liquor
specialties.desc: A potent traditional ferment that both peoples make, separately, and both insist they invented. One of the very few things Hakari and Jaulaus have in common, and they will fight you about that too.

specialties.name: Knapped Glass Blades
specialties.desc: Traditional Mangaran weapons worked from volcanic jungle glass, wickedly sharp and deeply personal to their makers. Prized by offworld collectors who mostly do not grasp what they are holding.

hooks: Diplomatic analysts who study the Mangara situation note that every negotiated ceasefire between the Hakari and Jaulaus in recorded history has been undermined from within by factions on both sides who benefit from the continuation of the conflict. The pattern is consistent enough that observers now treat ceasefire attempts as a reliable signal that a significant escalation is coming from one side or the other shortly afterward.

Port Neutral on Mangara is understood by Alliance intelligence to function as the primary point of entry for corporate extraction operations that violate the embargo, a fact the Alliance is aware of and has chosen not to act on, which is itself the subject of considerable speculation among analysts who study the system.

The phenomenon of Hakari and Jaulaus diaspora members in Alliance Space inheriting leadership positions in ancestral clans they have never lived among is well-documented and creates a recurring problem for both communities, leaders who hold cultural authority but lack cultural knowledge, and traditional communities that must decide how much weight to give inherited position versus lived experience.
planets.desc: Mangara's history is one of the most uncomfortable chapters in Alliance records. Five hundred years ago the Hakari and Jaulaus were technologically undeveloped, a fact the Nerulian Empire exploited without hesitation, treating both species as an inexhaustible labour resource. Corporate interests followed when the Empire fell. The Alliance eventually placed Mangara under embargo in an attempt to slow outside interference. Enforcement is imperfect. The civil war is continuous, deeply rooted in centuries of grievance and competition, and the Alliance's official position is that it does not get involved. The planet is simultaneously embargoed and ignored, protected on paper, exploited in practice, and burning from within.

planets.name: Mangara II
planets.atm_note: Marginal breathable, thin CO2 mix with trace oxygen, requires supplemental filtration
planets.temperature: Arid, large day-night swings, roughly 0°C to 45°C
planets.faction: None, Alliance considers it within embargo zone
planets.access_note: Falls within the Mangara embargo zone. Alliance patrol ships apply the same access restrictions as the primary world.
hazards: Within Alliance embargo zone, approach will attract patrol interest
No infrastructure or rescue capability
Thin atmosphere provides minimal radiation protection
planets.desc: A small, arid outer world in the Mangara system, barren and largely featureless. The Alliance embargo technically covers the entire system, but enforcement at this remote body is minimal. Corporate survey teams have landed here covertly to use it as a waystation when running supplies through the embargo.

planets.name: Mangara Outer Giant
planets.atm_note: Dense hydrogen-helium gas envelope
planets.temperature: Cryogenic cloud tops, roughly -110°C to -180°C; far hotter in the deep atmosphere under pressure
planets.access_note: Alliance embargo coverage is unclear at this range, but Alliance patrols have intercepted vessels here before.
hazards: Alliance patrol presence in system
Gas giant hazards
planets.desc: A large gas giant at the outer edge of the Mangara system. Its moons have been used by smugglers running the Alliance embargo as staging points and fuel dumps, a use the Alliance is aware of and periodically disrupts.

catalogue_systems.name: Carach System
catalogue_systems.desc: The Carach system is the seat of Skalan civilisation. Caragh, the homeworld, is closed. The system perimeter is enforced by Skalan patrol vessels without legal framework or diplomatic negotiation. Non-Skalans who approach uninvited are turned away or fired upon. The distinction between the two outcomes is not always communicated in advance.
catalogue_systems.subtitle: The Closed Homeworld of a Dying, Honourable People
catalogue_systems.quote: "We were made to fight, and then made to end. We have decided to end well. That is our whole philosophy, and we find it sufficient." (Caragh proverb)
catalogue_systems.history:
Carach is the Skalander homeworld, though the Skalander were made before they were born. The Patriark, when they were still the Arcor, engineered them as a warrior race to survive the Nemanian threat, and once that threat had passed the makers set quietly about unmaking them, editing the Skalander genome toward a slow and deliberate extinction. The Skalander know exactly what was done to them. They have chosen to meet it with dignity rather than fury, and that choice is the thing that defines them.
Carach itself is advanced and contemplative, a world that looks forward and backward at the same time. Its people built a high technology and wrapped it in ceremony and discipline and a code of honour that governs everything from warfare to conversation. They have spent their borrowed centuries preserving what they can and settling their affairs with the patience of a people who know, roughly, when the end will arrive.
Carach is closed. Every world in the system is shut to outsiders, with a single exception, one deliberately unremarkable world set aside for the limited diplomacy the Skalander still consent to conduct. The galaxy sees almost nothing of Carach, which suits everyone. The Skalander guard their privacy and their grief, and the rest of the galaxy is spared the discomfort of watching a noble people arrange their own funeral.
catalogue_systems.politics:
Carach is self-governing and answers to no one, an arrangement the Alliance accepts because the Skalander are respected, few, and not worth the cost of bringing to heel. Authority runs through honour and lineage and the judgement of elders, in forms outsiders are rarely permitted to watch closely, and the system perimeter is held by Skalander patrols who turn away the uninvited and fire on the persistent.
What contact the Skalander allow happens on the one open world, on their terms and in their time. The closure is not hostility. It is curation. A people with limited years have decided precisely how much of themselves the galaxy is allowed to see.
The Alliance believes the Skalan Order, the dissident faction that refuses the quiet death, keeps a hideout somewhere on Carach. The Skalander deny it flatly and with evident disgust, insisting they would never shelter a group that threw away its honour to cling to survival. Whether the denial is the truth, or whether a dying people quietly looks away for the one of its children still willing to fight, is a question the Skalander will not discuss and the Alliance cannot answer.

dominant_race.name: Skalander
dominant_race.lore:
The Skalander are a made people, engineered from the Arcor genome as warriors and then edited back down toward extinction once the war was won. They are massive, formidable, and increasingly rare, and like the Patriark they carry a Veil, though where the Patriark's projects trust the Skalander's projects dread. To stand before one is to feel, below the level of thought, that you are in the presence of something built to end you.
What defines them is not the violence they were made for but the dignity they chose afterward. Skalander culture rests on honour and duty and the keeping of one's word, held with a seriousness that shorter-lived and less doomed peoples find almost unbearable. They are courteous, genuinely dangerous, and quietly occupied with finishing what they can before the end. A Skalander's word is the most reliable thing in known space, which is part of why their slow disappearance is mourned even by those who fear them.
They do not discuss their extinction with outsiders, and they discuss the Skalan Order less still. The Order is the open wound of the species, the children who looked at the same fate and chose fury over grace, and the rest of the Skalander regard it as a disgrace precisely because it abandoned the one thing they all have left.

race_standing.note: Home, and the only people permitted across most of the system. To be Skalander on Carach is to be among the last of your kind, with everything that carries.

The makers, who built the Skalander to fight and then built them to die. A Patriark is received on the one open world with flawless courtesy and bottomless buried grievance, the most fraught relationship in known space conducted entirely in good manners.
Tolerated on the diplomatic world and nowhere else. The Skalander respect human institutions and find human haste a little sad, and they treat human envoys as honoured and closely watched guests.
Heirs of the empire the Skalander were built to fight. Old enemies, and welcome on no world of Carach, diplomatic or otherwise.
Fellow warriors whose endurance the Skalander respect, granted limited contact and counted among the few peoples who understand what it means to hold a line.
Respected as warriors and held at the same careful distance as everyone else. Courtesy, and the door no further than the threshold.
A mind that feels nothing and reads everything is an uneasy guest for a people guarding their privacy and their grief. Admitted rarely, and watched throughout.

A people engineered into being has complicated feelings about people grown to order. The Skalander extend the Non-Born a sober, unexpected sympathy, one made thing to another, while keeping them, like all outsiders, off the closed worlds.

relations.name: The Patriark
relations.note: Creators and executioners at once, who built the Skalander as a weapon and then legislated their slow end. The relationship is correct, courteous, and unforgivable, and neither side says so aloud.

relations.name: The Alliance
relations.note: Recognises Carach's independence and leaves it alone, partly from respect and partly because coercing a proud, dying, heavily armed people is a poor use of a fleet. Officially, it also hunts the Skalan Order here.

relations.name: The Skalan Order
relations.note: The dissident children who chose survival over honour. The Skalander deny all association and mean the denial, though whether denial is the same as refusal is a question they will not entertain.

relations.name: Seigh
relations.note: The system's lethal sister world, where the Skalander test their young and outsiders test their luck. What Carach preserves, Seigh proves.

catalogue_systems.gm_notes: Run Carach as a closed door with impeccable manners. Almost the whole system is off-limits, and the single open world is where every Skalander story involving outsiders has to happen, on their terms and in their time. Play the dignity straight, because these are not bitter people but graceful ones, which is far more unsettling. The live wires are the Patriark relationship, all courtesy laid over a wound that will never close, and the Skalan Order: does Carach shelter it, and what does it cost a people of honour to look the other way for the one child still fighting? A Skalander's word is absolute, so an oath given or owed is the strongest hook you can hang on a player.

planets.name: Caragh
planets.atm_note: Pristine, no industrial pollution, ecosystem maintained as sacred
planets.temperature: Hot and humid, roughly 22°C to 42°C
planets.grav_note: Noticeably above standard, Skalan physiology adapted. Non-Skalans experience fatigue under extended exposure.
planets.demographics: Skalan exclusively, no known non-Skalan permanent residents
planets.tech_level: Advanced (selectively applied, industrial tech rejected in sacred zones)
planets.economy: Internal subsistence, cultural production, military training, nothing exported
planets.access_note: Non-Skalans not permitted. Not formally legislated, enforced by the certainty that testing it is inadvisable. Skalan patrol vessels intercept any unauthorised approach.
hazards: Extreme hostility to non-Skalan visitors throughout
Skalan warrior culture, insult has immediate physical consequences
Alliance legal structures do not apply here
No diplomatic protection for non-Skalans who enter without invitation

notable_locations.name: Temple of the First Warrior
notable_locations.desc: The most sacred structure in Skalan culture. Non-Skalans have never been permitted inside. Its location is known. Its contents are not.

notable_locations.name: Training Grounds
notable_locations.desc: Extensive martial training facilities covering much of the planet's northern continent. The quality of what is produced here is evident to anyone who has encountered Skalan warriors.

notable_locations.name: The City of Memory
notable_locations.desc: Built to commemorate every Skalan who died during the Patriarks' attempted genetic extinction. The records kept here are the most complete surviving documentation of what was done.

hooks: It is known among people who work with Skalan warriors that they occasionally seek outside contractors for tasks they cannot pursue through Skalan channels, not because the Skalans lack capability, but because involving their own institutions would make the matter a political issue within Skalan culture. This pattern of selective use of outsiders is established enough that certain contractors maintain ongoing relationships with Skalan clients specifically for this purpose.

The relationship between the Skalans and the Patriarks is one of the most closely watched bilateral dynamics in Alliance Space, a species that survived an attempted extinction by the Patriarks maintaining formal diplomatic relations with the perpetrators. Diplomatic exchanges between the two are never conducted publicly, and accounts of what happens in direct meetings between their representatives are not shared in any accessible record.

The City of Memory on Caragh is believed by historians and legal scholars to contain the most complete surviving documentation of the Patriarks' genetic modification program against the Skalans, records that would be legally significant in Alliance jurisdictions if they could be accessed. They cannot be accessed without Skalan permission, which has never been granted to any outside party.
planets.desc: Caragh is the Skalan homeworld and it is closed. Non-Skalans do not land here. This is not formally legislated, it is simply a boundary that the Skalans enforce and that everyone with any familiarity with Skalan culture understands not to test. The planet is covered in temples, training grounds, and shrines to warrior traditions that predate the Skalans' existence as a distinct species. The Patriarks created the Skalans as a warrior caste and later attempted to eliminate them through genetic modification. The attempt failed. The Skalans remember.

planets.name: Carach II
planets.atm_note: Unbreathable outside the sealed contact enclave; the enclave maintains its own atmosphere
planets.temperature: Arid, large day-night swings, roughly 0°C to 45°C
planets.grav_note: Standard gravity
planets.population: ~12,000, Skalan diplomatic staff and sanctioned visitors
planets.demographics: Skalan administration with a small, rotating population of vetted offworld envoys
planets.economy: Sanctioned diplomacy and the limited, supervised contact the Skalan permit
planets.access_note: The only Carach world open to outsiders, by Skalan invitation only. Straying beyond the enclave ends the visit, and sometimes the visitor.
hazards: Skalan jurisdiction, approach without invitation treated as hostile
Unbreathable atmosphere
No infrastructure
planets.desc: The one Carach world outsiders are ever allowed to set foot on, chosen for the purpose precisely because it means nothing. Carach II holds no sacred ground and no cultural weight, so the Skalander conduct what little diplomacy they permit here, in a sealed enclave on an unremarkable rock, where losing the place to a hostile guest would cost them nothing they value. Everything an outsider ever learns of Carach, they learn in this one room.

planets.name: Carach Outer Belt
planets.temperature: Vacuum; surface swings from roughly -150°C in shadow to +120°C in direct sunlight
planets.access_note: Skalan patrol vessels use the belt for positioning. Non-Skalan approach treated as intrusion.
hazards: Active Skalan patrol activity
Debris navigation hazards in denser belt sections
planets.desc: The outer belt of the Carach system. Skalan patrol vessels anchor among the larger bodies during long patrol rotations, using the belt as the de facto outer perimeter of territorial enforcement for the homeworld system.

catalogue_systems.name: Seigh System
catalogue_systems.classification: Self-Governed Territory, Skalan Training World System
catalogue_systems.desc: The Seigh system is administered by the Skalan as a separate closed territory from the Carach homeworld system. The primary body, Seigh, is the site of the Skalan rite of passage. Non-Skalans are not invited. The fauna does not check jurisdiction.
catalogue_systems.subtitle: The Deadliest World in Known Space, and the Test That Makes a Skalander
catalogue_systems.quote: "Seigh does not care what you have killed before. It is interested only in whether it kills you now." (Skalander rite-master)
catalogue_systems.history:
Seigh is self-governed Skalander territory, and unlike Carach it has no homes on it. Its fauna and flora have earned, honestly, the title of the deadliest world in known space, an ecology so uniformly lethal that the Skalander never tried to settle it. They set it aside instead for the one thing it does well, which is to test people.
For the Skalander, a tour on Seigh is a rite of passage. A young Skalander who means to prove themselves goes to Seigh and returns, or does not, and the ones who come back carry a standing nothing else in the culture confers. The military trains here too, on the sound logic that a soldier who can survive Seigh can survive anything a war will think to do to them.
Seigh's reputation draws another kind of visitor. Wealthy outsiders pay enormous sums for illegal safaris, hoping to carry home a trophy from the deadliest world there is, and a steady fraction of them stay forever, feeding the ground they came to conquer. The Skalander tolerate the hunters with thinly veiled contempt and the occasional quiet profit, and the wildlife goes on balancing the ledger.
catalogue_systems.politics:
Seigh has no government, because it has no settled population to govern, only the Skalander military that trains on it and the rite-masters who oversee the proving. Skalander law applies in the sense that the Skalander decide who is allowed to come here and die, and largely ignore those who come anyway.
The illegal safari trade is the one persistent outside presence, run by offworld outfits that bribe, smuggle, and occasionally get eaten. The Skalander could stamp it out and mostly do not, partly because the planet does their enforcement for them, and partly because a rich fool who wishes to die on Seigh is, to the Skalander mind, exercising a freedom no one has the standing to deny him.

dominant_race.name: The Tested and the Trespassers
dominant_race.lore:
Seigh has no true population, only two kinds of visitor. The first are the Skalander, young warriors come to earn their standing and soldiers come to be hardened, overseen by rite-masters who have survived the world themselves and expect no less of anyone else. To them Seigh is sacred ground of a brutal kind, the place that decides who a Skalander becomes.
The second are the trespassers, wealthy offworlders chasing a trophy from the deadliest world there is, and the outfits that smuggle them in. The Skalander regard them as the planet's livestock, and Seigh, with no opinion on the matter either way, obliges.

relations.name: Carach
relations.note: The Skalander homeworld and the seat of everything Seigh exists to serve. Carach preserves the Skalander; Seigh proves them, and the two systems are run as one closed territory in all but name.

relations.name: The Skalander military
relations.note: Trains its young and its soldiers on Seigh because nothing else comes close. A Seigh tour is the credential behind every Skalander reputation worth the name.

relations.name: Safari outfits
relations.note: Offworld operations that smuggle rich hunters past the perimeter for a fortune. The Skalander permit them by inaction, and the planet thins their numbers without assistance.

catalogue_systems.gm_notes: Run Seigh as a world that is itself the antagonist. Nothing here needs a stat line to be terrifying; the ground, the air, the plants, and the things moving in them are all trying to kill everyone equally. Two ways onto the board: a Skalander rite of passage, where a player earns standing the culture grants no other way, or an illegal safari, where the real danger is rarely the trophy and often the other hunters. A surviving outsider gains a strange, grudging Skalander respect, and the phrase 'they came back from Seigh' carries weight in places the player will not expect.

planets.name: Seigh
planets.atm_note: Breathable but carries spores, pollen, and biological agents causing cumulative harm without proper filtration
planets.temperature: Hot and wet, roughly 26°C to 44°C, the climate as hostile as everything living in it
planets.grav_note: Above standard. Escape from predators is significantly harder than expected.
planets.demographics: Skalan young adults completing rite of passage
planets.tech_level: None (Skalans enter with minimal equipment by cultural mandate)
planets.access_note: Skalan jurisdiction. Non-Skalans are not invited and the fauna does not distinguish. Skalan vessels enforce no-entry for outsiders.
hazards: Most lethal natural environment in the known galaxy (consensus survey rating)
Multiple apex predator species with no natural fear of prey
Toxic and corrosive flora, skin contact with many plant species causes immediate harm
Acidic swampland, large sections physically corrosive to standard materials
Volcanic terrain with unpredictable activity
Biological spore agents requiring constant respiratory filtration
No rescue or medical extraction for non-Skalans, ever

notable_locations.name: The Deep Jungle
notable_locations.desc: The interior of the continent-scale jungle. Navigation is extremely difficult without cultural knowledge of the terrain. Predator density at this depth has never been successfully surveyed, no survey team has survived to report it.

notable_locations.name: The Acid Flats
notable_locations.desc: A vast expanse of chemical-saturated wetland that can dissolve standard armour alloys over a period of hours. The path through it is known to Skalan trainees and transmitted only orally.

notable_locations.name: The Summit
notable_locations.desc: The highest point on Seigh, the goal of the rite of passage. What is found there is known only to those who complete the training. No outsider has reached it and returned.

specialties.name: Seigh Trophies (Illegal)
specialties.desc: Hides, fangs, and preserved specimens from the deadliest fauna in known space, smuggled out at enormous cost for collectors who want proof that someone went and came back. Possession is illegal in Alliance space and prized accordingly.

specialties.name: Seigh-Tested
specialties.desc: The credential, not a cargo. A Skalander who has passed the rite, or the rare outsider who survived a season, carries a standing that opens doors across the galaxy. Few things are worth more, and few are harder to earn.

hooks: Among bounty hunters and fugitive recovery specialists, Seigh is treated as a terminal destination, the effective end of any trail. The combination of lethality and Skalan jurisdiction means that anyone who reaches Seigh is considered as inaccessible as if they had died. In practice, some do not survive it; but those who do are simply unreachable.

The exotic specimen trade has a standing, persistent market for live Seigh megafauna that has never been successfully supplied, the Skalans consider the planet's wildlife sacred and the environment ensures that any attempt at capture would likely kill the captor before the specimen. This has not reduced the offered prices, which continue to rise in proportion to the known impossibility of delivery.

Among Skalans living in Alliance Space, it is understood and never discussed that families who lose a child to Seigh's rite of passage cannot acknowledge the loss publicly. This creates a visible but unspoken grief that communities who know Skalans well learn to recognise and leave unaddressed, the correct response, in Skalan cultural terms, is silence.
planets.desc: Every credible environmental survey of Seigh has reached the same conclusion: it is the most lethal naturally occurring environment in the known galaxy. The jungle is dense, the flora is largely toxic on contact, the predators are large and have evolved over millions of years to kill anything that moves, and the terrain alternates between impenetrable canopy, acidic swampland, and sheer volcanic rock. The Skalans send their young here. Surviving Seigh for the required period is the rite of passage that marks the transition to adulthood in Skalan culture. The survival rate for uninvited visitors is low enough that most insurers classify Seigh as uninsurable.

planets.name: Seigh II
planets.temperature: Frozen, roughly -80°C to -30°C
planets.access_note: Skalan jurisdiction extends to all bodies in the system. Patrol vessels enforce exclusion.
hazards: Skalan jurisdiction, approach without invitation treated as hostile
Extreme cold
No infrastructure
planets.desc: A small, frozen rocky world at the outer edge of the Seigh system. The Skalans claim it as part of their territory. It holds no strategic or cultural significance; the Skalans simply do not permit others to operate in their systems on principle.

planets.name: Seigh Outer Belt
planets.temperature: Vacuum; surface swings from roughly -150°C in shadow to +120°C in direct sunlight
planets.access_note: Skalan patrol vessels use the belt for positioning. Non-Skalan approach treated as intrusion.
hazards: Active Skalan patrol activity
Debris navigation hazards in denser belt sections
planets.desc: The outer belt of the Seigh system. Skalan patrol vessels maintain a presence here as part of the broader perimeter enforcement around the training world.

catalogue_systems.name: San Tien System
catalogue_systems.desc: San Tien is the last world the Nerulians can call their own. When the Kravens obliterated the empire, survival came down to luck, those off-world, those on the fringes, those on ships fast enough to run. San Tien was remote enough to be overlooked and has remained so. It is a world haunted by what was lost.

planets.name: San Tien
planets.atm_note: Thin at altitude, breathable at ground level throughout
planets.temperature: Arid, large day-night swings, roughly 0°C to 45°C
planets.demographics: ~98% Nerulian, small number of permanent non-Nerulian residents, mostly academics and diplomats
planets.government: Nerulian Government in Exile (Council of Survivors)
planets.tech_level: Advanced (Nerulian technology predates Alliance, much is unique)
planets.economy: Cultural preservation, historical archiving, small-scale manufacturing, knowledge trade
planets.access_note: San Tien accepts visitors but screens them carefully. Nerulian distrust of outsiders is deep-rooted given their history.
hazards: Proximity to Kraven Space, the border is not immovable
San Tien pirates operate in nearby systems and occasionally probe the border
Internal political tensions, Government in Exile vs those who believe there is nothing left to govern
Nerulian technology not understood by outsiders, some remains active in unexpected locations

notable_locations.name: The Archive City
notable_locations.desc: The primary settlement on San Tien, built around the most comprehensive surviving collection of Nerulian cultural records, history, and pre-Kraven technology. The most important library the galaxy didn't know existed.

notable_locations.name: The Memorial Shore
notable_locations.desc: A coastal site maintained as a permanent memorial to the worlds lost in the Kraven invasion. The Nerulians count their dead here. The number is still being updated.

notable_locations.name: The Dry Docks
notable_locations.desc: Where the great fleet-cities that drift between systems are maintained and repaired when they return to San Tien. The technology here is unlike anything produced in Alliance Space, older, different, and in several cases more capable.

hooks: Nerulian archivists at the San Tien Archive City have long maintained, in private academic discourse, that pre-Kraven records contain references to technologies specifically developed to counter Kraven biological processes, technologies that were in development at the time of the invasion and never completed. The academic consensus is that the references are genuine. Whether anything retrievable survives is the question that has gone unresolved for decades.

Among the Nerulian diaspora communities that travel on fleet-cities, the loss of a fleet-city in transit is one of the most deeply feared outcomes, the combination of isolation, the Nemani Rift proximity on several routes, and the lack of rescue capability means that missing fleet-cities are almost never found. There are at least three fleet-cities that are known to be overdue and presumed lost in the past century.

The negotiation between the Nerulian Government in Exile and the Alliance over access to pre-Kraven technology records has been ongoing for over thirty years without resolution. Analysts who study the situation note that both sides appear to want an agreement and neither trusts the other enough to make the concessions one. The technology records are considered by Alliance naval intelligence to be potentially the most strategically valuable archive in existence.
planets.desc: San Tien is the last world the Nerulians can call their own. It is a world haunted by what was lost: libraries of Nerulian history, refugee camps that became cities, a government in exile that may never govern again. Most Nerulians encountered in the galaxy are from the great fleet-cities that drift between systems, but San Tien remains the spiritual and political home of the surviving people. The archive kept here is the most significant cultural repository of a civilisation that no longer has a civilisation, a last record of everything the Kravens destroyed.

planets.name: San Tien II
planets.temperature: Arid, large day-night swings, roughly 0°C to 45°C
planets.access_note: San Tien system is open to vetted visitors. No infrastructure at this body.
hazards: No atmosphere
No rescue capability at this distance from San Tien
planets.desc: A small, airless rocky world catalogued in early Nerulian surveys under the designation Tien-Bav (Second Stone). The Nerulians have never developed it, their resources and attention are entirely on the inhabited world. It orbits in silence as it has for millions of years.

planets.name: Vel-Aroth
planets.atm_note: Hydrogen-helium envelope with distinctive green-amber bands, named in old Nerulian charts
planets.temperature: Cryogenic cloud tops, roughly -110°C to -180°C; far hotter in the deep atmosphere under pressure
planets.access_note: No restrictions. Nerulian navigators historically used it as a reference point on approach to San Tien.
hazards: Standard gas giant hazards
planets.desc: A large gas giant known in old Nerulian navigation as Vel-Aroth, meaning roughly "the watcher at the edge." Nerulian navigators traditionally gave it a silent acknowledgement on approach to San Tien, a custom maintained by the Government in Exile's fleet-cities as a gesture of continuity with the civilisation they carry in memory.

catalogue_systems.name: Ishtar System
catalogue_systems.desc: Ishtar exists to produce. The volcanic geology provides near-limitless geothermal energy. The crust is mineral-dense enough that raw materials are extracted metres from where they are processed. The atmosphere is permanently toxic from centuries of unregulated industrial output. The weapons that come out of Ishtar's foundries are carried by soldiers on every side of every war in the galaxy.
catalogue_systems.subtitle: The Galaxy's Forge: A World You Pay For in Lungs and Years
catalogue_systems.quote: "Ishtar makes everything the galaxy points at the galaxy. We breathe the difference." (foundry-floor saying, Ishtar Prime)
catalogue_systems.history:
Ishtar was always going to be industrial. The geology is volcanic and dense with ore, with near-limitless geothermal power and raw metal lying close to where it is smelted, and Arms Corp built its empire on exactly that. Over centuries it made the whole world into one continuous factory, and centuries of unregulated output ruined the sky. You cannot breathe Ishtar's air now without a filter.
It became the galaxy's forge. Most of known space's heavy manufacturing, and the great majority of its weapons, come off Ishtar's lines and into the hands of soldiers on every side of every war. Arms Corp sells to all of them and calls it neutrality. The furnaces never cool, and the workforce that keeps them lit pays for the privilege a breath at a time.
catalogue_systems.politics:
Ishtar has no government, only management. The Arms Corp Industrial Directorate runs the planet as a single company state. There are no citizens, only employees; no civic rights, only contracts. Law is corporate policy, and the police are Arms Corp's private military, which is better equipped than most national navies.
The bargain is plain. Arms Corp pays well because it has to, since the work is lethal and the air is poison and bodies wear out fast. In return it owns your hours, your housing, your medical care, and a fair share of your future. It is a gilded cage with excellent dental, and most of the galaxy's working poor would still sign, because a short well-paid life on Ishtar beats a long hungry one elsewhere.
Ishtar is built in tiers, and the tiers map who matters. The upper levels hold the skilled trades, the management, and the filtered air, and for them the well-paid bargain is real. The lower you go, the worse the air and the work and the contract, down to levels the corporation does not advertise. There the foundry-born talk about debt-bond labour: workers whose housing and care and breather rations are advanced against wages they can never quite clear, so they are held by arithmetic rather than by law. Officially it does not exist. Officially the lower tiers simply have very loyal, very long-serving employees. No one who has worked them calls it anything but slavery, and no one with the clearance to investigate has found it convenient to look.
The one thing Arms Corp fears is its own workforce. It watched the Worker Clans of Damph slip the corporate leash and take a whole planet, and it has no intention of letting Ishtar become the second example. Organising is watched, infiltrated, and broken before it can harden, and the Directorate spends more on keeping its workers content or contained than any outsider would guess.

dominant_race.name: The Foundry-Born
dominant_race.lore:
Ishtar's people are its workforce, generations of them born into Arms Corp company towns and raised to the line. They are mostly human, with a large Hakari contingent on the hazardous floors and an enormous Non-Born population doing the work that kills fastest. They call themselves the foundry-born, and they carry the name with the grim pride of people who know exactly what they are worth and exactly what it costs.
Foundry culture is hard and fatalistic, leavened by the black humour of people who can hear the meter running on their own lungs. No one here pretends the work is anything but a trade of years for credits, and there is a strange dignity in how clearly they make the trade. The galaxy carries Ishtar's guns and rides in ships Ishtar built, and the foundry-born know, with some bitterness, that everything out in the clean air was made by someone down here who could not breathe it.

race_standing.note: The backbone of the skilled lines. Valued for exactly as long as they are productive, and looked after exactly as far as the contract specifies.
A huge labour contingent whose reflexes suit the fast, dangerous machinery. Arms Corp draws its floor enforcers from the same pool.
Built to last on the hottest and most toxic floors, and handed exactly those jobs. Respected, and used hard.

Ishtar runs on Non-Born labour and uses it up. They crew the lethal stations no one else will, the Ishtar II mines among them, and Arms Corp treats them as inputs to be replaced rather than people to be kept. The cruelty is in the accounting, not the malice.
Their menace makes them natural floor overseers, and Arms Corp puts it to work keeping the lines in order. Feared on the floor, which is the point.
Precise, tireless, and untroubled by the misery, which makes them ideal for process work and quality control. Management likes them and the workers find them ghoulish.
Rare and respected. Honest hands in a place that runs on contracts find steady, well-paid work and little trouble.
Found in Arms Corp's upper management and its arms-dealing diplomacy, brokering the sales that arm every side. The foundry-born distrust the suits on principle, and the Patriark suits most of all.

relations.name: The Alliance
relations.note: The Alliance navy carries Arms Corp weapons, so the Alliance does not discipline Arms Corp. The corporation helped write the laws it obeys, and the relationship runs on terms that favour the side holding the guns.

relations.name: Damph / Worker Clans
relations.note: Ishtar builds the ships and Damph fuels them, and neither works without the other. But Ishtar's workers stayed under the boot while Damph's seized their world, and the contrast has curdled into a real and personal rivalry, fought hardest for now over whose beer is better.

relations.name: Zang'Hai
relations.note: Cheap Zang'Hai copies of Arms Corp weapons flood the black market, pirated through the same clan networks that supply the originals' fuel. Arms Corp litigates, Zang'Hai shrugs, and the cycle continues.

relations.name: Every belligerent
relations.note: Arms Corp arms all sides of all wars and calls it neutrality. From Ishtar's vantage, a war with only one armed side is a market failure.

catalogue_systems.gm_notes: Make the players feel Ishtar in their lungs. The air is hostile, a breather is not optional, and the company owns everything, including the law. Almost everything is made here and most of it is for sale, including weapons most worlds would never licence, through or around the Arms Corp permit system. The strongest plots are arms deals, industrial sabotage, and the thing Arms Corp dreads most, organising that might turn Ishtar into a second Damph. Ishtar Gold flows everywhere and costs nothing; ordering a Damph Cold on a foundry floor is the quiet way to start a fight. And the lower tiers are a campaign of their own: debt-bonded workers who cannot afford to leave, an open secret the company files under loyalty, the kind of place a crew can do real good or vanish entirely.

planets.name: Ishtar
planets.atm_note: Permanently toxic from centuries of unregulated industrial output, breathers mandatory outside sealed zones
planets.temperature: ~35°C to 70°C; hotter near active foundry and vent zones
planets.demographics: Mixed, predominantly human, significant Hakari labour contingent
planets.economy: Weapons manufacturing, heavy industry, geothermal energy, raw material extraction
planets.access_note: Arms Corp employment credential or contractor license required. Tourist access does not exist.
hazards: Toxic atmosphere, breather mandatory at all times outside sealed zones
Volcanic activity, eruption zones shift without reliable warning
Acid precipitation in certain atmospheric bands
Industrial accident rate significantly above Alliance average
Arms Corp security forces with lethal escalation policy
Geothermal venting, some districts are periodically unworkable

notable_locations.name: The Foundry Districts
notable_locations.desc: The core of Ishtar's weapons production capacity. Dozens of enormous manufacturing complexes producing the full range of Arms Corp weaponry. The noise and heat are extreme even inside sealed areas.

notable_locations.name: Arms Corp HQ (Ishtar Campus)
notable_locations.desc: The primary administrative and research hub for the largest weapons manufacturer in the galaxy. Security is military-grade. Visitor access is not offered.

notable_locations.name: Residential Sealed Zones
notable_locations.desc: The pressurised living areas where the workforce spends its off-shifts. Designed for efficiency, not comfort. The waiting list to transfer out is years long. Arms Corp pays well because it has to.

notable_locations.name: The Extraction Front
notable_locations.desc: The active mining zones where raw materials come out of the crust. Geologically unstable, worked in shifts around the clock, and statistically the most dangerous workplace in Alliance Space.

specialties.name: Ishtar Gold
specialties.desc: The cheap, harsh workers' lager brewed in the shadow of the foundries and, against all reason, the single best-selling beer in the galaxy. The number one blue-collar drink in known space: it tastes like the floor it is brewed on, it costs almost nothing, and it is absolutely everywhere.

specialties.name: Vent-Grilled Skewers
specialties.desc: Street food seared on the exhaust grilles of the smelting lines and sold from carts between shifts. Smoky, cheap, faintly metallic, and the taste of home to anyone foundry-born.

specialties.name: Ishtar-Pattern Sidearm
specialties.desc: The definitive mass-produced Arms Corp pistol: cheap, ugly, and utterly reliable, carried on every side of every war in the galaxy. If you have seen a gun, you have probably seen this one.

hooks: It is well-established among weapons dealers and military procurement officers that Arms Corp production from Ishtar consistently exceeds what appears on any filed export manifest, a discrepancy that has persisted across multiple audit cycles and is understood in the trade to represent an ongoing internal diversion operation that Arms Corp has chosen to manage quietly rather than expose.

Labour organising on Ishtar has a documented history spanning over a century: attempts are made, participants are transferred to less accessible work sites, and the organising effort dissolves. The cycle is consistent enough that experienced labour advocates consider it part of Arms Corp's standard operating procedure rather than a response to any specific threat.

Arms Corp's Ishtar research division is known in materials science circles to produce significant advances that never appear in publicly accessible literature, innovations that go directly into proprietary production rather than academic publication. The gap between what is observed in their manufactured output and what can be explained by known metallurgy has been widening for decades.

Labour auditors and Alliance inspectors have for decades filed reports noting that a large fraction of Ishtar's lower-tier workforce carries company debt that mathematically cannot be cleared within a working lifetime, and that these workers are not permitted to leave until it is. Arms Corp characterises the arrangement as voluntary credit against future earnings. Everyone who has actually seen the lower tiers characterises it as debt-bond slavery, and the inspections that might settle the question are scheduled, announced, and routed carefully through the breathable upper levels.
planets.desc: Ishtar is one of the most productive worlds in the known galaxy and one of the least pleasant to live on. Nobody who works here chose it for the scenery. Arms Corp pays well because it has to, the working conditions are brutal, the life expectancy is below average, and the waiting list for transfer off-world is years long. The sky is a permanent orange-brown. The air outside a sealed zone will kill you. The weapons produced here are on every battlefield in the galaxy.

planets.name: Ishtar II
planets.atm_note: Negligible atmosphere, trace nitrogen
planets.temperature: Swings from ~-90°C in shadow to ~160°C in sun (negligible atmosphere)
planets.population: ~80, automated extraction station, minimal crew rotation
planets.demographics: Non-Born operators with small human technical team
planets.economy: Raw material extraction, titanium, chromium, rare earths for weapons manufacturing
planets.access_note: Arms Corp property. No civilian access. Station crew only.
hazards: Arms Corp security protocols, unrequested approach treated as industrial espionage
Automated mining equipment operates in unsecured surface zones
Low gravity and no atmosphere, full EVA
planets.desc: A small barren world close to Ishtar that Arms Corp uses as a raw material extraction site. Automated mining equipment operates almost without human presence, a small crew rotation maintains the extraction station and manages ore transport. The materials go directly to the Ishtar foundry complexes.

planets.name: Ishtar Outer Belt
planets.temperature: Near-vacuum, ~-120°C in shadow to ~120°C in direct sun
planets.demographics: Mixed, contract workers from various corporations
planets.economy: Bulk ore extraction, primarily ferrous and nickel-iron asteroids
planets.access_note: Commercial mining licenses required. Alliance licensing authority is strict about claim boundaries.
hazards: Multiple competing mining operations with disputed claim boundaries
High-velocity industrial equipment
Debris from mining operations creates navigation hazards
Labour disputes in isolated stations can become violent
planets.desc: A moderately dense asteroid belt in the middle reaches of the Ishtar system, parcelled out under Alliance mining licenses to half a dozen corporations and independent operators. The ore quality is good but not exceptional, Arms Corp dominates the most valuable asteroids and leaves the rest to smaller operators who accept the dangerous working conditions in exchange for the proximity to Ishtar's market.

planets.name: Ishtar Outer Giant
planets.atm_note: Banded hydrogen-helium atmosphere
planets.temperature: Cryogenic, around -150°C
planets.economy: Potential fuel skimming, no licensed operation established
planets.access_note: No infrastructure. Alliance survey completed.
hazards: Standard gas giant hazards
planets.desc: A large gas giant at the outer boundary of the Ishtar system. Arms Corp surveyed it for potential fuel skimming operations and concluded the logistics did not justify the investment given Sirius's existing fuel infrastructure. It orbits largely unobserved at the edge of the system's navigational charts.

catalogue_systems.name: Damph System
catalogue_systems.desc: Damph is a frozen hellhole that happens to sit on the only known deposits of Coronthia in the galaxy. Without Damph, a significant portion of the galaxy's most powerful ships stop moving. The workers who extract it know exactly how much leverage that gives them. Governed by a patchwork of worker clans, tough, territorial, deeply suspicious of outsiders, and fiercely proud of what they do.
catalogue_systems.subtitle: Crime Families on a Frozen World, and the Coronthia the Galaxy Cannot Replace
catalogue_systems.quote: "The corps think they run Damph because they own the freighters. We own the cold, the seams, and the only thing in civilized space that makes those freighters move. They can keep the paperwork." (Boss Maela Vurn, Vethara Clan Council, recorded during the third licensing renegotiation)
catalogue_systems.history:
Damph kills careless workers by the shift. For most of its history that was the whole of its story, a cold world worth the trip only for cheap labour and the companies that came to use it. The miners survived the seams the way the desperate usually do, by banding together, and their family blocs hardened over generations into hereditary clans, each with its own courts and its own long memory.
Their power came from a collapse, not a boom. When modern ships moved to cold fusion, demand for coronthia fell, and the companies that ran Damph's extraction lost interest and let their grip slacken. The clans took the seams while no one was guarding them, and they held them well before the Tronik Wars, half a century ago. Then the predicted death of coronthia failed to arrive. The compound was still the only thing that would drive a ship across real distance, so demand never fell the way the companies had feared, and the clans were left owning the sole reliable supply of something the galaxy had already written off.
catalogue_systems.politics:
Damph is run by the Clan Council, where a seat's weight depends on how much coronthia the family pulls, so the largest producer is heard first and loudest. On paper it is a labour council. In practice it is a sit-down of bosses dividing a planet.
Each clan runs its territory as a family concern. Extraction is the legitimate face. Protection and smuggling are the body of the business, and violence settles whatever the other two cannot. Among themselves the clans feud without pause, over seam rights and over debts older than anyone now living, but against an outsider they close ranks at once, because the one thing every clan agrees on is that no company and no government takes Damph.
The monopoly is what makes all of it work. The Alliance cannot move against Damph without freezing its own long-haul fleets, so it tolerates from the clans what would have any other organisation declared criminal. The families have spent fifty years turning muscle into respectability. Clan money funds senators, clan lawyers sit in on Alliance hearings, and a boss can reach a lawmaker faster than most planetary governors can. They are still blue-collar criminals. They are simply criminals the galaxy cannot afford to arrest.

dominant_race.name: The Worker Clans
dominant_race.lore:
Damph's people are the clans, and a clan is a family before it is anything else. Most are human, with a large Hakari minority that took to the territorial, loyalty-bound life and to the lethal work of the Deep Seams. You do not join a clan. You are born into one, marry into one, or spend a lifetime paying off a debt to one. Nearly everyone on Damph belongs to a clan or works for one, and the few who belong to none are tolerated only while they stay useful and quiet.
They are proud and profane, and they do not take to being looked down on. A world that punishes carelessness with death produced a people who respect competence and nerve and have no patience for anyone who has never earned a callus. To a clansman the polish of corporate society looks like weakness in good clothes, which is a dangerous assumption to make about people who have learned to buy the institutions that look down on them.
Nothing shows clan pride better than what they drink. Damph Cold, the sub-zero lager brewed in the deep facilities, is the second best-selling beer in the galaxy, and every clansman will tell you it ought to be first. First place belongs to Ishtar Gold, the cheap standard poured in every working system in known space, and on Damph that ranking is taken as a standing insult. Order an Ishtar in a clan bar and you will learn, quickly and in person, that some rivalries are not a joke here.

race_standing.note: The blood of the clans is mostly human, so a human who is clan, or vouched for by clan, is home. A human in a corporate uniform is something else, and is treated as such.
The largest minority, and valued for it. Their loyalty and their nerve suit clan life and the Deep Seams, and many of Damph's hardest crews are Hakari.
Respected as muscle and as heavy labour, able to take the seams' punishment better than most. Trusted in proportion to the work they put in, like everyone else here.
Rare on Damph, but a people who keep their word travel well in a culture that prizes the same. A Skalander who works honestly is left alone, which here is high praise.
Smooth offworld operators are the thing the clans have learned hardest to distrust. A Patriark is assumed to be working an angle and watched on that assumption, whatever courtesy he is shown.
Menace is a language the clans understand, and a Nerulian can find work as an enforcer. But the clans trust blood, and an outsider who trades on fear is kept on a short contract.
Useful for the brutal arithmetic of extraction and impossible to read across a table, which unsettles the clans about equally. Hired for the work and never asked to the table.

A clan is blood, and the Non-Born have none, which leaves them outside the family however long they work the seams. Worse, the companies ship in Non-Born crews to undercut clan labour, so a Non-Born on Damph inherits the resentment of a wage war he did not start.

relations.name: Zang'Hai
