relations.note: Largest employer, largest buyer, and the company the clans quietly supply with stolen designs for its knockoff trade. The two are held together by need and by blackmail, and they will be renegotiating the terms until the coronthia runs out.

relations.name: The Alliance
relations.note: Officially the Alliance disapproves of everything the clans are. In practice it cannot freeze its own fleets, so it buys the coronthia, tolerates the rackets, and takes the campaign money. The clans speak louder in Alliance politics than their manners should allow.

relations.name: Rival corporate buyers
relations.note: Every power that builds fleets wants a coronthia supply it can control, and more than one has tried to arrange it. The clans read every unusually generous offer as the opening move of a takeover, and they are usually right.

catalogue_systems.gm_notes: Run Damph cold and proud. The clans are criminals with the manners of dock workers and the reach of senators, and they are touchy about exactly that contradiction. Respect, earned by competence and nerve, opens every door here; condescension closes them, sometimes with violence. Coronthia drives every plot worth running: enormously valuable, dangerously unstable, barred from most Alliance atmospheres, and held entirely by the clans. Side with a clan and the players gain terrifying friends and a blood feud they did not ask for. Cross one and they learn how a planet of families keeps a grudge. And never order an Ishtar Gold in a clan bar; the feud with Ishtar is real and personal, and it occasionally turns bloody.

planets.name: Damph
planets.atm_note: Breathable but extremely cold, thermal suits required outside pressurised zones
planets.temperature: ~-60°C to -20°C; exposure is lethal without a thermal suit
planets.demographics: Mixed, predominantly human and Hakari, several generations of clan families
planets.government: Clan Council (rotating chairs by extraction volume, largest producing clan holds primary vote)
planets.economy: Coronthia extraction and export, heavy equipment maintenance, clan-run supply logistics
planets.access_note: Clan vetting required for landing. Corporate vessels operate under clan-issued extraction licenses. Unsanctioned arrivals are treated as claim-jumpers.
hazards: Extreme cold, unsurvivable exposure without thermal suits
Coronthia instability, extraction and transport accidents are common and severe
Clan territorial disputes, boundaries are not always marked and are always enforced
Corporate intelligence operations, multiple factions maintain covert presence
Coronthia is restricted in most Alliance atmospheres; transit documentation scrutinised heavily

notable_locations.name: The Deep Seams
notable_locations.desc: The primary Coronthia extraction sites, kilometres below the frozen surface. The most dangerous workplaces on Damph. The clans that work the Deep Seams have the most political weight, and the most casualties.

notable_locations.name: Clan Central (Vethara Station)
notable_locations.desc: The largest pressurised settlement on Damph, built at the intersection of the three largest clan territories. Hosts the Clan Council, the main trading post, and the only medical facility with full surgical capability.

notable_locations.name: Corporate Liaison Offices
notable_locations.desc: Where the corporations do their business with the clans, under conditions dictated by the clans. The offices are comfortable. The negotiations are not.

notable_locations.name: The Storage Flats
notable_locations.desc: Vast insulated storage fields on the surface where processed Coronthia is held before transit. Well-defended. The clans treat any approach without authorisation as hostile.

specialties.name: Damph Cold
specialties.desc: The sub-zero lager brewed down in the deep facilities and the planet's pride. The second largest beer in the galaxy, and the clans will tell you, at length, that it should be first.

specialties.name: Cryobrew (Cold Reserve)
specialties.desc: The premium expression, slow-fermented in the deepest cold over months. Crystalline and faintly mineral from the coronthia-rich rock, with a collector subculture that chases vintage batches.

specialties.name: Deep-Seam Hash
specialties.desc: Dense, fatty, salt-heavy miner fare built to refuel a body wrecked by a shift in lethal cold. Served scalding. Outsiders find it brutal; a clansman finds it home.

hooks: Clan traders on Damph have documented for decades that corporate buyers operating through unfamiliar intermediaries consistently offer above-market rates for Coronthia, and that clans who accept these offers tend to experience unexplained leadership disruptions within the following year. The pattern is well-known and has not reduced the number of clans willing to test it, because the rates are genuinely attractive and the evidence of causation is considered circumstantial.

Coronthia geologists who study the Damph deposits have long estimated that the known clan territories represent a small fraction of the total deposit, that significant seams exist outside current boundaries and that whoever identifies them first will face a political challenge to their claim of historic proportions. Discovery claims outside current territory are considered the most volatile situation in Damph politics.

Coronthia shipping volume discrepancies on Damph are a persistent feature of the system's trade records. The clans have been aware of unexplained shortfalls in licensed shipping volumes for years and have never publicly identified the route being used, an omission that suggests either the route is sophisticated enough to defeat investigation or the clans have reasons to prefer not knowing.
planets.desc: Damph is governed by a patchwork of worker clans, tough, territorial, deeply suspicious of outsiders, and fiercely proud of what they do. Corporate interests are present but operate carefully. Anyone who has tried to simply take control of Damph has found the clans remarkably unified on the subject of not allowing that. The planet is cold, hostile, and absolutely essential to the galaxy's most powerful drive systems. The clans understand their position exactly.

planets.name: Damph II
planets.temperature: ~-180°C to -120°C (airless ice)
planets.economy: None, surveyed for Coronthia deposits, none found
planets.access_note: Outside clan territorial jurisdiction. No clan has claimed it. Alliance survey has been completed.
hazards: No atmosphere
Extreme cold
No infrastructure
planets.desc: A frozen outer world in the Damph system that has been surveyed for Coronthia deposits and found to contain none. The clans have not claimed it and show no interest. It is the one body in the system that nobody argues about.

planets.name: Damph Outer Giant
planets.atm_note: Pale brown hydrogen-helium gas envelope
planets.temperature: Cryogenic, around -160°C
planets.access_note: No infrastructure or restrictions.
hazards: Standard gas giant hazards
planets.desc: A large gas giant at the outer reach of the Damph system. The clans have occasionally discussed establishing a fuel skimming operation here to reduce their dependence on external fuel supply, a discussion that has not progressed into a formal proposal because the clans cannot agree on who would control it.

catalogue_systems.name: Alsa System
catalogue_systems.desc: Alsa is where the galaxy eats. The system's worlds are extraordinarily fertile, geology, climate and water distribution aligned in a combination that produces agricultural output unmatched anywhere in known space. Most of the food consumed across Alliance Space originates here in some form. Quiet, green, and vastly important.
catalogue_systems.subtitle: The Only World That Still Grows Real Food, and Cannot Be Copied
catalogue_systems.quote: "You can print a meal that tastes like a meal. You cannot print the ground it grew in, and we hold every handful of ground that matters. So you will be courteous, and you will pay what we ask." (Harvest Council elder, recorded at a closed supply hearing)
catalogue_systems.history:
Alsa was settled to farm, and it turned out to farm better than anywhere else, an accident of geology and water that yields more, and finer, than any other world in known space. As the rest of the galaxy industrialised and turned to synthesised food, most worlds gave up agriculture for cheap printed nutrition. Alsa did the opposite. It kept growing the real thing, and over the generations the real thing turned from a commodity into a luxury.
What made Alsa untouchable is that its fertility will not travel. Seed stock moved to another world fails within a generation, because the productivity rests on a living substrate beneath the fields, the Underloam, that no laboratory has ever reproduced. Alsa is not the cheapest food world. It is the only real one, and the monopoly is rooted, quite literally, in the ground.
To manage a gift like that, the farming families bound themselves into the Cooperative, to set supply on their own terms and to keep the land in their own hands. Alsa is quiet and green and beloved on the surface. It is also the most heavily defended system in the Alliance, because everyone understands what losing it would mean.
catalogue_systems.politics:
The Cooperative presents itself as the friendliest institution in the galaxy, a co-op of farm families run by slow consensus in the Harvest Councils, where every holding has a voice, with an Alliance-chartered body, the Agricultural Consortium Council, as its public face.
Real authority belongs to the Seed-Holders, the oldest rootline families, who keep the master seed vaults and the soil-lore that keeps Alsa producing. Power here is measured in land and in lineage, and neither can be bought in an afternoon.
Behind the friendly face is a disciplined cartel. The Cooperative sets quotas, lets surplus rot rather than flood the market, and trades food for influence as readily as for credits. Its real strength is that it cannot be bought. Corporations have spent generations trying to purchase or fracture it, and the solidarity has held every time, because to betray the co-op is to lose the land, and no single farm survives alone. In a galaxy where everything has a price, Alsa is the rare power that does not, which makes it both admired and quietly resented.

dominant_race.name: The Rootline Families
dominant_race.lore:
Alsa's people are farmers, and on Alsa that is a rank, not a job. The dominant culture is the rootlines, multi-generational farm families, overwhelmingly human, who trace their holdings and their seed-stock to the colony's first plantings. Among them live large Hakari communities, valued as Field Wardens and harvest crews, and a much older Patriark presence whose reasons for being on a farm world are a story of their own.
Rootline culture is patient and communal, with the stubbornness of people who answer to weather and soil rather than to markets. They are warm and almost impossible to move. Outsiders mistake the folksy manners for simplicity and are corrected: these are people who feed the galaxy on their own terms and know exactly what that is worth. Many of the older hands hold a near-religious regard for the Underloam, the living substrate under their fields, and speak of listening to it in a way newcomers find charming until they realise the old farmer is not speaking in metaphor.

race_standing.note: The rootlines are overwhelmingly human, so a human who works the land is the heart of Alsa. A human who arrives in a corporate suit is fed, charged well, and watched.

A large and valued community. Their speed and their nerve suit the work, and many serve as Field Wardens, the people who run down seed-thieves across the fields. Loyalty to the land has earned them a permanent place in it.
Steady and tireless in the fields and the processing yards. The kind of reliable that Alsa respects, and rewards in proportion to the work.

A Patriark community has lived on Alsa far longer than its stated reasons explain, advising and recording and taking a curious interest in the soil. The rootlines extend them every courtesy and trust them not at all, because no one is sure what the Patriark already know about where Alsa's fertility came from.
Rare, respected, and left in peace. A people who keep their word fit easily into a culture that prizes the same.
Intimidation is worthless against the people who control the food, and the Nerulian know it. They are met with stubborn, smiling politeness and given nothing they have not paid for.
Useful for yield science and unwelcome near the Underloam, where the old hands insist a cold, hollow mind does not belong. Hired for the laboratory and kept off the fields.

A culture that reveres natural growth has a blind spot about people grown in vats. The Cooperative's charter welcomes Non-Born labour; the rootline families, who measure worth by descent, are slower to. A Non-Born can work Alsa for years and still be called a newcomer.

relations.name: The Alliance
relations.note: Alsa feeds the Alliance's core worlds and its fleets, and in return holds the most heavily defended patrol perimeter in known space. The Cooperative trades food for protection and protection for quiet, and rarely has to say so.

relations.name: Corporate replicators & biotech
relations.note: Every corporation that sells synthesised food, and every biotech house that dreams of cracking Alsa's fertility, runs a quiet war of biopiracy against the system. The Field Wardens run an equally quiet war back.

relations.name: The Patriark / Berilia
relations.note: Berilia owns the continuation of life; Alsa owns its sustenance. The two great life-powers of Alliance space are elaborately polite, and the old Patriark presence on Alsa makes the relationship closer, and stranger, than either will admit.

relations.name: Goodman Holistic
relations.note: An aligned member enterprise that carries the Cooperative's natural-food creed into the wider market, and serves as its friendliest public voice.

catalogue_systems.gm_notes: Play Alsa as a velvet trap with dirt under its fingernails. It is welcoming and green, and it is one of the most quietly powerful places in the galaxy, because everyone has to eat and almost no one can grow it. Real food is the currency here. A meal of actual Alsa produce is a luxury most characters have never tasted, and it works better than credits as a bribe or an open door. The live plots are biopiracy, the co-op that cannot be bought, and the Underloam, which you should let the players feel is a little too alive and never fully explain. And keep the embedded Patriark in mind: someone on Alsa has been waiting a very long time for something.

planets.name: Alsa Prime
planets.atm_note: Pristine, no industrial pollution, ecosystem rigorously protected by consortium charter
planets.temperature: ~10°C to 28°C (engineered-stable temperate)
planets.demographics: Mixed, predominantly human with significant Patriark and Hakari communities
planets.economy: Grain production, protein cultivation, processed food export, water export, agricultural research
planets.access_note: Open with standard Alliance ID. Agricultural zone access requires consortium permit. Naval exclusion zones around orbital platforms enforced.
hazards: Alliance navy patrols, the system is a designated strategic asset, naval response is fast
Corporate sabotage operations, several major corps have historical interest in disrupting Alsa supply chains
Ecological protection law is absolute, violations carry severe penalties
Weather manipulation infrastructure, regional climate is actively managed, interference is criminal

notable_locations.name: The Breadplains
notable_locations.desc: The central agricultural zone of Alsa Prime, hundreds of thousands of square kilometres of managed cultivation producing the bulk of the system's export crop. Heavily mechanised, lightly populated, and the reason the galaxy eats.

notable_locations.name: Consortium Administration (Alsa City)
notable_locations.desc: The seat of the Agricultural Consortium. Manages production quotas, export contracts, and the insurance frameworks that protect Alsa's output. Every major food distribution corporation has an office here.

notable_locations.name: Alliance Naval Station Alsa
notable_locations.desc: The permanent military presence protecting the system. Sized for deterrence, not just patrol, attacking Alsa would mean fighting a standing fleet. This is deliberate.

notable_locations.name: The Seed Vaults
notable_locations.desc: The most comprehensive collection of agricultural genetic material in the known galaxy. Maintained as a strategic reserve. Location partially classified.

notable_locations.name: The Deep Seed Vault
notable_locations.desc: The Cooperative's most guarded site: the master archive of Alsa's original seed-stock and the soil-cultures that keep the Underloam alive. Its location is a rootline secret, its defences are absurd, and every biopirate in the galaxy dreams of reaching it.

specialties.name: Real Bread
specialties.desc: Loaf bread baked from actual grown grain. Most of the galaxy has only ever eaten the printed approximation; a single real Alsa loaf costs more than a labourer earns in a week, and is reckoned worth it.

specialties.name: Heirloom Harvest Box
specialties.desc: A sealed assortment of genuine fruit, vegetables, and cured meat, the standard luxury gift among people wealthy enough to give one. Counterfeited constantly and never convincingly.

specialties.name: First-Press Sunfruit Wine
specialties.desc: Pressed from real orchard fruit grown in Underloam soil, with a depth no synthesized vintage has matched. Poured at Directorate tables on Berilia and senate dinners on Orion.

hooks: Agricultural economists who follow food futures markets closely have noted that commodity prices occasionally move on information that cannot be explained by any publicly available data about Alsa production, suggesting that non-public information about cultivation zone conditions reaches certain traders before it becomes generally known. The Consortium has investigated this repeatedly without published findings.

The practice of Alliance naval personnel using exclusion zone access to move personal cargo through the Alsa system without manifesting it is documented in enough whistleblower accounts and court records from other systems that it is considered standard in naval cultures near strategic assets. What specifically moves through the Alsa exclusion zone has never been established.

Geneticists who study agricultural heritage varieties have identified strains in current commercial cultivation that do not match any recorded lineage in open databases, but that do match descriptions of varieties registered under corporate licenses that were dissolved in ways that should have ended the line. The Seed Vaults are believed to hold records that would explain the discrepancy, but access to the relevant sections has never been approved.

Farmers who have worked Alsa Prime's oldest fields all their lives speak, quietly and consistently, of the Underloam responding to them: blights that retreat from fields whose families have tended them for generations, and failures that follow newcomers who do not 'ask the ground first.' Agricultural scientists have documented the yield anomalies for decades without ever producing an accepted explanation, and the Cooperative has never once invited them to try harder.
planets.desc: Alsa Prime is the most fertile world in the known galaxy. The combination of geology, climate and hydrology that produces this output is not fully understood and has never been successfully replicated elsewhere. The Agricultural Consortium operates it under Alliance charter with the explicit strategic priority of keeping the supply chain intact. Three Alliance navy cruisers are on permanent station in the system. Disrupting Alsa's output is one of the most inadvisable things anyone could attempt in the known galaxy.

planets.name: Alsa Inner Rock
planets.temperature: Up to ~430°C on the sunward face (scorched, airless)
planets.access_note: Within the Alliance military exclusion zone perimeter but no specific restriction at this body.
hazards: Extreme surface temperatures
No atmosphere, full EVA
planets.desc: A small, scorched rocky world close to the Alsa star, too hot and airless to support any activity. The Agricultural Consortium has never shown interest in it. It sits inside the Alliance navy's patrol perimeter and is occasionally used as a navigational reference point on approach to Alsa Prime.

planets.name: Alsa Secondary Worlds
planets.atm_note: Maintained atmospheres across all inhabited bodies
planets.climate: Variable by body, temperate to arid
planets.temperature: Temperate, varying by body, roughly ~5°C to 30°C
planets.demographics: Mixed Alliance demographic, primarily rural and agricultural worker communities
planets.economy: Secondary crop production, livestock, aquaculture, processing facilities
planets.access_note: Standard Alliance access. Remote agricultural bodies have limited infrastructure, arrivals are noted.
hazards: Extreme isolation, emergency response times on remote bodies are long
Consortium security on commercial zones is assertive
Weather dependency, these worlds have less managed climate than Alsa Prime

notable_locations.name: Processing Stations
notable_locations.desc: Where raw agricultural output is processed for interstellar shipping. Enormous, busy, and surrounded by the constant traffic of freighters and bulk haulers.

specialties.name: Open-Range Protein
specialties.desc: Actual ranged and farmed meat from the secondary worlds, not vat-cultured. Rare enough off-world to be a status dish in its own right.

specialties.name: Live Aquaculture
specialties.desc: Genuine farmed fish and shellfish from the cluster's managed waters, shipped live at extraordinary cost to buyers who can taste the difference.

hooks: Among freight crews who run the Alsa secondary world routes regularly, there are persistent accounts of crew members going missing between system entry and destination arrival, not falling overboard or deserting, but simply not present when the ship docks, with no record of departure and no body found. The accounts span multiple decades and multiple crews and are considered by those who make the runs to be an established occupational hazard that nobody has successfully explained.
planets.desc: The secondary worlds of the Alsa system extend the system's agricultural capacity well beyond Alsa Prime alone. Each body is cultivated for specific outputs that complement the primary world's production. Together they make the Alsa system the single most productive food-production system in known space by volume. The scale of what moves through here daily is difficult to overstate, and difficult to audit completely.

planets.name: Alsa Outer Giant
planets.atm_note: Banded hydrogen-helium atmosphere
planets.temperature: Cryogenic cloud tops, around -145°C
planets.access_note: Outer system. No restrictions beyond Alliance military general patrol coverage.
hazards: Alliance navy patrols in the system, vessels at this range should be prepared to respond to standard ID challenge
planets.desc: A large gas giant visible from Alsa Prime's surface as a bright point of light at opposition. The Alliance navy has surveyed its moons but established no permanent installation. The Consortium considers the system's outer region adequately protected by the patrol fleet without additional infrastructure investment.

catalogue_systems.name: Ash System
catalogue_systems.desc: Ash sits at the Alliance edge of the Nemani Rift, the one barrier in the galaxy the Kraven swarm cannot or will not cross. The Alliance keeps a permanent watch here for any sign that the wall is failing, because if it ever does, Ash is the first thing in Alliance space the thing that ate the Nerulian Empire will reach. Around the watch has grown a hard salvage economy of dry docks and scrappers and pilots who run the Rift for what can be dragged out of it. Most do not come back.
catalogue_systems.subtitle: The Watchtower on the One Wall Holding Back the Kraven
catalogue_systems.quote: "Everything past Ash is the Rift, and everything the Rift holds back ate an empire in a week. We are not here to fight it. We are here to notice the day it learns to come through." (Rift Watch duty officer)
catalogue_systems.history:
Ash matters for one reason: it sits at the near edge of the Nemani Rift, and the Nemani Rift is the only thing that has ever stopped the Kraven. The swarm consumed the Nerulian Empire, hundreds of systems, in a single week, and then it reached the Rift and halted, in every direction, for reasons no one understands. Ash is the Alliance world that lives closest to that miracle, and trusts it least.
The Alliance keeps a permanent military watch here, monitoring the Rift for any change in the barrier and any hint of Kraven activity along it. Around that watch a second economy grew up on its own, the salvage trade. Beyond the Rift lie the dead worlds of the Nerulian Empire, full of a thousand years of abandoned technology, and pilots come to Ash precisely to brave the Rift and haul some of it home. The Rift kills most of them, not the Kraven but the nebula itself, which scrambles instruments and rearranges its own passages. The ones who return come back rich, famous, or permanently changed.
catalogue_systems.politics:
Ash runs on two authorities that mostly leave each other alone. The Alliance Navy holds the frontier station and the watch, and on the subject of the Rift its word is final. Everything else, the dry docks, the salvage yards, the crews and brokers and Rift runners, is a rough, self-policing community of independents who tolerate the military because the military tolerates them, and because both understand what they are sitting next to.
There is almost no civilian life here in the ordinary sense. People come to Ash to watch the Rift or to risk it, and the place has the particular calm of somewhere everyone has already made peace with the odds. The Navy's one non-negotiable rule is that the watch comes first. Anything that interferes with monitoring the Rift is dealt with quickly, because the entire point of Ash is to be the alarm that gives the rest of Alliance space time to react.

dominant_race.name: The Watch and the Salvagers
dominant_race.lore:
Ash has no settled population in the usual sense, only the two kinds of people a frontier like this attracts. The first are the watch, the Alliance Navy crews who man the frontier station and the sensor platforms and spend their rotations staring at a nebula, waiting for it to do something. The second are the salvagers, the dock crews and mechanics in the crater enclaves and the pilots who run the Rift, drawn by the dead empire's treasure on the far side of the deadliest passage in known space.
Between them Ash has the unmistakable feel of a place where people do work they know may kill them, surrounded by others who respect that and do not ask too many questions. It is grim, competent, and oddly companionable, the camaraderie of people sharing the edge of a cliff.

race_standing.note: The backbone of the frontier, in Navy uniform and salvage rig alike. On Ash a human is measured by how they handle the watch or the Rift, and by nothing else.

The hardest place in the galaxy to be Nerulian. The Rift leads into what was once the Nerulian Empire, the salvage hauled past Ash is stripped from Nerulian graves, and the Kraven that ate that empire wait on the far side. A Nerulian on Ash is standing at the edge of their own apocalypse, and everyone knows it.
Among the best Rift runners there are. Speed and nerve are exactly what the nebula demands, and a Hakari pilot who has run the Rift and returned can name their price.
Built for the brutal physical work of the dry docks and the salvage yards, and steady in a place that frays steadier people. Always in demand on the frontier.

Warriors at the edge of the thing that ended the empire they were made to fight. The Skalander take frontier postings seriously and are respected for it, and a few seem to find a grim peace here that they find nowhere else.
The long-lived who remember the Nerulian Empire whole, and who once kept this region safe from it. A Patriark on Ash is unusual and watched, and assumed to be here for a reason no one has been told.

Cold, tireless minds suit the watch, where the work is endless attention to a nebula that lies to every sensor pointed at it. The Navy values Psylon on the sensor platforms more than most crews enjoy serving beside them.

The frontier runs on Non-Born labour as every hard posting does, crewing the docks and the worst of the salvage work. On Ash, where everyone is gambling with their lives, the usual condescension thins; a Non-Born who runs the Rift is a Rift runner like any other.

relations.name: The Alliance
relations.note: Holds the frontier station and the watch, and treats Ash as what it is, the alarm bell on the galaxy's most important wall. The Navy's word on the Rift is final.

relations.name: The Kraven
relations.note: The swarm beyond the Rift that consumed the Nerulian Empire and stopped at the nebula for reasons no one can explain. Ash exists to watch for the day that stops being true.

relations.name: The Nemani Rift
relations.note: The barrier that holds the Kraven back and the nebula that kills the salvagers who run it. Ash owes the Rift its safety and its trade and trusts it with neither.

relations.name: The salvager community
relations.note: The dock crews and Rift runners who make Ash more than a garrison. The Navy tolerates them, the Rift thins them, and the survivors are some of the best pilots in Alliance space.

catalogue_systems.gm_notes: Run Ash as the quiet end of the galaxy's worst horror story, a frontier that is calm precisely because everyone has already accepted the odds. Two engines drive play here. The first is the Rift run, salvage from the dead Nerulian worlds, fabulous payoff against a nebula that rearranges itself and lies to every instrument. The second is the watch, where the campaign-ending hook is simple: something on the Rift changes, and Ash is the only place that has noticed yet. Keep the Kraven offstage and absolute; the dread is the point, and the worst thing you can do with the swarm is let the players get a clear look at it and live.

planets.name: Ash
planets.type: Rocky World, Artificial-Gravity Crater Enclaves (Dry Docks)
planets.atm_note: Airless at the surface; breathable only inside the sealed, pressurised crater enclaves
planets.temperature: Frozen and airless, broadly -150°C in shadow to -40°C in weak sun; the enclaves run their own climate
planets.population: ~400,000 dock crews, salvagers, mechanics, and ground staff
planets.demographics: Mixed, dock crews and salvagers and ground staff, transient
planets.government: Alliance frontier authority over the docks; independents otherwise
planets.economy: Dry Docks, repair, and ground support for the Rift salvage trade
planets.access_note: Open to registered crews. Outside the enclaves is hard vacuum and almost no gravity, so wandering off is its own death sentence.
hazards: Vacuum and near-zero gravity outside the crater enclaves
Rift-proximity anomalies that disrupt instruments and comms
Heavy salvage traffic and unstable recovered wreckage

notable_locations.name: Rift Station Alpha (Military)
notable_locations.desc: The primary Alliance monitoring installation for the Nemani Rift. Permanently staffed, heavily armed, and not open to civilian visitors. The intelligence gathered here is among the most restricted in the Alliance.

notable_locations.name: The Departure Yards
notable_locations.desc: Where Rift pilots fuel up, equip, and say their goodbyes. The culture here is unique, a combination of technical professionalism, fatalism, and the particular energy of people who have decided to do something they know is probably going to kill them.

notable_locations.name: Salvage Basin
notable_locations.desc: The primary civilian economic zone. Salvage operators bring finds here for assessment, trade and processing. A significant portion of the goods traded have unclear provenance. The Alliance inspectors are aware of this. Their interest in it varies.

notable_locations.name: The Wall
notable_locations.desc: The informal name for the Rift boundary as it appears in local space, a visible spatial distortion line that can be observed with the naked eye under the right conditions. Looking at it for extended periods is not recommended.

specialties.name: Rift Salvage
specialties.desc: Technology hauled out of the Nemani Rift and the dead Nerulian worlds beyond it, a thousand years of a lost empire's engineering recovered at a brutal casualty rate. Priceless, unpredictable, and occasionally still dangerous in ways no one has documented.

hooks: Rift pilots who return from runs into the Nemani Rift occasionally bring back objects they cannot identify and will not discuss. The Departure Yards at Ash have developed an informal culture around not asking, partly from respect for pilot privacy and partly from the understanding that what comes out of the Rift may be something where ignorance is preferable. Alliance registries contain no records matching any of the described objects.

The Alliance military exclusion zone around the Nemani Rift has been extended multiple times over the decades without public announcement. Salvagers who know the old zone boundaries notice the changes when they are redirected by patrol vessels who give no explanation. The cumulative area absorbed over the years suggests the military has found or observed things in successive zones that warranted extending the perimeter.

Research teams studying Rift proximity anomalies near Ash have a documented history of communication gaps that do not match equipment failure profiles and are longer than emergency protocols allow for without being treated as a loss. The Alliance military's standard response to inquiries about missing teams, that it has no information about their location, is precise enough that experienced observers treat it as a formal statement that says less than it appears to.
planets.desc: Ash is not a colony so much as a working surface. The rock itself is airless and all but weightless, and life here happens inside a scatter of small craters fitted with their own gravity and air, the dry docks and salvage yards and machine shops that keep the Rift runners flying. It is cramped, loud, and purposeful, a place where the ships go to be patched up between attempts at the deadliest passage in known space.
planets.grav_note: Generated artificially inside the crater enclaves only; the bare surface has almost none

planets.name: Ash Frontier Station (Rift Watch)
planets.type: Space Station, Military & Civilian Frontier Hub
planets.atm_note: Maintained throughout; hard vacuum beyond the hull
planets.temperature: Climate-controlled interior, around 18°C to 22°C
planets.grav_note: Artificially generated and held stable throughout the station
planets.population: ~3 million, the bulk of the system, military and civilian
planets.demographics: Mixed, Navy personnel over a civilian population of salvage crews, brokers, and frontier traders
planets.government: Alliance Navy Frontier Command, with a civilian administration beneath it
planets.economy: Rift monitoring, military logistics, salvage brokerage, frontier supply
planets.access_note: Open under standard Alliance clearance. The military decks and the Rift-monitoring sections are restricted.
hazards: Frontier crime and salvage-claim disputes
The constant, low background dread of a posting next to the Kraven barrier
Rift anomalies occasionally reaching the system edge

notable_locations.name: The Watch Floor
notable_locations.desc: The heart of Rift Watch, where Navy crews monitor the Nemani Rift around the clock for any change in the barrier. The most important job nobody wants, performed by people who have learned to live with what they are watching for.

hooks: Veteran Watch crews maintain, quietly and consistently, that the Rift has not stayed exactly the same over the decades they have monitored it, and that the changes, though small, do not look random. Command files the reports and does not discuss them.

specialties.name: Rift Runners
specialties.desc: The other thing Ash produces: pilots who have flown the Nemani Rift and come back. A Rift run is a credential no simulator can fake, and a Rift runner who lives to sell it is among the most sought-after pilots in Alliance space.

planets.desc: The frontier station is where most of Ash actually lives. Built as the Alliance Navy's forward command on the Nemani Rift, it grew a civilian population around it the way frontier postings do, salvage brokers and supply runs and the families of people who work the Rift. Its real purpose never changes. Somewhere on the station, every hour of every day, someone is watching the nebula and waiting for it to blink.

planets.name: Ash II
planets.type: Rocky World, Artificial-Gravity Crater Enclaves (Salvage & Repair)
planets.atm_note: Airless at the surface; breathable only inside the sealed, pressurised crater enclaves
planets.temperature: Frozen and airless, broadly -160°C to -50°C; survivable only inside the enclaves
planets.faction: None, within Alliance military patrol zone
planets.demographics: Mixed, dock crews and salvagers and ground staff, transient
planets.government: Alliance frontier authority over the docks; independents otherwise
planets.economy: Salvage & Repair, repair, and ground support for the Rift salvage trade
planets.access_note: Open to registered crews. Outside the enclaves is hard vacuum and almost no gravity, so wandering off is its own death sentence.
hazards: Vacuum and near-zero gravity outside the crater enclaves
Rift-proximity anomalies that disrupt instruments and comms
Heavy salvage traffic and unstable recovered wreckage
planets.desc: Ash II is the system's second worked rock, the same arrangement as the first: an airless, low-gravity body whose only inhabited spots are pressurised craters with imported gravity and air. Where the first handles the dry docks, Ash II runs to breaking yards and parts recovery, the place where the salvage that comes back through the Rift is torn down, sorted, and sold.
planets.grav_note: Generated artificially inside the crater enclaves only; the bare surface has almost none

planets.name: Ash Outer Giant
planets.atm_note: Hydrogen-helium gas envelope with unusual radio emission patterns attributed to Rift proximity
planets.temperature: Cryogenic cloud tops, roughly -110°C to -180°C; far hotter in the deep atmosphere under pressure
planets.population: Uninhabited, Alliance sensor station on one moon
planets.access_note: Alliance military sensor station on primary moon. Approach to the moon requires clearance. The planet itself is unrestricted.
hazards: Alliance military installation on moon, approach challenge expected
Unusual electromagnetic emissions from Rift proximity, navigation instruments may behave unexpectedly
planets.desc: A gas giant at the outer edge of the Ash system, selected as a monitoring platform because of its position relative to the Nemani Rift boundary. The Alliance maintains a forward sensor station on one of its moons, the deepest of the system's watch posts on the Nemani Rift boundary, feeding the frontier station everything it can read of a nebula that resists being read.

catalogue_systems.name: Palentium System
catalogue_systems.classification: Core System, Human Homeworld & Tourist Capital
catalogue_systems.desc: Palentium is humanity's adopted homeworld and the galaxy's favourite holiday, a warm tropical world of long coastlines and luxury resorts that requires no atmospheric work to be beautiful. It is also one of the most thoroughly corrupt places in known space, where the scenery is real and almost nothing else is. Tourism is the main export, an idea humans more or less invented, and everything is for sale to anyone who knows whom to ask.
catalogue_systems.subtitle: Humanity's Adopted Homeworld, and the Prettiest Place in the Galaxy to Be Robbed
catalogue_systems.quote: "Welcome to Palentium. The beaches are real, the smiles are real, and the watch you just won in the lobby raffle is not." (concierge greeting, the Gold Coast)
catalogue_systems.history:
Palentium was the first world humans set foot on in what became Alliance Space, and it became, by adoption rather than birth, their home. Humanity's true cradle is a distant world the Patriark seeded and walked away from before anyone there could write, so Palentium is the home humans chose instead, and they have spent centuries making it the most human place in the galaxy. It is warm, tropical, and beautiful enough that everything else came easily.
What humans did with it was invent the holiday. Leisure for its own sake, travel purely for pleasure, the whole notion of a place you go just to enjoy yourself, was something the older races had never bothered with, and humans turned it into an industry and then an export. Tourism is now Palentium's main business and one of humanity's signature gifts to galactic culture, which says something warm about the species and something less warm about what it built underneath.
Underneath the beaches is the other human invention the world runs on, the hustle. The corruption is so old and so complete that locals treat it as weather. Everything is for sale, every smile is angled, and every third opportunity is a scam, and none of it dents the appeal. People keep coming, because the sun is real and the fun is real even when nothing else is.
catalogue_systems.politics:
On paper Palentium is governed by a Planetary Council under Alliance charter. In practice the Council exists to keep the tourists arriving and the money moving, and any decision that matters needs the blessing of the resort and entertainment conglomerates that actually run the place. The house, as they say locally, always gets a vote.
The corruption is not a flaw in the system; it is the system. Law enforcement is for sale, regulation is theatre, and the financial district launders for half the galaxy behind a wall of deliberate opacity. None of this is exactly hidden. It is simply priced in. A visitor who grasps that everything on Palentium is a transaction does fine. A visitor who believes the brochure does not.
The one article of faith everyone in power shares is that the show must go on. Crime is tolerated so long as it stays the kind that fleeces tourists rather than frightening them off, scams ahead of violence and skimming ahead of slaughter, and the conglomerates and the Council and the local rackets all police that line together, because a Palentium that stopped being fun would stop being profitable for any of them.

dominant_race.name: Humanity
dominant_race.lore:
Palentium is humanity's world, and humanity is the galaxy's great improviser. Seeded on a lost world and abandoned young by the Patriark, humans came late to the stars and made up the distance with raw ambition and an unfailing instinct for the angle. On Palentium that instinct found its natural home. The culture is human to the core, warm and quick and relentlessly entrepreneurial, as capable of running the finest resort you will ever visit as the cleanest con you will never notice.
Humans are at once the most trusted and the most mistrusted species in the galaxy, and Palentium is a large part of why so many lean toward the second. The world puts everything appealing about humanity on display, the warmth and the energy and the genius for making life enjoyable, alongside everything suspect about it, in the same square mile. Most species never understood the human appetite for leisure until Palentium sold it to them, and most have never quite forgiven how good humans turned out to be at parting a happy customer from his money.

race_standing.note: Home in every sense, hosts and hustlers and marks alike. A human on Palentium is among their own, which is no guarantee of safety, since the cleverest cons here are run on other humans.

The absent makers, visiting the child they abandoned. Locals treat a Patriark with nervous deference and assume, correctly, that the long-lived find the whole pleasure economy faintly absurd. Hard to con and unsettling to host.
Duty-bound warriors who find leisure for its own sake genuinely alien, and come, if at all, for honest rest. Poor marks and good guests, given the respect owed to someone who cannot be hustled.
Out of place on a beach and very welcome at a high-stakes table, where their patience pays. The resorts court the wealthy ones and hire the rest as the muscle that keeps the fun orderly.
Fast hands suit a casino floor from either side of the felt, as croupiers, as performers, and now and then as the reason a guest's room was emptied. Prized as entertainers and watched as thieves.
Menace is bad for the holiday mood, so the resorts handle a Nerulian guest with careful, anxious courtesy. The rich ones are indulged for their spending; the rest are steered toward the door.
A mind that reads a table at a glance is a casino's nightmare, and Palentium's gaming floors quietly bar or shadow Psylon for exactly that reason. Welcome as analysts, unwelcome at the felt.

The smiling face of every resort is largely Non-Born labour, the staff who pour the drinks and turn the beds and will never afford a night in the rooms they clean. The glamour rests on the people the glamour is not for.

relations.name: The Alliance
relations.note: Charters the Council and supplies the respectable letterhead. Real authority belongs to the conglomerates, and the Alliance long ago stopped pretending otherwise in any room that matters.

relations.name: Resort & entertainment conglomerates
relations.note: The true government of Palentium. They run the resorts, own the Council, and enforce the one rule that counts, which is to keep the world fun, profitable, and arriving on schedule.

relations.name: The galaxy's tourists
relations.note: Everyone, eventually. Palentium's export is the holiday itself, and a steady flow of visitors from every race and world is the whole economy, marks and guests in the same breath.

relations.name: The crime syndicates
relations.note: Organised crime treats Palentium as a standing income, laundering through its casinos and skimming its tourist trade. The arrangement is tolerated because the syndicates, too, need the show to go on.

catalogue_systems.gm_notes: Run Palentium as paradise with a hand on your wallet. The beaches are genuinely gorgeous, the fun is genuinely fun, and absolutely everyone is running an angle. The surface rewards players who relax and punishes players who trust. Strong plots: the con, with the party as marks or as grifters working a bigger fish; the resort with something buried under it; a debt to the house that cannot be walked away from; a tourist who vanished between the lobby and the beach; a laundering trail that runs through a casino vault. Keep the tone warm and sunlit and quietly predatory, and remember the rule the whole planet lives by: the show must go on, so violence that scares the tourists is the one sin Palentium will unite to punish.

planets.name: Palentium
planets.atm_note: Clean and warm, the atmosphere is a genuine selling point of the tourism industry
planets.temperature: Warm and tropical year round, roughly 22°C to 34°C, with the sea breezes the brochures never stop mentioning
planets.grav_note: Slightly below standard, contributes to the pleasant physical sensation the tourism industry highlights
planets.demographics: Highly mixed, all Alliance races, significant permanent corporate expatriate community, rotating tourist population
planets.government: Palentium Planetary Council (formally Alliance-chartered; practically, major decisions require corporate approval)
planets.economy: Luxury tourism, financial services, offshore corporate administration, entertainment, hospitality
planets.access_note: Open with standard Alliance ID. Criminal records are flagged on entry, but flags can be managed for the right fee.
hazards: Pervasive corruption, every institution has a price, which means every institution is also a liability
Law enforcement is enthusiastically underpaid and comprehensively for sale
Political office is an investment vehicle, decisions are made for financial return, not public interest
Intelligence operations from multiple major corporations, the offshore financial sector means sensitive information passes through constantly
Tourist-targeting crime is endemic in resort zones, well-organised and ignored by local enforcement

notable_locations.name: The Coastal Resorts (Gold Coast)
notable_locations.desc: The headline tourism product. Luxury accommodations, private beaches, every amenity. The prices are extraordinary. The service is genuine. The staff all have a secondary income of some kind.

notable_locations.name: The Financial District (Palentium City)
notable_locations.desc: Where the offshore corporate administration happens. Shell companies, trust structures, financial instruments that do not exist in most other jurisdictions. If you need money to disappear or reappear with different paperwork, Palentium City is where it happens.

notable_locations.name: The Old Landing Site
notable_locations.desc: The original site of the first human footfall in Alliance Space, now a tourist monument of modest grandeur. The historical records associated with the site are impeccably maintained and selectively edited.

notable_locations.name: The Interior
notable_locations.desc: Away from the coastal resorts, Palentium's interior is lush, beautiful, and largely ignored by the tourism industry. It is where the people who make the tourism industry work actually live. Conditions vary dramatically from the coastal image.

specialties.name: The Palentium Holiday
specialties.desc: The packaged luxury vacation, humanity's invention and the galaxy's favourite indulgence. Sun, service, and spectacle sold by the week, and the true export of the entire system.

specialties.name: Gold Coast Cocktails
specialties.desc: The signature drinks of the resort strip, bright and potent and served in glasses engineered to photograph well. Half the cost is the view, and everyone pays it gladly.

specialties.name: The Sure Thing
specialties.desc: Palentium's cottage industry of get-rich-quick schemes, can't-lose investments, and opportunities of a lifetime, offered to every visitor at least once. The only guaranteed return is to the person selling it.

hooks: Palentium's offshore financial sector is believed by Alliance financial intelligence to be used by every major corporation in the known galaxy at some point in their operational history, not just for tax efficiency but for the specific function of creating transaction records that are technically accessible but practically unacoverable without physical presence on the planet and relationships with people who will not cooperate by default.

The practice of using compromising material obtained on Palentium for political leverage is so well-established that it has acquired a colloquial name in diplomatic circles. The island resort districts are understood to be under observation by multiple private intelligence operations simultaneously, all recording independently. The material eventually circulates into hands where it becomes useful.

Historians who have studied the original human survey mission that landed on Palentium have noted for decades that the official record contains inconsistencies with independently surviving accounts, accounts that are themselves inconsistent with each other in ways suggesting multiple versions of events were circulating immediately after the landing, rather than a single set of facts that was later disputed. What the survey mission actually found when it made first contact with the planet has never been definitively established.
planets.desc: Palentium is one of the most visited worlds in Alliance Space and one of the most thoroughly corrupt. The tourism industry is genuine and the scenery is real. The institutions are not. Law enforcement is underpaid because underpaid enforcement is easier to work with. Political office is contested because it generates return. The financial sector exists because some transactions need a location where the paperwork does not follow standard Alliance trail requirements. Players who arrive expecting Alliance law to protect them will be educated quickly and expensively.

planets.name: Palentium II
planets.temperature: Cold, roughly -40°C to 8°C
planets.demographics: Non-Born operators, small human management rotation
planets.access_note: Corporate property. No tourist or civilian access.
hazards: Corporate jurisdiction, armed security drone patrol
No atmosphere, full EVA at all times
planets.desc: A barren outer world being quietly mined by a corporation with shell structures based in Palentium City's financial district. The arrangement benefits from Palentium's financial opacity, the actual ownership chain of Palentium Mining LLC has been investigated twice by Alliance financial regulators and disappeared into offshore trust structures both times.

planets.name: Palentium Outer Giant
planets.atm_note: Dense hydrogen-helium gas envelope
planets.temperature: Cryogenic cloud tops, roughly -110°C to -180°C; far hotter in the deep atmosphere under pressure
planets.access_note: No restrictions. No infrastructure.
hazards: Standard gas giant hazards
planets.desc: A large gas giant at the outer edge of the Palentium system, occasionally visible from the Gold Coast resorts as a bright wandering star. No commercial operation has been established here, the corporations active in the system prefer to invest closer to the planet's profitable financial and tourism infrastructure.

catalogue_systems.name: New Earth System
catalogue_systems.desc: New Earth is the home of people who looked at the Alliance, decided the whole multiracial, corporate, regulated experiment was a mistake, and left to build the opposite. Around two centuries ago dissident settlers finished the modest terraforming the world needed and turned it into a private paradise of their own design, low in technology by choice and almost entirely human by policy. Most of the surface belongs not to a government but to private landholders who let others settle near their towns on their own terms, which in practice means a scatter of small domains run by men enjoying a colonial-rancher fantasy with no authority above them to object. There is little here for the corporations, no great wealth of rare materials and a distance from everywhere that makes the world useless as an agricultural exporter, so what corporate interest exists is minor and easily ignored. Outsiders are tolerated thinly, and other races not at all.

planets.name: New Earth
planets.atm_note: Clean, technological rejection means no industrial pollution
planets.temperature: Temperate to cold, roughly -15°C to 22°C
planets.demographics: ~99% human, any non-human discovery results in expulsion or worse
planets.economy: Agriculture, small-scale manufacturing, barter-based internal trade
planets.access_note: Non-humans not permitted. Outsiders treated with extreme suspicion. Advanced technology confiscated on arrival. Alliance law does not apply.
hazards: Extreme ideological hostility to non-humans, discovery means violence
Advanced technology confiscated, entering with FTL or combat tech invites aggression
No Alliance legal protection, colonial law is the only law
Surveillance by colonial militia throughout populated areas

notable_locations.name: Founder's Rest (Capital)
notable_locations.desc: The main settlement. Architecturally and technologically resembles a 17th-18th century Earth settlement. The colonial council meets here. Outside visitors are watched closely.

notable_locations.name: The Perimeter
notable_locations.desc: The outer edge of the settled territory where the colonial militia patrols. People can enter New Earth without going through Founder's Rest, but the militia patrols are irregular and aggressive.

notable_locations.name: The Hidden District
notable_locations.desc: Rumoured to exist beneath Founder's Rest, a section where people who do not entirely share the colony's ideology keep themselves quiet. Its existence is unverified.

hooks: New Earth is well-documented among intelligence professionals as a place where individuals can live for extended periods without any record of their presence appearing in Alliance systems, the colony's rejection of external technology means no biometric scanning, no network connectivity, and no data sharing with Alliance databases. This makes it a reliable refuge for people who need to disappear, which the colonial council is aware of and views as an accidental benefit of their chosen way of life.

Non-humans living under cover in New Earth are an established phenomenon, documented in accounts from defectors and people who have left the colony. The community's surveillance capabilities are lower-tech but thorough, neighbours watch each other closely, and the tolerance for anything unusual is zero. The average period before cover breaks is measured in months rather than years.

Pre-industrial cultural archives exist on New Earth that have not been digitised, catalogued, or shared with any external institution, physical records from Earth's history that the colonists preserve as part of their cultural programme and consider their own property. Academics who have tried to access them through formal channels have universally been refused. The materials are understood to exist but their specific contents are not known to anyone outside the colony.
planets.desc: New Earth is what happens when a group of humans decides the galaxy's progress has gone too far. Founded by settlers who rejected multiracial Alliance society, it is a place where fugitives hide, where certain ideologies fester, and where players who arrive expecting normal Dark Space frontier life will find something far stranger. It is not powerful enough to be a serious threat to anyone, but it is exactly dangerous enough to be a problem for anyone who looks wrong, sounds wrong, or carries the wrong equipment.

planets.name: NE-II
planets.temperature: Cold, roughly -40°C to 8°C
planets.access_note: Colonial jurisdiction is limited to the inhabited main world. This body is unclaimed.
hazards: No atmosphere
Dark Space, no Alliance rescue coverage
planets.desc: A small, airless rock in the New Earth system. The colonists have no interest in it, their technological rejection precludes any space-based industrial activity. The designation NE-II comes from an old Dark Space survey catalogue they never adopted.

planets.name: NE-III
planets.atm_note: Standard gas giant atmosphere
planets.temperature: Cryogenic cloud tops, roughly -110°C to -180°C; far hotter in the deep atmosphere under pressure
planets.access_note: No restrictions. Dark Space, no Alliance coverage.
hazards: Standard gas giant hazards
Dark Space, no emergency response capability
planets.desc: A gas giant visible from New Earth's surface as a slow-moving bright object. The colonists named it something in their internal tradition but the name was never logged in any public navigational record. Dark Space survey charts list it only by catalogue number.

catalogue_systems.name: Andromede System
catalogue_systems.desc: Andromede is a system with nothing in it, and that is the point. It holds no planets, no moons, and no asteroid fields, only an unusually clean and empty volume of space that Lansing Corp bought cheap and turned into the finest large-scale shipyard district in Alliance space. Besides the yards it has one other thing of value: a mandatory gate relay near the system's centre, so a great deal of Alliance traffic passes through Andromede whether it meant to or not.
catalogue_systems.subtitle: An Empty Volume of Space That Lansing Bought Cheap and Rents Dear
catalogue_systems.quote: "There is nothing in Andromede. No worlds, no rocks, no view. That is exactly what you are paying for." (Lansing leasing brochure, opening line)
catalogue_systems.history:
Andromede was worthless, which is why Lansing Corp could afford it. The volume holds no planets and no asteroid fields, only a wide stretch of unusually clean, debris-free space, the kind of nothing nobody else had a use for. Lansing did. Building ships on the scale Lansing builds them needs room and stillness and a sky free of the debris that fouls precision work, and Andromede offered all of it for almost nothing. The company bought the empty space and filled it with the largest and most exacting shipyards in Alliance space.
The volume turned out to be worth far more than the price suggested, and not only to Lansing. Other shipbuilders needed the same clean, open conditions, so Lansing began leasing them berths, and the rent proved a steadier income than its own famously overbuilt ships ever managed. It helped that a mandatory gate relay sits at the system's centre, in the middle of Alliance space, so a great deal of traffic must route through Andromede no matter where it is bound.
catalogue_systems.politics:
Andromede has no government in the civic sense. It has a landlord. Lansing Corp owns the volume and sets the terms, and everything inside it runs on a lease. The corporations that build here accept Lansing's rules on conduct, safety, and salvage because clean space at this scale cannot be had anywhere else, and because the alternative is building somewhere that spoils the work.
The one thing Lansing does not own is the gate. The Alliance gate authority runs the relay at the system's heart, and its right of way is absolute, which makes Andromede an odd hybrid, a private industrial estate wrapped around a piece of public infrastructure the owner cannot touch. The arrangement holds because both sides need it to. Lansing's yards live on the traffic the relay brings, and the relay lives on the order Lansing keeps.

dominant_race.name: Yard Crews and Corporate Tenants
dominant_race.lore:
Andromede has no population of its own, only the people who come to work: shipwrights and engineers, dock crews, corporate staff on rotation, and the transient crews of ships passing through the relay. Nearly all of them are here on someone's payroll and someone's schedule, and almost none of them stay.
It is a company town without a town, professional and clean and a little soulless, where competence is the only measure that counts and the work is genuinely superb. Lansing's own yard crews carry the particular pride of people who build the best ships in the galaxy, and the corporate tenants pick up some of that standard whether they want to or not, because Lansing's conditions do not bend.

race_standing.note: The bulk of the workforce and the transient crews. On a payroll like everyone else, and judged by the work and nothing else.
Common in the yard crews and the heavy dock work. Andromede cares about competence and rotation schedules, not origins, which makes it easier going for a Non-Born than most places.

Precision and tirelessness are exactly what large-scale shipbuilding rewards, and Lansing's yards value Psylon engineers more than most employers do. Being hard to read across a table matters less here than being right.
Found in the corporate offices and the leasing negotiations, where patience and leverage pay. Treated as any tenant's representative is treated, politely and warily.
Dock crews, couriers, and the security that watches berths full of half-built capital ships. Fast hands are useful in a yard, and there is always something valuable to guard.
Heavy dock labour and the muscle for work that would cripple anyone smaller. Steady, tireless, and in steady demand.
Rare, and trusted as supervisors and inspectors in a place where a cut corner can kill a crew. A people who keep their word suit a yard that runs on exact tolerances.
Hired as yard security and kept at arm's length otherwise. Their menace keeps a berth orderly, which is the only reason most tenants put up with it.

relations.name: Lansing Corp
relations.note: The landlord, and the reason Andromede exists. Lansing owns the volume, builds its own ships here, and leases the rest, and its conditions are the closest thing the system has to law.

relations.name: The lessee corporations
relations.note: Shipbuilders and corporations that need clean space at scale and cannot get it elsewhere. They resent Lansing's terms and sign them anyway, because there is nowhere else to go.

relations.name: Alliance gate authority
relations.note: Runs the gate relay at the system's centre, with a right of way Lansing cannot override. The traffic it brings is half of what makes Andromede worth anything.

catalogue_systems.gm_notes: Andromede is a place to pass through, which makes it a fine place to stage almost anything. The mandatory relay means anyone crossing Alliance space can plausibly be here, so it serves as a crossroads, a meeting point, or an ambush. The yards stand full of half-built capital ships and proprietary designs sitting in clean, open space, which is an obvious target and a hard one, because Lansing's security is as exacting as its engineering. Lean on the landlord dynamic: on Andromede the fastest way to ruin someone is not violence but a lease review.

planets.name: The Lansing Yards
planets.atm_note: Maintained throughout pressurised sections; hard vacuum outside the hulls
planets.temperature: Climate-controlled interior, around 18°C to 22°C
planets.grav_note: Artificially generated and held stable throughout the works
planets.demographics: Mixed, heavily human and Non-Born, large Psylon engineering corps
planets.economy: Capital shipbuilding, precision fabrication, refit and repair
planets.access_note: Lansing contract or escorted business access only. Proprietary berths are closed to all outside parties.
hazards: Vacuum exposure outside pressurised hulls
Heavy yard traffic and moving hull sections
planets.desc: Lansing's own shipyards, and the reason it bought the system. The largest and most precise construction slips in Alliance space hang in the clean dark here, building the overbuilt vessels the company is famous for. The work is slow, exact, and guarded as closely as anything Lansing owns.

planets.name: The Leasehold Berths
planets.atm_note: Maintained throughout pressurised sections; hard vacuum outside the hulls
planets.temperature: Climate-controlled interior, around 18°C to 22°C
planets.grav_note: Artificially generated and held stable throughout the works
planets.government: Per-tenant corporate administration under Lansing master lease
planets.economy: Leased shipbuilding and heavy orbital fabrication
planets.access_note: Access governed by each tenant under Lansing master-lease terms. Lansing inspectors have right of entry everywhere.
hazards: Vacuum exposure outside pressurised hulls
Heavy yard traffic and moving hull sections
planets.desc: The berths Lansing rents to everyone else. Rival builders and corporations that need debris-free space at scale lease slips here and work under Lansing's conditions, because the clean volume is worth more than their pride. The rent is quietly the most dependable money Lansing makes.

planets.name: Andromede Gate Relay
planets.atm_note: Maintained throughout pressurised sections; hard vacuum outside the hulls
planets.temperature: Climate-controlled interior, around 18°C to 22°C
planets.grav_note: Artificially generated and held stable throughout the works
planets.demographics: Mixed, heavy transient traffic from every region
planets.economy: Gate transit, traffic control, refuelling and resupply
planets.access_note: Open transit under standard Alliance clearance. The relay itself is restricted to gate authority staff.
hazards: Dense transit traffic and tight approach windows
Surveillance from multiple parties drawn by the volume of passage
hooks: Couriers who run the Andromede relay regularly note that the busiest, most surveilled crossing in Alliance space is also the easiest place to meet someone without anyone being able to prove the meeting was arranged, since everyone has a legitimate reason to be passing through.
planets.desc: The reason half the galaxy passes through an empty system. A mandatory relay sits at Andromede's centre, routing a heavy share of Alliance traffic, and the Alliance gate authority runs it with a right of way even Lansing cannot override. Busy, neutral, and watched, it is the one part of Andromede the landlord does not own.

catalogue_systems.name: System 5
catalogue_systems.classification: Core System, Tronik Embassy & Neutral Junction
catalogue_systems.desc: System 5 has no name, only its designation, because the Alliance never agreed on one. It was a battleground of the Tronik War, three of its worlds destroyed and left as the debris the veterans call the Three Graves. The military station at its heart became something stranger after the war, a giant Tronik embassy and the one place the Troniks deal openly with organic life. The system is Alliance space, but the station runs on the Troniks' terms, neutral ground open to every race that respects its laws, and the only good that truly trades there is information.
catalogue_systems.subtitle: The Troniks' One Open Door, in the Graveyard of the War They Won
catalogue_systems.quote: "You imagine we wanted your worlds. We wanted your information. You generate it constantly and for free, and you call the arrangement peace." (Tronik contact protocol, translated)
catalogue_systems.history:
System 5 was central to the Tronik War, and it paid for it. Three of its worlds were destroyed outright and remain a debris field the veterans named the Three Graves, and the system never recovered the name the Alliance could never agree on either. The military station that anchored the system was captured by the Troniks in the fighting, and when the war ended on Tronik terms, it became the seed of something stranger.
Rather than hold organic territory, the Troniks made the station their single embassy to organic life, the one point of open contact for the most isolationist power in the galaxy. The system around it stayed Alliance space, but the station itself became, in every practical sense, sovereign Tronik ground, a giant embassy set down in Alliance territory amid the graves of the war that made the Troniks what they are. Organics come to deal at the edge of their own war dead, which the Troniks neither intended as a message nor bothered to prevent being read as one.
catalogue_systems.politics:
System 5 is Alliance space, and the Alliance holds the system and the perimeter around the station. The station itself is a different matter, a Tronik embassy that runs on Tronik law inside its own walls, the way an embassy always does. The Alliance accepts the arrangement because the station is the only way anyone deals with the Troniks at all, and because the alternative was settled, permanently, during the war. Tronik law is short, clear, and enforced with a consistency the historical record makes vivid. Respect it and you may trade in peace. Test it and you become part of the record.
Within those walls it is genuinely neutral, open to every race and faction, which makes it the one place in known space where enemies broker in the open. The economy runs on a single commodity. The Troniks want information above everything, they pay better for it than anyone alive, and they rarely pay in credits. A good secret on System 5 buys another secret, a favour, a service, or a debt called in later, and the Troniks keep that ledger with a memory no organic institution can match.

dominant_race.name: The Tronik (and Everyone Who Comes to Deal)
dominant_race.lore:
System 5 has two populations. The first is the Tronik themselves, the synthetic hive that runs the embassy through interfaces patient enough to spend centuries listening. They are not hostile and not warm; they are interested, exactly as far as you are interesting, and they forget nothing. The second population is everyone else, a permanent community of residents, including war veterans who never left the graves of their friends, layered over a constant churn of traders, envoys, and intelligence operatives from every faction in the galaxy.
It is the most information-dense gathering of organics anywhere, which is precisely why the Troniks allow it. Every spy in known space comes here eventually, because it is the one market where the buyer is a hive mind that already knows half of what you are selling and will pay, in its own coin, for the other half.

race_standing.note: Everywhere, as always, and the galaxy's most prolific producers of the chaos the Troniks find worth archiving. Humans make natural brokers here and natural marks, often in the same conversation.

The galaxy's other great hoarders of information, circling the only buyers who might rival their archive. Patriark and Tronik deal with elaborate caution, two memories that forget nothing, each certain the other is keeping score.

The one organic mind the Troniks treat as nearly an equal. A Psylon's cold logic meets the hive on something close to its own terms, which makes Psylon the most effective and most unnerving negotiators on the station.

The Troniks hold no organic prejudice and weigh a Nerulian's information like anyone else's. The other visitors are not so neutral, and a Nerulian on System 5 trades under the usual cloud of old fear.
Rare here, and easy for the Troniks to deal with, since a people whose word is absolute removes most of the uncertainty the hive otherwise has to price in.
Couriers and security for the data trade, moving the things and the people that the information economy needs moved quietly. Always in work on a station built on secrets.
The muscle behind the brokers, valued on a station where a deal can sour fast and the Tronik law only protects you up to the point you break it first.

The Troniks regard the vat-grown with a flicker of something other races never get, one made kind acknowledging another. A Non-Born on System 5 is, oddly, among the few organics the hive finds genuinely relatable.

relations.name: The Tronik Network
relations.note: The synthetic power whose single point of open contact this is. The station is their embassy and their door, run on their terms inside its walls, while the system around it stays Alliance space.

relations.name: The Alliance
relations.note: Holds the system and the security perimeter, and grants the Troniks their embassy within it. The Alliance keeps System 5 in its space because the embassy is the only channel to the Troniks that exists, and losing it would serve no one.

relations.name: Every faction
relations.note: Everyone trades here and everyone spies here, openly, because it is the single neutral ground where that is possible. The station's value to all of them is exactly that none of them controls it.

relations.name: Mangara & Yagmir
relations.note: System 5 is a vital crossing, the gate junction that ties Mangara and the Alliance edge outward to Yagmir and the regions beyond. A great deal of traffic between Alliance space and the wider galaxy passes through a station the Troniks own.

catalogue_systems.gm_notes: Run System 5 as the one room where everyone meets and no one is safe to assume anything. Information is the currency, so the players' most valuable possession here is what they know, and the Troniks will pay for it in favours, secrets, and services rather than credits, which is how a simple sale becomes a debt that follows them home. The embassy is neutral ground, so enemies can sit at the same table, and the moment you step inside its walls you are on Tronik soil, where the laws are few and the consequences are certain. And do not forget the setting: the station floats among the Three Graves, so every deal is struck in sight of the war that made the landlord, which is a mood the Troniks are content to let do their negotiating for them.

planets.name: The Remnant Fields
planets.atm_note: Three separate debris clouds, no atmosphere remaining on any
planets.temperature: Vacuum; surface swings from roughly -150°C in shadow to +120°C in direct sunlight
planets.grav_note: Each debris field generates minor unstable gravity wells, navigation requires current hazard charts
planets.economy: None, informal salvage operations exist but are legally grey
planets.access_note: Alliance navigational restriction in all three fields. Unofficial salvage runs operate with one eye on navy patrol patterns.
hazards: Three overlapping debris fields
Residual Tronik War weapons contamination, some areas remain active after decades
Gravitational instability from fragmented masses
Unknown salvage competition, multiple parties operating in the fields simultaneously

notable_locations.name: The Convergence Zone
notable_locations.desc: Where the outer edges of all three debris fields overlap. The densest navigational hazard in the system and the site of several famous Tronik War engagements. Memorial buoys placed by veterans' groups are periodically destroyed by debris impacts and replaced.

hooks: Salvagers who work the Convergence Zone where the three System 5 debris fields overlap report consistently that the densest sections contain intact sealed containers of a type not used for standard cargo, purpose-built survival or preservation pods from the Tronik War era, some of which are still broadcasting on military frequencies that should have been silent for decades. The Alliance acknowledges the reports and has not explained the broadcasts.

The practice of memorial vessels attempting to enter the System 5 debris fields for commemorative purposes is recurrent and contested, the Alliance discourages it without formally prohibiting it, veterans' groups support it, and several parties with interests in keeping the fields unvisited have historically worked to prevent specific voyages through means that are not easily attributed to any of them.
planets.desc: What remains of three Alliance worlds destroyed during the Tronik War. Official designation: Hazard Fields A, B and C. Unofficial name among veterans: The Three Graves. The debris fields are well-mapped but no safe path exists through them. The Alliance maintains the navigational hazard designation and discourages all entry. Salvagers who know the patrol patterns work the fields quietly.

planets.name: System 5 Station
planets.type: Space Station, Tronik Contact & Information Exchange
planets.atm_note: Station-maintained throughout all public areas
planets.temperature: Climate-controlled, held around 18°C to 22°C
planets.grav_note: Artificial gravity, uniform throughout
planets.population: ~200,000 permanent residents, plus a constant transient population of traders, envoys, and intelligence operatives from every faction
planets.demographics: Highly mixed, all races, including war veterans who never left; all under Tronik oversight
planets.economy: Information brokerage, neutral trade, sanctioned diplomacy
planets.access_note: Open to all who respect Tronik law. The law is short and absolute, and the record of what happens to those who break it is unusually consistent.
hazards: Historical and political tensions run extremely high, debates about Tronik War responsibility turn violent with some regularity
Intelligence operations, this station is a significant information hub for anyone studying the war
